target: Vivimos entre West Sussex y Bretaña, con el canal de por medio.
english: We live between West Sussex and Brittany, with the Channel in between.
grammar: No pronoun needed: 'vivimos' – the ending already says we, so 'nosotros' appears only for emphasis.

target: La luz de la mañana es la mejor para pintar.
english: Morning light is the best for painting.
grammar: 'Es la mejor para pintar' – 'la mejor' stands without its noun: the article alone carries 'luz' forward.

target: Swansea es una ciudad maravillosa: tan bella, tan impoluta.
english: Swansea is a marvellous town – so beautiful, so pristine.
grammar: 'Tan bella, tan impoluta' – 'tan' before an adjective means so, and repeating it piles the praise higher.

target: A mediodía el agua del lago se ve de un azul tan oscuro que casi parece negro.
english: At midday the lake water looks such a dark blue it's almost black.
grammar: 'Se ve de un azul tan oscuro' – 'verse' is how something looks, and 'de un' + colour names the shade it shows.

target: En esta familia, la falta de coordinación es hereditaria y nos enorgullece.
english: In this family, a lack of coordination is hereditary, and we're proud of it.
grammar: 'Es hereditaria' – a defining trait takes 'ser': hereditary is what the trait is, not a passing state.

target: La gente con opiniones políticas aburridas puede arruinar una cena.
english: People with boring political opinions can ruin a dinner party.
grammar: 'La gente' (people) is grammatically singular – so it takes 'puede', never 'pueden'.

target: Brannagh es, sencillamente, la mejor yegua de todos los tiempos.
english: Brannagh is, quite simply, the greatest horse of all time.
grammar: What she is by nature takes 'ser': 'es, sencillamente, la mejor yegua' – a defining fact, not a passing state.

target: Como es de lino, esta camisa se arruga a los cinco minutos de ponértela.
english: Being linen, this shirt creases within five minutes of putting it on.
grammar: 'Es de lino' – 'ser de' gives the shirt's material, a permanent trait, so 'ser' rather than 'estar'.

target: El clima puede ser impredecible cuando haces senderismo en el Lake District.
english: The weather can be unpredictable when you're hiking in the Lake District.
grammar: The 'tú' form can speak generally: 'cuando haces senderismo' – when you (anyone, really) hike.

target: Brannagh la yegua tiene un carácter muy noble.
english: Brannagh the horse has a really kind nature.
grammar: Personality is had, not been: 'tiene un carácter muy noble' – 'tener' + noun where English uses is + adjective.

target: Estoy muerta de cansancio, pero es el cansancio bueno, el de un día bien aprovechado.
english: I'm shattered, but it's the good kind of tired – the kind you get from a day well spent.
grammar: 'Estoy muerta' is the passing state, 'es el cansancio bueno' the definition – estar and ser dividing the work.

target: Los quebequenses usan todo tipo de expresiones distintas en francés.
english: Québécois speakers use all kinds of different expressions in French.
grammar: 'Todo tipo de' keeps the type singular – all kinds of is literally every type of, even before plural 'expresiones'.

target: Sean y John pueden ser poco confiables y quizás un poco egocéntricos.
english: Sean and John can be slightly unreliable and perhaps a little self-centred.
grammar: Before an adjective, 'poco' flips it negative: 'poco confiables' = unreliable.

target: El español es mi tercer idioma, después del francés y el inglés.
english: Spanish is my third language, after French and English.
grammar: Before a masculine noun 'tercero' clips to 'tercer': 'mi tercer idioma'. 'Primero' does it too.

target: Lord Egremont es nuestro señor y salvador.
english: Lord Egremont is our lord and saviour.
grammar: 'Es nuestro señor y salvador' – identity, what someone is, calls for 'ser' rather than 'estar'.

target: Tu suéter no es negro, es azul marino, se nota a la luz del sol.
english: Your jumper isn't black, it's navy – you can tell in the sunlight.
grammar: 'No es negro, es azul marino' – ser for the colour a thing actually is: its standing identity, not a passing state.

target: La cáscara ya está más naranja que verde, o sea que el mango está listo.
english: The skin's more orange than green now, which means the mango's ready.
grammar: 'Ya está más naranja que verde' – estar for a colour caught mid-change: ripening is a passing state, not identity.

target: La película es triste, sí, pero yo no estoy triste: me pareció preciosa.
english: The film is sad, yes, but I'm not sad – I thought it was lovely.
grammar: 'Es triste' vs 'no estoy triste' – one adjective, two verbs: 'ser' for what the film is like, 'estar' for your mood.

target: PapyLou lee todos los letreros con todo detalle.
english: Papylou reads every sign in great detail.
grammar: 'Todos los' before a plural means every: 'todos los letreros' – all-the-signs is how Spanish says every sign.

target: En nuestra casa, Berlusconi no es un político: es un plato con vainitas.
english: In our house, Berlusconi isn't a politician – he's a dish involving green beans.
grammar: Classifying uses 'ser': 'es un plato' – what a thing is, as opposed to where it is or how it seems.

target: Es generosa hasta cuando no le sobra nada: siempre encuentra algo para compartir.
english: She's generous even when she has nothing to spare – she always finds something to share.
grammar: 'Es generosa' – 'ser' states character, and character holds even when 'no le sobra nada' (nothing to spare).

target: Pierre aloja a solicitantes de asilo en hoteles.
english: Pierre houses asylum seekers in hotels.
grammar: 'Aloja a solicitantes' – when the ones on the receiving end are people, Spanish slips in a little 'a' before them.

target: Twig tiene las patas un poco calientes después del paseo.
english: Twig's paws are a little warm after his walk.
grammar: 'Tiene las patas' – body parts take the article, not a possessive; 'tiene' already says whose paws they are.

target: El horno no perdona las prisas.
english: The kiln doesn't forgive rushing.
grammar: 'No perdona las prisas' – rushing is a plural noun with its article: 'las prisas', haste in general.

target: Petworth Park es imponente, con sus lagos y sus colinas diseñados con esmero.
english: Petworth Park is very grand, with its carefully landscaped lakes and hills.
grammar: 'Es imponente' – 'ser' for a defining trait: grand is what the park is, not a mood it's in.

target: Brannagh la yegua tiene un bigote espléndido.
english: Brannagh the horse has a fine moustache.
grammar: Most descriptive adjectives follow their noun: 'un bigote espléndido', not 'un espléndido bigote'.

target: El ferry nocturno tiene su encanto, sobre todo si el mar está tranquilo.
english: The overnight ferry has its charm, especially if the sea is calm.
grammar: 'Está tranquilo' takes 'estar' for the sea's state today – 'es tranquilo' would make calm its character.

target: Este apartamento tiene poca luz natural, por eso todo está pintado de colores claros.
english: This flat doesn't get much natural light, which is why everything's painted in light colours.
grammar: 'Está pintado de colores claros' – 'estar' for the painted state the flat is in, and 'de' introduces the colour.

target: La marea decide a qué hora nadamos, no al revés.
english: The tide decides what time we swim, not the other way round.
grammar: 'Decide a qué hora' – the question word keeps its accent even folded inside a statement, so 'qué' stays marked.

target: ¿Su maleta es gris o negra? Hay dos muy parecidas en la banda.
english: Is your suitcase grey or black? There are two very similar ones on the belt.
grammar: 'Gris o negra' – colours agree like adjectives: 'negra' goes feminine for 'maleta', while 'gris' keeps one form.

target: Doy gracias a Lord Egremont durante el festival de la cosecha.
english: I give thanks to Lord Egremont during the harvest festival.
grammar: 'Doy gracias a' – thanks are given with 'dar', and the person thanked gets the little 'a'.

target: El pódcast de juegos de mesa de Pierre es excelente.
english: Pierre's board game podcast is excellent.
grammar: 'De juegos de mesa de Pierre' – Spanish has no apostrophe-s, so ownership stacks as a chain of 'de'.

target: El clarinete rojo de Ken tiene un sonido precioso.
english: Ken's red clarinet makes a lovely sound.
grammar: 'Tiene un sonido precioso' – qualities are often things you have: 'tener' describes as much as 'ser' does.

target: El refrigerador está lleno, pero no tenemos nada listo para comer.
english: The fridge is full, but we haven't got a single thing that's ready to eat.
grammar: 'Está lleno' – estar for the fridge's state right now, the kind of thing that changes with every shop.

target: La celebración es el sábado en la tarde y el lugar está a dos cuadras del parque.
english: The celebration is on Saturday afternoon, and the venue is two blocks from the park.
grammar: Events take ser for their when – 'es el sábado en la tarde' – while the venue's location takes 'está'.

target: Tengo sobrinas muy internacionales: una vive en la isla de Reunión y otra en Angola.
english: I have very international nieces – one lives on Réunion Island and one in Angola.
grammar: Another is just 'otra', no article in front: 'y otra en Angola' – never 'una otra'.

target: En esta familia comemos bastante rápido.
english: As a family, we eat fairly quickly.
grammar: 'Rápido' works as an adverb here – spoken Spanish often uses the bare adjective where 'rápidamente' sounds stiff.

target: PapyLou no atina con las notas, pero canta más fuerte y más contento que nadie.
english: PapyLou doesn't hit the notes, but he sings louder and happier than anyone.
grammar: 'Más contento que nadie' – after a comparison, Spanish says nobody ('nadie') where English says anyone.

target: Está muy gris el cielo para ser mediodía, seguro llueve en la tarde.
english: The sky's awfully grey for midday – it's bound to rain this afternoon.
grammar: 'Está muy gris el cielo' – with estar the subject often trails the verb: the state comes first, the sky second.

target: Parece tímido, pero no es tímido: está incómodo porque todavía no conoce a nadie.
english: He seems shy, but he isn't shy – he's uncomfortable because he doesn't know anyone yet.
grammar: 'No es tímido: está incómodo' – 'ser' for the sort of person he is, 'estar' for the state the room put him in.

target: ¿Seguro que vas lo suficientemente abrigado? Hace frío afuera.
english: Are you sure you're dressed warmly enough? It's cold out.
grammar: 'Abrigado' matches whoever is heading out – said to a man here, but a woman would go 'abrigada'.

target: Hay muchísima historia en esta zona.
english: There's so much history in the local area.
grammar: 'Hay' covers both there is and there are – one fixed form, here before 'muchísima historia'.

target: Keir Starmer me tiene bastante decepcionada, la verdad.
english: Keir Starmer has been quite a disappointment, honestly.
grammar: 'Me tiene bastante decepcionada' – the '-a' ending shows the person let down is a woman, here the speaker.

target: Está celoso porque felicitaron a su compañero y no a él, cosa rara, porque celoso no es.
english: He's jealous because his colleague got the praise and he didn't – odd, really, because he isn't the jealous type.
grammar: 'Está celoso' ties the mood to one incident – 'celoso no es' uses 'ser' to say jealousy isn't his character.

target: La dueña del café es alegre de por sí, pero hoy está que se ríe sola: algo bueno le habrá pasado.
english: The owner of the café is cheerful by nature, but today she keeps laughing to herself – something good must have happened.
grammar: 'Es alegre de por sí' – 'ser' plus 'de por sí' (by nature) claims the trait, so today's laughing takes 'está'.

target: ¿La cajera está enojada o simplemente es seria? Nunca sé cómo tomarla.
english: Is the cashier cross, or is she just a serious sort? I never know how to take her.
grammar: 'Está enojada' or just 'es seria' – the whole question sits in the verbs: 'estar' asks mood, 'ser' asks character.

target: El comedor está pintado de un verde apagado que combina bien con la madera.
english: The dining room's painted a muted green that goes well with the wood.
grammar: 'Un verde apagado' – give a colour an article and it becomes a noun that adjectives can shade: a muted green.

target: Twig es un cachorro, pero también es la última esperanza de la democracia occidental.
english: Twig is a puppy, but he is also the last hope of Western democracy.
grammar: Identity runs on 'ser' – 'es un cachorro' and 'es la última esperanza' both state what Twig is.

target: El teclado nuevo es inalámbrico y no tiene ni un cable, pero está descargado la mitad del tiempo.
english: The new keyboard is wireless, not a single cable, but it's out of charge half the time.
grammar: 'Es inalámbrico' is what it is, 'está descargado' how it stands – ser and estar split the sentence between them.

target: Pierre negocia con la matriarca gitana.
english: Pierre negotiates with the gypsy matriarch.
grammar: Adjectives of origin or group follow the noun and stay lowercase: 'la matriarca gitana'.

target: Coates Common es bastante arenoso y perfecto para pasear a los perros.
english: Coates Common is pretty sandy and perfect for dog walks.
grammar: 'Pasear a los perros' – beloved animals get the personal 'a' just as people do.

target: Tengo la garganta irritada y estoy un poco afónica desde ayer.
english: My throat is sore and I've been a bit hoarse since yesterday.
grammar: 'Tengo la garganta irritada' – body parts take 'la', not a possessive: 'tengo' already says whose throat it is.

target: En primavera, los corderitos corren por ahí en pandillas.
english: In spring, the lambs run around in little gangs.
grammar: 'Por ahí' – 'por' paints vague movement through an area: running around-there, no destination in mind.

target: Los juegos de mesa de Pierre están muy bien diseñados.
english: Pierre's board games are very well designed.
grammar: 'Están muy bien diseñados' – 'estar' describes the state the games are in now, not the act of designing them.

target: La rana de la boca grande tiene opiniones firmes sobre la mermelada.
english: The frog with the big mouth has strong opinions about marmalade.
grammar: 'De la boca grande' – adding the article turns the trait into an identifier: the frog we already know.

target: El deporte es el pegamento de esta familia.
english: Sport is the glue of this family.
grammar: 'Es el pegamento' – naming what a thing is, even as a metaphor, is ser's job, so 'es', never 'está'.

target: Este año es bisiesto, así que febrero tiene veintinueve días en vez de veintiocho.
english: This year's a leap year, so February has twenty-nine days instead of twenty-eight.
grammar: 'Es bisiesto' takes 'ser' – naming which kind of year it is classifies it, and classifying belongs to 'ser'.

target: Para el dormitorio, esta lámpara tiene una luz demasiado brillante, es más de escritorio.
english: For the bedroom this lamp gives too bright a light – it's more of a desk lamp.
grammar: 'Tiene una luz demasiado brillante' – tener carries description: qualities are things you have in Spanish.

target: Yo no soy nerviosa, pero hoy sí estoy nerviosa: el examen de manejo es en una hora.
english: I'm not a nervous person, but today I really am nervous – my driving test is in an hour.
grammar: 'No soy nerviosa' rules the trait out with 'ser', 'sí estoy nerviosa' owns today's state – same word, two claims.

target: El plazo de entrega siempre llega antes de lo que una piensa.
english: The deadline always arrives sooner than you think.
grammar: 'Antes de lo que una piensa' – comparing with a whole idea (sooner than you think) needs 'de lo que', not just 'que'.

target: Los Pérez tienen unas opiniones políticas de lo más interesantes.
english: The Pérez family have some really interesting political opinions.
grammar: 'Los Pérez' – the surname itself stays singular; the plural article alone makes it the Pérez family.

target: Anna teje con muchísima destreza.
english: Anna knits with great skill.
grammar: 'Con' + a noun does the work of an English -ly adverb: 'con muchísima destreza' – with great skill.

target: Pierre tiene un alijo secreto de Mini Eggs escondido en alguna parte.
english: Pierre has a secret stash of Mini Eggs hidden somewhere.
grammar: 'Escondido' (hidden) matches 'un alijo' the way any describing word would – masculine and singular to fit the stash.

target: Los topos son el gran enemigo de Ken: le están dejando el jardín hecho un desastre.
english: The moles are Ken's great enemy: they're leaving the garden in a terrible state.
grammar: 'son' states what the moles are, 'están dejando' tracks what's currently under way – 'ser' and 'estar' in one line.

target: Bear tiene dos velocidades: dormido y misil.
english: Bear has two speeds: asleep and missile.
grammar: 'Tiene dos velocidades' – 'tener' states built-in traits, the standard way Spanish describes features.

target: El tren de Pulborough te deja en Victoria en poco más de una hora.
english: The train from Pulborough gets you to Victoria in just over an hour.
grammar: 'El tren de Pulborough' – plain 'de' marks the train's starting point: 'de', not 'desde', is the usual link.

target: West Sussex es un condado verde, entre las colinas de los South Downs y el mar.
english: West Sussex is a green county, between the South Downs hills and the sea.
grammar: Descriptive adjectives trail the noun: 'un condado verde' – after, not before, is the default position.

target: Estoy pintando un paisaje de la costa bretona.
english: I'm painting a landscape of the Breton coast.
grammar: Actions in progress use 'estar' + -ando: 'estoy pintando' – painting right now, not a general habit.

target: Orgullosa no es, para nada, pero está orgullosísima de cómo quedó la cocina recién pintada.
english: She's not one to boast, not at all, but she's terribly proud of how the freshly painted kitchen turned out.
grammar: 'Orgullosa no es' puts the adjective first for emphasis – proud is the last thing this person is.

target: Estoy probando acuarelas después de años de pintar al óleo.
english: I'm trying watercolours after years of painting in oils.
grammar: 'Estoy probando' – 'estar' + '-ando' makes the in-progress tense: trying right now, not in general.

target: No es una región espectacular, es algo mejor: es tranquila y no tiene nada que demostrar.
english: It's not a spectacular region – it's something better: it's calm, with nothing to prove.
grammar: Double negatives are correct Spanish: 'no tiene nada que demostrar' – the two negatives reinforce, not cancel.

target: Cuento un chiste buenísimo sobre una rana de boca grande.
english: I tell a very funny joke about a frog with a big mouth.
grammar: Features hang off 'de': 'una rana de boca grande' – a frog of big mouth, no word for with needed.

target: Henri tiene colmenas al fondo del jardín.
english: Henri has beehives at the bottom of the garden.
grammar: 'Al fondo del jardín' packs both of Spanish's only two contractions – 'a el' fuses to 'al', 'de el' to 'del'.

target: Ken está aprendiendo galés en un pueblito de los valles.
english: Ken is learning Welsh in a small village in the valleys.
grammar: 'Pueblito' – the '-ito' ending shrinks 'pueblo' fondly; Latin American Spanish uses diminutives constantly.

target: Esta olla es pesadísima, pero tiene la ventaja de que reparte bien el calor.
english: This pot is seriously heavy, but it does have the advantage of spreading the heat evenly.
grammar: 'Es pesadísima' – 'ser' because the weight is built into the pot, not a passing state for 'estar'.

target: Las finanzas de Pierre están más ordenadas que la biblioteca nacional.
english: Pierre's finances are more organised than the national library.
grammar: 'Más ordenadas' matches 'las finanzas' – describing words agree, so it goes feminine and plural with '-as'.

target: Un lienzo en blanco impone un poco, ¿no?
english: A blank canvas is a little intimidating, isn't it?
grammar: '¿No?' – the all-purpose tag: one word where English cycles through isn't it, right and don't you think.

target: El salar de Uyuni es el desierto de sal más grande del mundo.
english: The Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world.
grammar: 'Más grande del mundo' – the biggest in the world comes out as the biggest of the world: 'de', not 'en'.

target: Benoît es un jugador encantador, con una relación flexible con las reglas.
english: Benoît is a charming player with a flexible relationship with the rules.
grammar: 'Es un jugador encantador' – 'ser' introduces what someone is by nature, charm counted as character.

target: Cerca de Marescot hay un montón de iglesitas históricas.
english: There are lots of small historic churches near Marescot.
grammar: 'Un montón de' – literally a heap of – is the everyday loads of, with a plural noun after the 'de'.

target: Cuando pasamos por el canal, siempre buscamos a Swonky entre los cisnes: con ese cuello es imposible confundirlo.
english: When we walk along the canal we always look for Swonky among the swans: with that neck you can't miss him.
grammar: 'Siempre buscamos' – the plain present is the routine tense: every time we pass the canal, the looking repeats.

target: A veces mezclo el francés y el español sin darme cuenta.
english: Sometimes I mix up French and Spanish without realising.
grammar: After 'sin', the verb is an infinitive: 'sin darme cuenta' = without (me) realising.

target: En Bretaña compramos el pan en la panadería del pueblo.
english: In Brittany we buy our bread at the village bakery.
grammar: The plain present states a routine – 'compramos el pan' is what happens every visit, no habit word needed.

target: Disculpe, ¿esto cómo se come, crudo o hay que cocinarlo?
english: Excuse me, how do you eat this – raw, or does it need cooking?
grammar: 'Se come' asks how one eats it – the impersonal 'se' leaves the eater out entirely.

target: Cuando salgo del agua, me envuelvo en la toalla como un burrito.
english: When I get out of the water, I wrap myself in my towel like a burrito.
grammar: 'Me envuelvo' – the reflexive 'me' says wrapper and wrapped are the same person.

target: Me cambio rapidísimo cuando salgo del agua: con los años una aprende a vestirse debajo de la toalla.
english: I get changed in no time when I come out of the water: over the years you learn to dress under your towel.
grammar: 'Cambiar' changes something else – the reflexive turns it inward: 'me cambio' is I get changed.

target: Por la mañana nado en el mar con un grupo de amigas.
english: In the morning I swim in the sea with a group of friends.
grammar: 'Por la mañana' – parts of the day take 'por': morning, afternoon and night all use it.

target: Entre el mercado y la cocina, el domingo se me pasa volando.
english: Between the market and the kitchen, Sunday simply flies by on me.
grammar: 'Se me pasa volando' – the 'se me' combo makes Sunday the doer and me the bystander it slips past.

target: Anna se ocupa de los parques de Newbury.
english: Anna looks after Newbury's parks.
grammar: The verb owns its preposition: 'se ocupa de' – 'ocuparse de' = to look after, 'de' included.

target: Entre semana me despierto antes de las siete para adelantar los quehaceres.
english: On weekdays I wake up before seven to get a head start on the chores.
grammar: 'Me despierto' – waking is reflexive, something you do to yourself, like much of the daily routine.

target: El pódcast The Rest Is Politics me ayuda a formarme una opinión sobre la actualidad.
english: The Rest Is Politics podcast helps me make my mind up about current affairs.
grammar: 'Formarme una opinión' – opinions are formed for yourself: the reflexive 'me' rides on the infinitive.

target: Antes de ponerme a pintar, me pongo el delantal.
english: Before I sit down to paint, I put my apron on.
grammar: After a preposition like 'Antes de', Spanish uses the infinitive: 'ponerme a pintar', never an -ing form.

target: ¿Y tú a qué te dedicas? Yo me dedico a la traducción y trabajo desde la casa.
english: And what do you do? I'm in translation myself – I work from home.
grammar: 'Me dedico a' – 'dedicarse a' is the standard occupation verb: reflexive, and the 'a' comes built in.

target: Antoine siempre camina en el sentido contrario al salir de la tienda.
english: Antoine always walks the wrong way after leaving the shop.
grammar: 'Al' + infinitive gives a when: 'al salir de la tienda' – on leaving the shop, right at that moment.

target: De vuelta en la casa, lo primero es quitarme la chaqueta y colgarla detrás de la puerta.
english: Once I'm back home, the first thing is to take my jacket off and hang it behind the door.
grammar: 'Quitarme' and 'colgarla' – each infinitive carries its own pronoun glued on: 'me' for me, 'la' for the jacket.

target: El agua está helada en abril, pero una se acostumbra.
english: The water is freezing in April, but you get used to it.
grammar: 'Una se acostumbra' – a woman speaking generally says 'una', your version of the impersonal one.

target: Me pongo el casco, me ajusto los guantes y respiro hondo un par de veces antes de subirme al caballo.
english: I put my hat on, adjust my gloves and take a couple of deep breaths before getting on the horse.
grammar: Clothing works reflexively: 'me pongo el casco' – the 'me' already says whose, so no 'mi casco'.

target: Todavía escondemos huevitos de chocolate cada año para la búsqueda de Pascua.
english: We still hide chocolate eggs for the yearly Easter egg hunt.
grammar: 'Todavía' + present keeps a habit alive: 'todavía escondemos' – still doing it, year after year.

target: El arroz se cocina solo: olla tapada, fuego bajito y paciencia para no destaparla.
english: Rice cooks itself: lid on the pot, heat down low, and the patience not to lift the lid.
grammar: 'El arroz se cocina solo' – 'se' lets the rice do its own cooking, leaving the cook out of the sentence.

target: PapyLou se asegura de documentarlo todo con esmero.
english: Papylou makes sure he documents everything meticulously.
grammar: 'Documentarlo todo' – when 'todo' is the object, Spanish doubles it with 'lo' on the verb: document-it all.

target: Me mareo en los vuelos largos, así que me siento cerca del ala y trato de no leer.
english: I get queasy on long flights, so I sit near the wing and try not to read.
grammar: 'Me mareo' – 'marearse' is reflexive, as body-feeling verbs often are: the queasiness happens to you.

target: En Bretaña me despierto con las voces de los turistas que pasan, en Sussex con los pájaros del jardín.
english: In Brittany I wake up to the voices of the passing tourists, in Sussex to the birds in the garden.
grammar: 'Me despierto' – waking is done to yourself in Spanish: reflexive 'despertarse', the usual shape of routine verbs.

target: Antes de entregar, me leo el texto completo en voz alta: así se me escapan menos errores.
english: Before I deliver anything I read the whole text aloud to myself: fewer mistakes get past me that way.
grammar: 'Me leo el texto completo' – the optional 'me' signals reading it right through, start to finish.

target: Aquí se acostumbra quitarse los zapatos en la entrada y dejarlos junto a la puerta.
english: Here it's the custom to take your shoes off at the entrance and leave them by the door.
grammar: 'Se acostumbra' – the impersonal 'se' states the local custom: what's done here, no one in particular doing it.

target: En cuanto refresca un poco, la gente se abriga con bufanda y guantes como en pleno invierno.
english: As soon as it cools down a little, people wrap up in scarves and gloves as if it were deepest winter.
grammar: Wrapping up warm is 'abrigarse': 'la gente se abriga' – you bundle yourself, so the verb keeps its 'se'.

target: ¿Usted no se prueba los pantalones antes de comprarlos? Las tallas cambian mucho de una marca a otra.
english: Don't you try trousers on before buying them? Sizes vary a lot from one brand to another.
grammar: 'Se prueba los pantalones' – trying on is reflexive 'probarse', and with usted the pronoun is 'se'.

target: Cuando vamos a Josselin, solemos quedarnos unas cuantas semanas.
english: When we go to Josselin, we usually stay for a few weeks.
grammar: 'Soler' builds usually – 'solemos quedarnos' is we usually stay, the reflexive glued onto the infinitive.

target: En otoño, los bosques del Weald se llenan de hongos y de gente que los fotografía.
english: In autumn the Weald's woods fill up with mushrooms, and with people photographing them.
grammar: 'Se llenan de hongos' – llenarse makes the filling happen by itself, and 'de' introduces the filler.

target: Después de freír, el olor se queda en la cocina por horas, así que siempre abro la ventana antes de empezar.
english: After frying, the smell hangs around the kitchen for hours, so I always open the window before I start.
grammar: 'El olor se queda' – 'quedarse' means to stay on: the reflexive turns being-somewhere into lingering.

target: Nunca me acerco mucho al borde de la acera: los buses pasan pegaditos.
english: I never get too close to the edge of the pavement – the buses skim right past.
grammar: 'Me acerco' – to near something is 'acercarse a', reflexive with its preposition included: 'al borde'.

target: Nos organizamos temprano para aprovechar el día entero en la ciudad.
english: We get ourselves organised early to make the most of a full day in the city.
grammar: 'Nos organizamos' – organizar pointed at ourselves: the reflexive does the job of English get organised.

target: Andy Burnham me da cierta esperanza, aunque prefiero no hacerme ilusiones.
english: Andy Burnham gives me some hope, though I'd rather not get carried away.
grammar: 'Cierta esperanza' – before the noun 'cierto' means some; after it ('esperanza cierta') it would mean definite.

target: Siempre que cocino me pongo el delantal, es una costumbre de años.
english: Whenever I cook I put my apron on – it's a habit of many years.
grammar: 'me pongo el delantal' – dressing uses reflexive 'ponerse': the apron goes onto yourself, so 'me' comes along.

target: En Bolivia se habla español, quechua y aimara.
english: In Bolivia they speak Spanish, Quechua and Aymara.
grammar: Impersonal 'se' hides the doer: 'se habla español' = Spanish is spoken.

target: A Béa se le está dando muy bien encuadernar libros.
english: Béa is getting really good at binding books.
grammar: Being good at something is 'dársele bien': 'se le está dando muy bien' – bookbinding is going well for her.
ttsText: A Bea se le está dando muy bien encuadernar libros.

target: Hasta me acuerdo de los nombres de todos sus amigos.
english: I even remember the names of all their friends.
grammar: 'Acordarse' (remember) is reflexive and takes 'de': 'me acuerdo de los nombres' – both bits required.

target: Henri se pone el traje de apicultor con la solemnidad de un astronauta.
english: Henri puts on his beekeeping suit with the solemnity of an astronaut.
grammar: Dressing is reflexive: 'se pone el traje' – ponerse for putting clothes on, with 'el' where English says his.

target: En Latour de France, los viejitos del pueblo se instalan en la plaza a vigilar a los recién llegados.
english: In Latour de France, the village elders install themselves in the square to keep watch on newcomers.
grammar: 'Se instalan' – the reflexive turns install into settle in: they install themselves in the square.

target: Los mitos llegan todos juntos, se quedan un minuto y se van igual de rápido.
english: The long-tailed tits arrive all at once, stay a minute, and leave just as quickly.
grammar: 'se quedan un minuto' – 'quedarse' means to stay: without the 'se', 'quedar' covers what remains or where things sit.

target: Cuando pinto, se me pasan las horas volando.
english: When I'm painting, the hours fly by.
grammar: 'Se me pasan las horas' – the hours are the subject and 'me' the person affected, two pronouns before the verb.

target: Todavía me acuerdo del olor de las colchonetas del club de judo, en eso Lyon y Storrington eran idénticos.
english: I can still remember the smell of the judo mats – Lyon and Storrington were identical in that.
grammar: Remembering runs reflexive: 'me acuerdo del olor' – 'acordarse de' carries its pronoun and its 'de'.

target: Ken y yo hacemos nuestro PPE todas las mañanas, casi sin falta.
english: Ken and I do our PPE every morning, basically without fail.
grammar: 'Todas las mañanas' – every morning is all the mornings: 'todas las' + plural noun marks the routine.

target: Mi caballo se pone nervioso cuando hay mucho viento.
english: My horse gets nervous when it's very windy.
grammar: 'Se pone nervioso' – 'ponerse' + adjective covers becoming: a change of mood, not a lasting trait.

target: Antoine y Pierre se inventaban mundos enteros y se pasaban la tarde jugando en el trampolín.
english: Antoine and Pierre would make up entire worlds and spend the whole afternoon playing on the trampoline.
grammar: The reflexive adds a for-themselves shade: 'se inventaban mundos enteros' – made up for their own use.

target: Pierre se mete en muchísimo detalle histórico cuando planifica sus juegos de mesa.
english: Pierre goes into a lot of historical detail when planning his board games.
grammar: 'Se mete en' – reflexive 'meterse' turns 'meter' (to put) into getting yourself into something: diving into detail.

target: Cuando algo me emociona, se me nota muchísimo.
english: When something excites me, you can really tell.
grammar: 'Se me nota' – the 'se' says it shows and the 'me' says who it shows on, both lined up before the verb.

target: Nos organizamos con dos listas, una para cada casa, y aun así siempre se nos olvida algo.
english: We organise ourselves with two lists, one for each house, and even so we always forget something.
grammar: 'Se nos olvida algo' – the thing does the forgetting: 'algo' is the subject and 'nos' marks who it slips from.

target: Este suéter pica un poco, así que siempre me lo pongo con una camisa debajo.
english: This jumper is a bit itchy, so I always wear it with a shirt underneath.
grammar: 'Me lo pongo' – 'ponerse' keeps its 'me' even when 'lo' (the jumper) joins, the person pronoun coming first.

target: El día que se van los invitados, me dedico la mañana entera a lavar sábanas y ventilar los cuartos.
english: The day our guests leave, I spend the whole morning washing sheets and airing the rooms.
grammar: 'Me dedico... a lavar' – 'dedicarse a' is reflexive, devoting yourself to whatever follows the 'a'.

target: Pierre se sienta cada domingo con sus hojas de cálculo como quien asiste a misa.
english: Every Sunday Pierre sits down with his spreadsheets like a man attending mass.
grammar: 'Se sienta' – sitting down is reflexive 'sentarse': you seat yourself, so the 'se' comes built in.

target: Si voy al centro, no me complico: me bajo en la plaza y sigo a pie.
english: If I'm going into the centre I keep it simple – I get off at the square and carry on on foot.
grammar: 'Me bajo en la plaza' – plain 'bajar' is to go down, and the 'me' of 'bajarse' makes it getting off.

target: Cuando estamos en Sussex, extraño la sidra bretona, y cuando estamos en Bretaña, extraño las colinas.
english: When we're in Sussex I miss Breton cider, and when we're in Brittany I miss the hills.
grammar: 'Extraño' is the everyday Latin American verb for missing things – in Spain you'd hear 'echo de menos'.

target: A Pierre no se le da muy bien llamar, y lo niega, pero no pasa nada.
english: Pierre isn't great at calling, and he's in denial about it, but that's okay.
grammar: 'No se le da muy bien' – 'dársele bien' is the skill idiom: calling isn't given-well to Pierre, so he's bad at it.

target: Beni se dedica a un arte precioso: prensa algas marinas y las enmarca sobre fondo blanco.
english: Beni does the most beautiful art: she presses seaweed and frames it against a white background.
grammar: 'se dedica a' – 'dedicarse a' is the verb for what someone devotes themselves to, and its 'a' comes built in.

target: A principios de cada mes me siento con la agenda y dejo apuntados todos los pagos que vienen.
english: At the start of each month I sit down with my diary and note down all the payments coming up.
grammar: 'Me siento con la agenda' – 'sentarse' is reflexive: sitting down is done to yourself, hence the 'me'.

target: Apenas llego a la casa me quito la ropa de calle y me pongo algo cómodo.
english: The minute I get home I take off my outdoor clothes and put on something comfortable.
grammar: 'Me quito la ropa' – with clothes the reflexive already says whose, so Spanish uses 'la', not 'mi ropa'.

target: Béa se pone sus audífonos y escucha techno camino al trabajo.
english: Béa puts her headphones on and listens to techno on the way to work.
grammar: 'Se pone sus audífonos' – kit goes on with reflexive 'ponerse': the action lands on her own body.
ttsText: Bea se pone sus audífonos y escucha techno camino al trabajo.

target: Todos se ríen del chiste y yo recién me estoy enterando. Siempre entiendo con retraso.
english: Everyone's laughing at the joke while I'm still catching up – I'm always a beat behind.
grammar: 'Me estoy enterando' – 'enterarse' (to find out) comes with its pronoun attached: drop the 'me' and the meaning changes.

target: Beni sale a caminar conmigo todas las mañanas.
english: Beni comes for a walk with me every morning.
grammar: Going out to do something is 'salir a' + infinitive: 'sale a caminar' – the 'a' links the outing to its purpose.

target: Los domingos me levanto temprano y camino por la ciclovía, a esa hora casi no hay nadie.
english: On Sundays I get up early and walk along the cycleway – at that hour there's hardly anyone about.
grammar: 'Los domingos' – a plural article turns the day into a habit: every Sunday, with no word for on.

target: Cuando ando triste, me obligo a salir a caminar un rato y vuelvo como nueva.
english: When I'm feeling down, I make myself go out for a walk and I come back a new woman.
grammar: 'Me obligo a salir' – reflexive 'obligarse': the same person forces and gets forced, I make myself go out.

target: Casi siempre me preparo un jugo de naranja recién exprimido antes del desayuno.
english: I almost always make myself a freshly squeezed orange juice before breakfast.
grammar: 'Me preparo un jugo' – the extra 'me' says who the juice is for: me, Spanish likes to name who benefits.

target: ¿Te vas a probar el vestido aquí o prefieres llevártelo y decidir con calma en tu casa?
english: Are you going to try the dress on here, or would you rather take it home and decide at your leisure?
grammar: 'Te vas a probar' – the reflexive can climb ahead of 'ir a' or glue onto the infinitive: 'vas a probarte'.

target: En las calles empinadas me canso rápido, así que me detengo cada dos cuadras a tomar aire.
english: On the steep streets I tire quickly, so I stop every couple of blocks to catch my breath.
grammar: 'Me canso' – 'cansar' means to tire someone out, and the reflexive turns it inward: I get tired.

target: ¿Podemos sentarnos en la terraza, o esas mesas se reservan?
english: Can we sit out on the terrace, or are those tables reserved?
grammar: 'Se reservan' is the passive 'se' – the tables get reserved, and nobody says by whom.

target: Los domingos nos juntamos a ver el partido, y eso no se negocia.
english: On Sundays we get together to watch the match, and that's non-negotiable.
grammar: 'Nos juntamos' – juntar means to join, and pointed back at ourselves it becomes we get together.

target: PapyLou se toma su tiempo cuando apila la leña.
english: PapyLou takes his time when he's stacking the logs.
grammar: The reflexive adds a for-himself flavour: 'se toma su tiempo' – he takes his own sweet time.

target: Desde Marescot se ven los South Downs a lo lejos.
english: From Marescot you can see the South Downs in the distance.
grammar: 'Se ven' is plural because 'los South Downs' are the subject – with this 'se', the thing seen does the agreeing.

target: Antes de montar, siempre reviso la silla y los estribos.
english: Before riding, I always check the saddle and the stirrups.
grammar: 'Antes de montar' – 'antes de' takes a bare infinitive where English switches to -ing: before riding.

target: Me fijo dos veces antes de cruzar, porque aquí las motos aparecen de la nada.
english: I look twice before crossing, because round here the motorbikes appear out of nowhere.
grammar: 'Me fijo' – looking carefully is 'fijarse', the 'me' built in: plain 'fijar' just means to fasten.

target: PapyLou vino también a Japón con nosotros y no se perdió ni una visita.
english: PapyLou came to Japan with us too, and didn't miss a single outing.
grammar: 'no se perdió ni una visita' – 'perderse' means to miss out on something, while plain 'perder' is just to lose.

target: Todo el invierno me pongo dos pares de calcetines, porque el piso de la cocina es helado.
english: All winter I put on two pairs of socks, because the kitchen floor is freezing.
grammar: Putting clothes on is 'ponerse': 'me pongo dos pares' – you put them onto yourself, so the 'me' is built in.

target: Los domingos Ken se va en la moto un par de horas y vuelve de muy buen humor.
english: On Sundays Ken goes off on his motorbike for a couple of hours and comes back in a very good mood.
grammar: 'se va en la moto' – 'irse' means to head off: the 'se' supplies the leaving, plain 'ir' would want a destination.

target: Se nos antoja algo dulce a las dos. ¿Cuál es el postre de la casa?
english: We both fancy something sweet – what's the house pudding?
grammar: 'Se nos antoja' works like 'gustar' – the sweet thing does the tempting, we just feel the craving.

target: Estamos pensando en alquilar una parte de la casa de Josselin por Airbnb, aunque todavía nos da un poco de cosa.
english: We're thinking about renting out part of the Josselin house on Airbnb, though we're still a bit unsure about it.
grammar: Like 'gustar', 'dar cosa' flips the roles: in 'nos da un poco de cosa' the unease is the subject and 'nos' receives it.

target: Puede ser agotador conversar con Gilles Darmont.
english: Talking to Gilles Darmont can be exhausting.
grammar: The infinitive subject can come last: 'puede ser agotador conversar' – and 'agotador' stays masculine.

target: Quedar mal con la gente no me gusta nada, pero decir que sí a todo tampoco es sano.
english: I really don't like letting people down, but saying yes to everything isn't healthy either.
grammar: 'Quedar mal con la gente' is the subject of 'no me gusta nada' – with 'gustar' the disliked thing drives the verb.

target: Caminar por los Wild Brooks de Pulborough con Beni es una rutina matutina encantadora.
english: Walking through the Pulborough Wild Brooks with Beni is a lovely morning routine.
grammar: 'Caminar por los Wild Brooks' – however long the infinitive phrase, it counts as one singular subject.

target: Me encanta subir a Londres desde Pulborough para ver una exposición.
english: I love going up to London from Pulborough to see an exhibition.
grammar: 'Me encanta subir' – an infinitive counts as one thing, so encantar stays singular, never 'encantan'.

target: Me emociona la idea de hablar español en Bolivia.
english: I'm excited to speak Spanish in Bolivia.
grammar: 'Emocionar' runs like 'gustar': 'me emociona la idea' – the idea is the subject doing the exciting.

target: Lo que más me gustó de Nara fue ver los ciervos paseando sueltos entre la gente.
english: What I liked best in Nara was watching the deer wandering loose among the people.
grammar: 'Lo que más me gustó' – with 'gustar' the pleaser is the subject, and here it's a whole action: 'ver los ciervos'.

target: Véro vive cerca, aquí en Bretaña, y es una maravilla poder verla.
english: Véro lives nearby, here in Brittany, and it's wonderful to be able to see her.
grammar: Pronouns glue onto infinitives: 'poder verla' – 'ver' plus 'la' (her) written as one word.
ttsText: Vero vive cerca, aquí en Bretaña, y es una maravilla poder verla.

target: A Antoine no le gustan nada los trámites ni el papeleo.
english: Antoine isn't a fan of paperwork or administrative tasks.
grammar: Adding 'nada' after the verb intensifies: 'no le gustan nada' = he doesn't like them at all.

target: Lo mejor de Londres es volver: cultura de día, colinas de noche.
english: The best bit of London is coming home: culture by day, hills by night.
grammar: Neuter 'lo' makes an adjective into a thing: 'lo mejor de Londres' – the best bit, no noun required.

target: Elegir el regalo me gusta casi más que darlo, puedo pasar horas mirando opciones.
english: I enjoy choosing the present almost more than giving it – I can spend hours browsing.
grammar: 'Elegir el regalo' is the subject of 'me gusta' – a whole infinitive phrase counts as singular.

target: ¿Té o café? Me da igual, lo que quiero es sentarme un rato después de tanta caminata.
english: Tea or coffee? I honestly don't mind, what I want is to sit down for a bit after all that walking.
grammar: 'Me da igual' follows the 'gustar' pattern – the choice does the giving, so the verb stays third person with 'me'.

target: Me encanta cuando una palabra encaja tan bien que la oración entera se acomoda sola.
english: I love it when a word fits so well that the whole sentence settles into place on its own.
grammar: 'Me encanta cuando' – the whole 'when a word fits' idea counts as one thing, so 'encanta' stays singular.

target: Cepillar al caballo después del paseo es parte del ritual.
english: Brushing the horse after the ride is part of the ritual.
grammar: 'Cepillar' opens the sentence as its subject – Spanish gives that job to the bare infinitive, not an -ing form.

target: Me pone un poco nerviosa hablar español por teléfono, pero cada vez me sale mejor.
english: Speaking Spanish on the phone makes me a bit nervous, but I'm getting better every time.
grammar: Gustar-style, the activity is the subject: 'me pone un poco nerviosa hablar' – the speaking does the unnerving.

target: Hacer contactos con otros traductores es más fácil decirlo que hacerlo.
english: Networking with other translators is easier said than done.
grammar: 'Decirlo que hacerlo' – each infinitive carries its own 'lo' on the end: to say-it than to do-it.

target: Me encantan las tonterías que Pierre y Antoine mandan al chat del grupo, aunque no siempre las entiendo.
english: I love the silly messages Pierre and Antoine send to the group chat, even if I don't always understand them.
grammar: 'Me encantan' is plural because 'las tonterías' are the subject – the loved thing does the agreeing, not the lover.

target: Estamos emocionados de ir a visitar a Antoine otra vez a Nueva York.
english: We're excited to go and visit Antoine again in New York.
grammar: Emotion adjectives link with 'de': 'emocionados de ir' – excited to needs 'de' before the infinitive.

target: Viajar a la isla de Reunión desde el Reino Unido es toda una odisea.
english: Travelling to Réunion Island from the UK is quite an odyssey.
grammar: 'Viajar' stands as the subject of 'es' – the bare infinitive is how Spanish names an activity.

target: Ir a Londres es solo un viaje corto en tren.
english: Going to London is only a short train ride.
grammar: To go is the subject: 'Ir a Londres es' – Spanish starts with a bare infinitive where English uses going.

target: Nadar en el mar por la mañana me despierta mejor que el café.
english: Swimming in the sea in the morning wakes me up better than coffee.
grammar: 'Me despierta' works like 'gustar' – the swimming is the subject and I'm the 'me' it wakes up.

target: A Pierre y a Antoine les encanta decorar el pastel de Navidad, aunque nadie entienda el tema que eligen.
english: Pierre and Antoine love decorating the Christmas cake, even if nobody understands the theme they've picked.
grammar: 'les encanta decorar' – 'encantar' works like 'gustar': the decorating is the subject, 'les' marks the fans.

target: ¿Me podría dar una cita para esta semana? Me duele una muela desde el viernes.
english: Could I have an appointment this week? I've had toothache since Friday.
grammar: 'Me duele una muela' – 'doler' works like 'gustar': the tooth does the hurting and you take the 'me'.

target: Me encanta ese olor a tierra mojada que queda después de un aguacero.
english: I love that smell of damp earth you get after a downpour.
grammar: 'Me encanta ese olor' works like gustar – the smell is the subject doing the delighting.

target: A Pierre le encanta tomar leche en cantidades abundantes.
english: Pierre loves drinking abundant quantities of milk.
grammar: In Latin America drinking is 'tomar': 'tomar leche' – 'beber' is understood but sounds more formal.

target: Leer en esa pantalla tan chica me cansa la vista. Para las noticias prefiero la computadora.
english: Reading on such a tiny screen tires my eyes. For the news I'd rather use the computer.
grammar: 'Me cansa la vista' runs on the 'gustar' pattern – the screen does the tiring, I just receive it.

target: Después de nadar, un té caliente sabe a gloria.
english: After a swim, a hot tea tastes like heaven.
grammar: 'Sabe a gloria' – 'saber a' means to taste of, with 'a' introducing the flavour.

target: Disfruto traducir para organizaciones internacionales y ONG.
english: I enjoy translating for international organisations and NGOs.
grammar: 'Disfruto traducir' – 'disfrutar' can take the infinitive directly, with no preposition in between.

target: A Ken le emociona mucho la idea de otro carro antiguo, y yo todavía no sé si es buena idea.
english: Ken's really excited about the idea of another vintage car, and I still don't know if it's a good idea.
grammar: 'A Ken le emociona' – 'emocionar' follows the 'gustar' pattern: 'la idea' does the exciting and 'le' marks Ken.

target: Es asombroso cuando una ballena enorme aparece de la nada frente al barco.
english: It's astonishing when a huge whale appears out of nowhere right in front of the boat.
grammar: 'Cuando una ballena enorme aparece' – 'cuando' plus the plain present describes what generally happens.

target: Tengo muchas ganas de ir de viaje con Antoine.
english: I'm really looking forward to going on a trip with Antoine.
grammar: 'Tengo muchas ganas de' – desire is something you have: 'ganas' + 'de' + infinitive is everyday looking-forward-to.

target: Hacer azulejos es más difícil de lo que parece.
english: Making tiles is harder than it looks.
grammar: 'Más difícil de lo que parece' – comparing with a whole idea (than it seems) needs 'de lo que', not just 'que'.

target: Ver deporte juntos nos une más que cualquier conversación seria.
english: Watching sport together brings us closer than any serious conversation.
grammar: An infinitive subject counts as singular – 'ver deporte' is the subject, so the verb is 'une', never 'unen'.

target: Me encanta tener invitados, pero también disfruto ese momento en que la casa vuelve a quedar en silencio.
english: I love having people to stay, but I also enjoy that moment when the house falls quiet again.
grammar: 'Me encanta tener' – the subject is the infinitive 'tener', and infinitive subjects are singular, hence no 'encantan'.

target: También me gusta pintar al aire libre en Josselin, cuando el pueblo está tranquilo y nadie te apura.
english: I also like painting outdoors in Josselin, when the town is quiet and nobody hurries you.
grammar: 'Me gusta pintar' – the infinitive is the subject of 'gusta', so the verb stays singular whatever follows.

target: Hoy me toca aspirar. ¿Por qué no sacudes tú los muebles?
english: It's my turn to hoover today – why don't you do the dusting?
grammar: 'Me toca aspirar' works like 'gustar' – the chore is the subject and 'me' marks whose turn it is.

target: En los mercados bolivianos conviene llevar efectivo.
english: In Bolivian markets it's best to carry cash.
grammar: 'Conviene' + infinitive = it's wise to: 'conviene llevar efectivo' – best to carry cash.

target: Me cuesta seguir la conversación cuando hablan varios a la vez. De a uno, perfecto.
english: I find it hard to follow when several people are talking at once – one at a time, I'm fine.
grammar: 'Me cuesta seguir' – 'costar' works like 'gustar': the effortful thing is the subject and the person appears as 'me'.

target: A Twig le gusta acomodarse junto a la cabeza de Pierre en el sofá.
english: Twig likes to perch right by Pierre's head on the sofa.
grammar: The liker is marked with 'a' and echoed by 'le': 'A Twig le gusta' – the perching pleases him.

target: Lo que más me gusta del frío es hornear: prender el horno calienta la casa entera.
english: What I like best about the cold is baking: turning the oven on warms the whole house.
grammar: 'Lo que más me gusta del frío es hornear' reads almost word for word: the thing I like most about the cold is baking.

target: Tachar los días en el calendario me da una alegría enorme cuando falta poco para un viaje.
english: Crossing the days off the calendar gives me such a thrill when a trip is getting close.
grammar: 'Tachar los días' – where English says 'crossing the days off', Spanish uses the plain verb 'tachar', to cross off.

target: Lo que me gusta de volver a Pulborough es retomar mis rutinas de siempre.
english: What I like about coming back to Pulborough is picking up my usual routines again.
grammar: 'Lo que me gusta de volver' – for 'what I like about coming back', Spanish uses 'de' where English says 'about'.

target: Me cuesta muchísimo pintar las manos, mucho más que las caras.
english: I find hands terribly difficult to paint, much harder than faces.
grammar: 'Me cuesta muchísimo pintar' – literally 'painting costs me a lot': the painting drives the verb, not the person.

target: ¿Sus nietos viven cerca o le toca viajar para verlos?
english: Do your grandchildren live nearby, or do you have to travel to see them?
grammar: 'Le toca viajar' – 'tocarle' deals out a turn or duty, gustar-style: the travelling falls to 'le'.

target: Quedarse sin aliento al ver salir una ballena es de lo más normal.
english: Gasping when you see a whale surface is perfectly normal.
grammar: The combo 'al ver' means on seeing – 'al' + infinitive pins an action to a moment.

target: Esmaltar es la parte que más me gusta: nunca sabes exactamente qué saldrá.
english: Glazing is the part I like best – you never know exactly how it will come out.
grammar: 'La parte que más me gusta' – 'más' + 'gustar' builds the favourite: the part that pleases me most.

target: Estrenar zapatos me encanta, aunque los primeros días siempre sale alguna ampolla.
english: I love wearing new shoes for the first time, even though the first few days a blister always appears.
grammar: 'Estrenar zapatos me encanta' – the infinitive is the thing doing the delighting, so 'encanta' stays singular.

target: Me encanta la calefacción de los asientos del carro.
english: I love the seat warmers in the car.
grammar: 'Encantar' is already strong – 'me encanta' means I love it, so no 'mucho' gets added on.

target: Lo que más me gusta es la vuelta al paso, cuando ya nadie tiene prisa, ni el caballo ni yo.
english: What I like best is the walk back at the end, when nobody's in a hurry any more, neither the horse nor me.
grammar: 'Lo que más me gusta' – Spanish says 'the thing that I like most' where English just says 'what I like most'.

target: Qué gusto da ver este puesto tan colorido. ¿Le molesta si le tomo una foto?
english: What a joy this colourful stall is – do you mind if I take a photo of it?
grammar: 'Qué gusto da ver' – 'ver' is the subject: the seeing itself gives the pleasure, gustar-style.

target: A Ken le encanta irse por ahí en la moto, aunque nunca va muy lejos ni muy rápido.
english: Ken loves going off on his motorbike, though he never goes very far or very fast.
grammar: 'A Ken le encanta' – 'encantar' works like 'gustar' but stronger, and what he loves is an infinitive: 'irse por ahí'.

target: Me relaja pelar papas con la radio puesta.
english: I find it quite relaxing peeling potatoes with the radio on.
grammar: 'Me relaja pelar papas' works like gustar – the peeling is the subject, so 'relaja' stays third person.

target: No me convence caminar sola por esta zona de noche. Vamos a pedir un taxi seguro.
english: I don't fancy walking round this area alone at night – let's order a registered taxi.
grammar: 'No me convence caminar sola' – 'convencer' works like 'gustar': the walk is the subject and you take the 'me'.

target: Las oraciones de esta aplicación me suenan sospechosamente familiares.
english: The sentences in this app sound suspiciously familiar.
grammar: Rings a bell is 'sonarle': 'me suenan sospechosamente familiares' – they sound familiar to me.

target: Lo que más me gusta es trazar el patrón a lápiz antes de tocar la pintura.
english: What I like best is drawing out the pattern in pencil before I touch the paint.
grammar: 'Lo que más me gusta es trazar' – 'lo que' wraps it all into one thing: the thing I like most is drawing.

target: Es fácil perder el rumbo en los bosques de Fittleworth con tanto helecho.
english: It's easy to lose track of where you are in Fittleworth Woods, with all the bracken.
grammar: 'Es fácil perder el rumbo' – adjective first, action after: 'es' + adjective + infinitive is the it's-easy-to frame.

target: Manejar en Georgia tiene su truco, con tantas vacas en la carretera.
english: Driving in Georgia is tricky, with so many cows on the road.
grammar: 'Manejar' is the Latin American word for driving – in Spain you'd hear 'conducir'.

target: Traducir es elegir: cada palabra desplaza a otra.
english: Translating is choosing – every word displaces another.
grammar: 'Traducir es elegir' – infinitives serve as nouns on both sides of 'es', where English wants -ing.

target: Me gusta ir a nuestro pequeño cine local a ver películas.
english: I like going to our little local cinema to watch films.
grammar: 'A ver películas' – after 'ir', purpose is a plain 'a' + infinitive; go-to-do needs nothing heavier.

target: A Ken le encantan los postres. Todos. En orden y sin excepciones.
english: Ken loves puddings. All of them. In order, and without exception.
grammar: 'Le encantan los postres' – the puddings do the delighting, so the verb agrees with them, not with Ken.

target: Traducir ficción no deja mucha plata.
english: Translating fiction doesn't bring in much money.
grammar: 'Plata', literally silver, is the everyday Latin American word for money – in Spain you'd hear 'dinero'.

target: Leer el libro es una parte importante de estar en un club de lectura.
english: Reading the book is an important part of being in a book club.
grammar: 'Leer el libro' is the subject – Spanish uses a bare infinitive where English says reading.

target: Saber francés ayuda mucho con el vocabulario del español.
english: Knowing French helps a lot with Spanish vocabulary.
grammar: Knowing a language is 'saber', not 'conocer': 'saber francés' – skills and facts belong to 'saber'.

target: La semana pasada terminé una traducción dos días antes del plazo, y me di el gusto de revisarla con calma.
english: Last week I finished a translation two days ahead of the deadline, and treated myself to an unhurried final read.
grammar: 'Me di el gusto' – 'dar' has the bare irregular preterite 'di', no accent, a one-off treat firmly in the past.

target: Anoche Gilles habló dos horas sin respirar, y eso que nadie le preguntó nada.
english: Last night Gilles talked for two hours without drawing breath, and nobody had even asked him anything.
grammar: 'Habló dos horas' – a counted stretch, start to finish, takes the preterite however long it dragged.

target: Ayer hice un pastel de manzana y no quedó ni una rebanada.
english: Yesterday I made an apple cake and there wasn't a single slice left.
grammar: 'Hice' – hacer's irregular preterite, the tense for yesterday's finished one-off, start to end.

target: La semana pasada me tocó un caballo distinto y tardé media clase en agarrarle el ritmo.
english: Last week I was given a different horse and it took me half the lesson to get the feel of him.
grammar: 'me tocó un caballo distinto' – 'tocar' here is about what you happen to get: a different horse fell to me.

target: Hubo una época en que un halcón peregrino vino a anidar en Latour de France.
english: There was once a time when a peregrine falcon came and nested in Latour de France.
grammar: 'Hubo' is 'hay' in the preterite – there-was as one closed chapter; 'había' would just set the scene.

target: Viajar por Chile fue increíble: hasta vimos pingüinos.
english: Travelling through Chile was incredible – we even saw penguins.
grammar: Besides until, 'hasta' can mean even: 'hasta vimos pingüinos' – we even saw penguins.

target: Ayer numeré toda la tanda por detrás para no perder el orden del patrón.
english: Yesterday I numbered the whole batch on the back so I wouldn't lose the order of the pattern.
grammar: 'Ayer numeré' – a task with a clear finish goes preterite: the numbering was done once and completed.

target: Floppy el hámster murió un viernes, y la familia todavía le encuentra significado a ese detalle.
english: Floppy the hamster died on a Friday, and the family still finds meaning in that detail.
grammar: 'Murió un viernes' – the preterite pins a single finished event to its date, the tense of one-off news.

target: El sábado hubo festival en la plaza, por eso cerraron la calle y el bus nos dejó a diez cuadras.
english: On Saturday there was a festival in the square, so they closed the road and the bus dropped us ten streets away.
grammar: 'Hubo festival' – 'hubo' is 'hay' in the preterite: the whole event came and went within its day.

target: Pierre se puso un conjunto amarillo para ir a esquiar.
english: Pierre wore a yellow outfit to go skiing.
grammar: Clothes go on with 'ponerse': 'se puso un conjunto amarillo' – he put a yellow outfit on himself.

target: Los ucranianos ganaron el torneo de tenis de mesa y no nos hizo mucha gracia.
english: The Ukrainians won the table tennis competition and we weren't too happy about it.
grammar: Amusement is 'hacer gracia' (to make grace): 'no nos hizo mucha gracia' = we didn't find it funny.

target: Me equivoqué de línea y terminé en la otra punta de la ciudad.
english: I got on the wrong line and ended up at the other end of the city.
grammar: One-off slips take the preterite: 'me equivoqué de línea' – a single finished event, not a running backdrop.

target: Tuve una entrevista rarísima con el gobierno irlandés.
english: I had a really weird interview with the Irish government.
grammar: The tail '-ísima' makes it really: 'rarísima' = really weird, stronger than 'muy rara'.

target: La entrevista para hacerse británica fue bastante invasiva.
english: The interview to become British was quite intrusive.
grammar: To become a nationality, Spanish says 'hacerse' – literally to make oneself: 'hacerse británica'.

target: El padre Paul prefirió no comentar los paralelos entre Floppy y la Pascua.
english: Father Paul declined to comment on the parallels between Floppy and Easter.
grammar: In this past form 'preferir' swaps its 'e' for an 'i' – 'prefirió', just as 'pedir' gives 'pidió'.

target: Llegué temprano a la panadería, escogí dos baguettes y de paso me enteré de todas las novedades del barrio.
english: I got to the bakery early, picked out two baguettes and caught up on all the local news while I was at it.
grammar: 'Me enteré de' – finding out is 'enterarse de', a one-moment verb: news lands in an instant, so the preterite fits.

target: La comida en Georgia me pareció un poco sobrevalorada, pero vimos cosas increíbles.
english: I found the food in Georgia a bit overrated, but we did see some incredible things.
grammar: 'Me pareció' – an opinion formed at the time takes 'parecer' in the preterite: that's how it struck me then.

target: El viaje a Japón para visitar a Antoine fue una maravilla: fuimos a Nara y a Kioto.
english: The trip to Japan to visit Antoine was wonderful: we went to Nara and Kyoto.
grammar: 'fue' and 'fuimos' – 'ser' and 'ir' share one preterite table, so only context says which verb you're seeing.

target: Ken estuvo en la RAF y tiene todo tipo de historias de esa época.
english: Ken used to be in the RAF and has all kinds of stories from that time.
grammar: 'Estuvo' – 'estar' in the preterite closes the chapter: the RAF years are a finished block of time.

target: Aprendí a cocinar por mi cuenta, y en esta casa nadie se queja.
english: I taught myself to cook, and nobody in this house complains.
grammar: 'Nadie se queja' – 'nadie' before the verb needs no 'no'; after the verb it would: 'no se queja nadie'.

target: Ken y yo no fuimos muy consecuentes a la hora de bautizar a nuestros hijos.
english: Ken and I weren't very consistent when baptising our children.
grammar: 'A la hora de' – literally at-the-hour-of: the set phrase for when-it-comes-to doing something.

target: Lord Waverley invitó a Ken a tomar el té en la Cámara de los Lores.
english: Lord Waverley invited Ken to tea at the House of Lords.
grammar: 'Invitó' – one completed invitation on one occasion: exactly the job of the preterite.

target: Enterramos a Floppy con honores. Tres días después, la jaula amaneció abierta.
english: We buried Floppy with full honours – three days later, we woke to find the cage open.
grammar: 'Enterramos' could be present or preterite – -ar we-forms look identical, so 'tres días después' settles it.

target: Yo trabajé en la audioguía de la Torre de Londres, así que ese lugar me lo sé de memoria.
english: I worked on the audioguide for the Tower of London, so I know the place off by heart.
grammar: A finished stint takes the preterite: 'trabajé en la audioguía' – that job is a closed chapter.

target: ¿A que no adivinas a quién me encontré en el café? A una señora que trabajó conmigo hace más de veinte años.
english: Guess who I ran into at the café? A woman who worked with me more than twenty years ago.
grammar: 'Me encontré' – reflexive 'encontrarse' is running into someone by chance, plain 'encontrar' just finding.

target: Se me cayó el celular en plena calle, y por suerte la pantalla no se rompió.
english: I dropped my phone in the middle of the street, and luckily the screen didn't break.
grammar: 'Se me cayó' – Spanish drops the phone, not the person: 'se' makes it happen by itself, 'me' names the victim.

target: Giramos donde nos indicaron y salimos justo frente al teatro.
english: We turned where they told us and came out right opposite the theatre.
grammar: A story moves in preterites: 'giramos' and 'salimos' – each a completed step that pushes the route on.

target: ¿Te acuerdas de aquella vez que las cigüeñas llegaron a Latour de France y se posaron en el techo?
english: Do you remember that time the storks came to Latour de France and perched on the roof?
grammar: 'Aquella vez' – 'aquel' points to the far-off: that time way back; 'esa vez' would feel closer at hand.

target: Antoine aprendió a leer mapas, administrar recursos y no rendirse jamás. Todo gracias a Pokémon.
english: Antoine learned to read maps, manage resources and never give up. All thanks to Pokémon.
grammar: 'aprendió a leer' – one 'aprendió a' covers the whole list that follows: reading, managing, never giving up.

target: Ayer estiré yo misma un lienzo por primera vez, y quedó más tenso de lo que esperaba.
english: Yesterday I stretched a canvas myself for the first time, and it came out tighter than I expected.
grammar: One finished action, done yesterday: preterite 'estiré' – the '-é' ending is the yo past for -ar verbs.

target: Mis hijos heredaron mi elegancia para tropezar con superficies completamente planas.
english: My sons inherited my elegance at tripping over completely flat surfaces.
grammar: 'Heredaron' is the preterite – the handover happened once and is complete, however long its effects run.

target: Ayer el plomero destapó la cañería de la cocina en media hora y dejó todo limpio.
english: Yesterday the plumber unblocked the kitchen drain in half an hour and left everything spotless.
grammar: 'Destapó' and 'dejó' are preterite – yesterday's job ran start to finish, two completed one-off actions.

target: Disculpe, creo que hubo una confusión: yo pedí el ceviche, no la sopa.
english: Excuse me, I think there's been a mix-up – I ordered the ceviche, not the soup.
grammar: 'Hubo una confusión' – 'hubo', the preterite of 'hay', reports one finished event: there was, and it's over.

target: ¡Ese peluquero se lució esta vez! El corte le quedó muy bien.
english: That hairdresser has outdone himself this time – the cut looks really good!
grammar: 'Se lució' – 'lucirse' means to outdo yourself, and the preterite pins it to this one haircut.

target: El último día cortamos el agua, vaciamos el refrigerador y dejamos las camas hechas.
english: On the last day we turned off the water, emptied the fridge and left the beds made up.
grammar: 'Cortamos', 'vaciamos', 'dejamos' – three finished acts ticked off in the preterite, the tense for a closing-up list.

target: Cuando me mudé al Reino Unido, la gente me decía 'my duck'.
english: When I moved to the UK, people called me 'my duck'.
grammar: 'Me mudé' marks the one-off move, while the imperfect 'decía' covers what people said again and again.

target: Para ir al Lake District empacamos un montón de hot cross buns.
english: Going to the Lake District involved packing a lot of hot cross buns.
grammar: 'Empacamos' could be present or preterite – -ar verbs share their we form, so context decides the tense.

target: Trabajé muchos años como traductora, así que elijo cada palabra con cuidado.
english: I worked as a translator for many years, so I choose every word with care.
grammar: 'Trabajé muchos años' – preterite even for a long stretch, because that chapter is closed.

target: Una media negra se me fue con la ropa clara y varias camisetas quedaron grises.
english: A black sock got into the light wash and several t-shirts came out grey.
grammar: 'Quedaron grises' – 'quedar' + adjective means ended up, and the preterite logs the outcome of that one wash.

target: Hice una serie de azulejos con motivos de conchas.
english: I made a series of tiles with shell motifs.
grammar: 'Hice' – 'hacer' goes irregular in the preterite (hice, hizo): a finished project takes the simple past.

target: Hice un álbum de fotos fantástico sobre la época que pasamos en Georgia.
english: I made a fantastic photo album about the time we spent in Georgia.
grammar: 'Hice' – 'hacer' goes irregular in the preterite: 'hice', 'hiciste', 'hizo', none carrying an accent.

target: El kilo de arcilla me salió en doce cincuenta, así que me llevé tres para tener de sobra.
english: The clay worked out at twelve fifty a kilo, so I took three to be on the safe side.
grammar: 'Me salió en doce cincuenta' – the price you ended up paying is a one-off result, so 'salir' goes preterite.

target: Ayer el vendedor me atendió de maravilla y al final no le compré nada, me dio no sé qué.
english: Yesterday the shop assistant couldn't have been more helpful and in the end I didn't buy a thing – I felt a bit bad about it.
grammar: 'Me atendió' and 'no le compré' are preterite – yesterday's scene runs as finished one-off events, told in order.

target: Nos quedamos tres noches en casa de unos amigos y el último día los invitamos a cenar afuera para agradecerles.
english: We stayed three nights at some friends' house, and on the last day we took them out to dinner to say thank you.
grammar: 'Nos quedamos tres noches' – a stay with a stated length is a closed chapter, so the preterite tells it.

target: Otra vez perdí los lentes de contacto y no veo nada.
english: I've lost my contact lenses again and I can't see a thing.
grammar: English says I've lost, but LatAm Spanish prefers the preterite: 'perdí', not 'he perdido'.

target: Primero se me olvidó la lista, después encontré la tienda cerrada y al final igual resolví la cena con lo que tenía en la casa.
english: First I forgot the list, then I found the shop shut, and in the end I sorted dinner out with what was in the house anyway.
grammar: 'Primero', 'después', 'al final' – the storytelling scaffold, each stage landing as its own fresh preterite.

target: Pierre y Anna tienen un huerto, y a Antoine le impresionó bastante.
english: Pierre and Anna have an allotment, and Antoine was quite impressed by it.
grammar: A reaction pinned to one moment takes the preterite: 'le impresionó' – the impression struck when he saw it.

target: Pierre y Anna se mudaron a una casa nueva.
english: Pierre and Anna moved into a new house.
grammar: A one-off completed event takes the preterite: 'se mudaron' – the move happened once and is done.

target: El mes pasado fuimos a una obra de teatro y volvimos en el último tren.
english: Last month we went to a play and came back on the last train.
grammar: 'Fuimos' is the preterite of both 'ir' and 'ser' – identical tables, and only context says went, not were.

target: El Brexit complicó bastante los trámites para vivir entre dos países.
english: Brexit made the paperwork for living between two countries a lot more complicated.
grammar: 'Complicó' is preterite – Brexit changed things at one point, and that change counts as one event.

target: El invierno pasado nevó tanto que cerraron varias carreteras durante días.
english: Last winter it snowed so much that several roads were closed for days.
grammar: 'El invierno pasado nevó' – a closed, dated time frame calls for the preterite: over and counted.

target: Hoy salimos a galopar por el campo y fue una maravilla.
english: Today we went out for a gallop through the fields and it was wonderful.
grammar: 'Salimos' spells both we go out and we went out – here 'fue' pins the whole outing in the past.

target: Aprendí viendo tutoriales y arruinando unas cuantas piezas.
english: I learned by watching tutorials and ruining quite a few pieces.
grammar: 'Aprendí viendo' – 'viendo' on its own means 'by watching': Spanish leaves out the word for 'by' entirely.

target: Ayer se me quemó el ajo por contestar el teléfono y tuve que empezar la salsa de nuevo.
english: Yesterday I burnt the garlic answering the phone and had to start the sauce all over again.
grammar: 'Tuve que empezar' – preterite 'tuve que' means the obligation was actually met: had to, and did.

target: Mi maleta no salió con las demás. ¿Dónde hago el reclamo de equipaje?
english: My suitcase didn't come out with the others – where do I report missing luggage?
grammar: 'No salió con las demás' – preterite: the unloading happened once and finished, and the case wasn't in it.

target: El brindis lo dio la dueña de la casa y le salió muy bien: breve, claro y sin leer nada.
english: The lady of the house gave the toast and it came out really well: short, clear and without reading a word.
grammar: In the preterite, dar borrows -er/-ir endings – 'dio', one syllable, so no written accent either.

target: Empecé a montar a caballo ya de grande, y no me arrepiento para nada.
english: I took up riding later in life, and I don't regret it one bit.
grammar: 'Empecé' – a start is a single moment, so it takes the preterite even if the riding went on for years.

target: Antoine y PapyLou volaron juntos en globo aerostático, y a la vuelta se pasaron semanas hablando del viaje.
english: Antoine and PapyLou went hot air ballooning together, and came back talking about it for weeks.
grammar: Even weeks fit in the preterite once finished: 'se pasaron semanas hablando' – the whole spell, wrapped up.

target: El año pasado traduje un informe entero sobre acceso al agua potable para una ONG.
english: Last year I translated a whole report on access to clean water for an NGO.
grammar: 'El año pasado' closes the time frame, so the verb goes preterite: 'traduje' – one finished job, viewed whole.

target: La caja fuerte se bloqueó y no hubo manera de abrirla con el código que me dieron.
english: The safe locked itself and there was no way to open it with the code they gave me.
grammar: 'No hubo manera' – 'hubo' is 'hay' in the preterite: the whole failed struggle wrapped up as one event.

target: Antoine y Ken fueron juntos a Letonia y vieron castillos, reliquias soviéticas y una playa.
english: Antoine and Ken went to Latvia together and saw castles, Soviet relics and a beach.
grammar: 'Fueron' is the preterite of both 'ir' and 'ser' – 'a Letonia' tells you this one means went, not were.

target: El primer día la altura me pegó durísimo: ¿a usted también le costó acostumbrarse?
english: The first day the altitude hit me really hard – did you find it hard to get used to as well?
grammar: 'Me pegó durísimo' – the preterite lands one finished blow: it hit on the first day, complete and done with.

target: No te vas a creer lo que me pasó hoy en el mercado: pedí un kilo de tomates y el señor me regaló un manojo de albahaca.
english: You'll never believe what happened to me at the market today: I asked for a kilo of tomatoes and the man threw in a bunch of basil for free.
grammar: 'Me pasó hoy' – LatAm keeps today's finished events in the preterite, where Spain would reach for 'ha pasado'.

target: Al llegar abrimos las ventanas de par en par y encendimos el calentador de agua.
english: When we arrived we threw the windows wide open and switched on the water heater.
grammar: 'Abrimos' could be present – nosotros -ir preterites share that form, and 'encendimos' pins the pair to the past.

target: Una delegación saudí ofreció una fortuna por Brannagh. La respuesta fue no.
english: A Saudi delegation offered a fortune for Brannagh. The answer was no.
grammar: One completed act, one preterite: 'ofreció una fortuna' – a single finished offer, story moved on.

target: Ayer borré un archivo sin querer y me pasé la tarde entera tratando de recuperarlo.
english: Yesterday I deleted a file by accident and spent the whole afternoon trying to get it back.
grammar: 'Ayer borré' – 'ayer' dates a finished event, so preterite, and 'me pasé la tarde' is just as closed.

target: Encontré la bufanda perfecta en una feria de artesanías y no me costó casi nada.
english: I found the perfect scarf at a craft fair and it cost me next to nothing.
grammar: 'Encontré' and 'no me costó' are preterites – single completed events, told as wrapped up and done.

target: Después de tantos años de judo en familia, por lo menos todos aprendimos a caer como se debe.
english: After all those years of family judo, we all at least learned how to fall properly.
grammar: The preterite marks it as achieved: 'aprendimos a caer' – the learning finally happened, complete.

target: En julio del año pasado recorrimos la costa y nos tocó un clima buenísimo.
english: In July last year we toured the coast and got glorious weather.
grammar: 'Nos tocó' is preterite – 'tocar' here means fell-to-us: luck arrives as a one-off event, so the completed past.

target: Pierre y Antoine decoraron el pastel de Navidad a su manera, y el resultado quedó bien raro.
english: Pierre and Antoine decorated the Christmas cake their own way, and the result was properly weird.
grammar: 'decoraron' – one finished Christmas job takes the preterite: done once, result and all.

target: Esta mañana entré de golpe, sin pensarlo dos veces, y resultó mucho mejor que ir de a poquito.
english: This morning I went straight in without thinking twice, and it was far better than easing in bit by bit.
grammar: One decisive act, so the preterite: 'entré de golpe' – a single completed plunge, not a scene or a habit.

target: Le marqué dos veces y las dos me mandó directo al buzón, así que mejor le escribí un mensaje.
