english: If I were you I wouldn't worry so much about the accent, what matters is being understood.
grammar: 'Si yo fuera tú' – an unreal 'si' takes imperfect subjunctive 'fuera', with the advice in conditional 'preocuparía'.

target: Si la casa tuviera un cuarto más, podríamos recibir a todos al mismo tiempo y no por turnos.
english: If the house had one more room, we could have everyone to stay at once instead of in shifts.
grammar: 'Tuviera' is past subjunctive for a room the house doesn't have – the unreal 'if' pairs with 'podríamos'.

target: Si de verdad quisieras convencerme, tendrías que darme un ejemplo concreto.
english: If you really wanted to win me over, you'd have to give me a concrete example.
grammar: An unreal if takes the imperfect subjunctive 'quisieras' – and its payoff 'tendrías' stays conditional.

target: Colgamos el cuadro donde le diera la luz.
english: We hung the painting where the light would catch it.
grammar: 'Donde le diera la luz' – a spot still being looked for takes the imperfect subjunctive after 'donde'.

target: Si tuviera que quedarme con un solo diccionario, sería el de sinónimos: me ha salvado mil veces.
english: If I had to keep just one dictionary it would be the thesaurus: it's saved me a thousand times.
grammar: 'Si tuviera' – an unlikely if takes the imperfect subjunctive, with the conditional 'sería' answering it.

target: Si la clase de pintura durara dos horas en vez de hora y media, terminaríamos el paisaje en una sola sesión.
english: If the painting class lasted two hours instead of an hour and a half, we'd finish the landscape in a single session.
grammar: 'Durara' imagines a longer class – past subjunctive in the 'si' half, conditional 'terminaríamos' in the result.

target: Si tuviera más tiempo, montaría todos los días.
english: If I had more time, I'd ride every day.
grammar: 'Si tuviera' – imperfect subjunctive for the unreal if, with conditional 'montaría' giving the result.

target: Los novios nos pidieron que no subiéramos fotos hasta el día siguiente.
english: The bride and groom asked us not to post any photos until the following day.
grammar: 'Pidieron que no subiéramos' – a request made in the past pulls the subjunctive into the past too.

target: Si Benoît no hiciera trampa, los juegos de mesa perderían parte de su encanto.
english: If Benoît didn't cheat, board games would lose part of their charm.
grammar: 'Hiciera' sets an unreal 'si' – imperfect subjunctive, with conditional 'perderían' carrying the result.

target: Asegurarme de que mis hijos fueran a una escuela anglicana era esencial para la integridad espiritual de la familia.
english: Making sure my sons attended a Church of England school was essential to our family's spiritual integrity.
grammar: 'Fueran' is imperfect subjunctive – the past trigger 'era esencial' drags the subjunctive into the past with it.

target: Si la travesía fuera más corta, iríamos y vendríamos mucho más seguido.
english: If the crossing were shorter we'd go back and forth much more often.
grammar: 'Fuera' is imperfect subjunctive – 'si' + an unreal condition takes it, with 'iríamos' replying in the conditional.

target: ¿Me haría un descuento si pagara todo en efectivo?
english: Would you give me a discount if I paid for the whole thing in cash?
grammar: The two halves can swap places: the result 'me haría' comes first, and the unreal if 'si pagara' trails behind.

target: Con un maestro que explicara más despacio, nadie tendría que quedarse después de clase.
english: With a teacher who explained things more slowly, nobody would have to stay behind after class.
grammar: 'Con un maestro que explicara' works like an if – the teacher is only imagined, so 'explicara', not 'explica'.

target: Si hiciéramos la fiesta en la terraza, cabría más gente y no habría que mover tantos muebles.
english: If we held the party on the terrace, more people would fit in and we wouldn't have to shift so much furniture.
grammar: 'Si hiciéramos' – the party is only imagined, which is exactly what the imperfect subjunctive flags.

target: Si hubiera anotado dónde estacionamos, no estaríamos dando vueltas por todo el estacionamiento.
english: If I'd made a note of where we parked, we wouldn't be going round and round the car park.
grammar: 'Si hubiera anotado' is unreal past, but the result is happening now – so 'estaríamos', not 'habríamos estado'.

target: Si viniera entre semana, ¿habría más pescado fresco?
english: If I came on a weekday, would there be more fresh fish?
grammar: The unreal if: 'si viniera' is imperfect subjunctive, and 'habría' answers it in the conditional.

target: Si el ferry se retrasa, aprovechamos para cenar en el puerto.
english: If the ferry is delayed, we make the most of it and have dinner at the port.
grammar: 'Si el ferry se retrasa' – a real, likely if keeps the everyday form: 'se retrasara' would make it a daydream.

target: Si viviéramos más lejos de la estación, lo pensaríamos dos veces. Por suerte, no es el caso.
english: If we lived further from the station, we'd think twice. Luckily, we don't.
grammar: An unreal if takes the imperfect subjunctive: 'si viviéramos', answered by the conditional 'lo pensaríamos'.

target: Me encantaría ayudar con la decoración si me avisaran con más anticipación.
english: I'd love to help with the decorations if they gave me a bit more notice.
grammar: The 'si' half can come last – 'si me avisaran' still takes imperfect subjunctive after 'encantaría'.

target: Si compráramos otro carro antiguo, no sé dónde lo meteríamos.
english: If we bought another vintage car, I don't know where we'd put it.
grammar: 'Si compráramos' – the -ra ending marks the imperfect subjunctive: an unreal purchase, answered by 'meteríamos'.

target: Sería bonito que cada invitado escribiera un deseo en una tarjeta.
english: It would be a lovely touch if every guest wrote a wish on a card.
grammar: A conditional judgement 'sería bonito que' pushes the next verb to imperfect subjunctive: 'escribiera'.

target: Si guardara los calcetines en pares desde el principio, no perdería diez minutos cada mañana buscando uno.
english: If I put the socks away in pairs from the start, I wouldn't lose ten minutes every morning hunting for one.
grammar: 'Si guardara' – the -ra form imagines a habit that isn't real, with 'no perdería' as the would-be payoff.

target: Si las instrucciones vinieran en un idioma normal, cualquiera podría conectar la impresora sin ayuda.
english: If the instructions came in normal language, anyone could set the printer up without help.
grammar: 'Si las instrucciones vinieran' – the unreal if takes imperfect subjunctive, and 'podría' answers with the result.

target: De haberlo sabido antes, habría reservado la excursión para otro día.
english: If I'd known sooner, I'd have booked the excursion for another day.
grammar: 'De haberlo sabido' squeezes a whole if I had known into three words – no 'si' needed at all.

target: Si viviéramos en el mismo huso horario, no tendría que hacer cuentas cada vez que quiero llamar.
english: If we lived in the same time zone, I wouldn't have to do sums every time I want to ring.
grammar: 'Si viviéramos' – an unreal 'if' takes the past subjunctive, and its result 'tendría' goes into the conditional.

target: Si hablara un poco más lento, le entendería todo. Lo mío es la velocidad, no el vocabulario.
english: If you spoke a little more slowly I'd understand everything – my problem is speed, not vocabulary.
grammar: 'Si hablara' pairs with 'le entendería' – imperfect subjunctive sets the unreal if, the conditional the result.

target: Si tuviera más espacio, pondría una huerta con tomates y hierbas aromáticas.
english: If I had more room, I'd put in a vegetable patch with tomatoes and herbs.
grammar: 'Si tuviera' imagines what isn't so – imperfect subjunctive for the if, with 'pondría' as the imagined result.

target: Si Ken dibujara a Trump, seguro que le pondría rodillas huesudas.
english: If Ken drew Trump, he'd definitely give him knobbly knees.
grammar: 'Le pondría rodillas' – Spanish says put knees to-him: 'le' does the job of English 'his' for body parts.

target: Si los postres contaran como verdura, Ken sería el hombre más sano de Inglaterra.
english: If puddings counted as vegetables, Ken would be the healthiest man in England.
grammar: 'Contaran' is just 'contaron' (they counted) with -ron swapped to -ran – that's how the unreal if is built.

target: Si tuviera un estudio con luz del norte, pintaría a cualquier hora sin pelearme con las sombras.
english: If I had a studio with north light, I'd paint at any hour without fighting the shadows.
grammar: Unreal present: 'si tuviera' – imperfect subjunctive – with the result in the conditional, 'pintaría'.

target: Si no fuera por los recordatorios del celular, se me pasaría la mitad de las citas.
english: If it weren't for the reminders on my phone, I'd miss half my appointments.
grammar: 'Si no fuera por' – the fixed frame for if it weren't for, with the fallout in conditional 'se me pasaría'.

target: Si los topos se fueran a otro jardín, Ken sería el hombre más feliz de Bretaña.
english: If the moles moved to someone else's garden, Ken would be the happiest man in Brittany.
grammar: 'se fueran' – 'si' plus imperfect subjunctive floats the unlikely dream, and 'sería' delivers the would-be result.

target: Si fuera por mí, las vacaciones largas serían en abril, cuando ya no hace tanto calor y todo está más barato.
english: If it were up to me, the long holidays would be in April, when it's not so hot any more and everything's cheaper.
grammar: 'Si fuera por mí' – the unreal-if pair: imperfect subjunctive 'fuera' in the if-half, conditional 'serían' answering.

target: Me encantaría que me recomendaras algún restaurante al que vayan los de aquí.
english: I'd love you to recommend a restaurant the locals actually go to.
grammar: 'Me encantaría que' hands the next verb the imperfect subjunctive: 'recomendaras', matching the conditional mood.

target: Si me hubieran avisado con tiempo, habría cambiado la cita sin ningún problema.
english: If they'd let me know in time, I'd have moved the appointment without any trouble.
grammar: 'Hubieran avisado' is pluperfect subjunctive – the warning never came, and unreal past events live in that form.

target: El jardinero me recomendó que no podara los rosales hasta fines del invierno.
english: The gardener advised me not to prune the rose bushes until late winter.
grammar: 'Recomendó que no podara' – a past-tense recommendation drags the verb into the imperfect subjunctive.

target: Si el pronóstico no anunciara tormenta, mañana haríamos la caminata larga.
english: If the forecast weren't showing a storm, we'd do the long walk tomorrow.
grammar: 'Si el pronóstico no anunciara' – picturing the forecast otherwise, so 'anunciara', with the plan in 'haríamos'.

target: Si no fuera por los videojuegos, quizás uno de mis hijos ya habría ganado el Nobel.
english: If it weren't for video games, perhaps one of my sons would have won a Nobel by now.
grammar: 'Si no fuera por' is the unreal if – imperfect subjunctive, answered by 'habría ganado' for the missed result.

target: Si el teleférico no estuviera en mantenimiento, llegaríamos en diez minutos.
english: If the cable car weren't down for maintenance, we'd be there in ten minutes.
grammar: 'Si' + 'no estuviera' sets an unreal now – imperfect subjunctive, with the result in conditional 'llegaríamos'.

target: Si dejáramos el comedero vacío unos días, los pájaros tardarían muy poco en desaparecer del jardín.
english: If we left the feeder empty for a few days, the birds would very soon disappear from the garden.
grammar: 'Si dejáramos' pairs with 'tardarían' – imperfect subjunctive for the imagined if, conditional for its result.

target: Ojalá hubiéramos apuntado el nombre de ese pueblito, porque ahora nadie se acuerda de cómo se llamaba.
english: I wish we'd written down the name of that little village, because now nobody can remember what it was called.
grammar: 'Ojalá hubiéramos apuntado' – 'ojalá' + pluperfect subjunctive wishes about a past that can't now change.

target: Si el cuarto tuviera algo para calentar agua, me prepararía mi té de la tarde.
english: If the room had some way of boiling water, I'd make my afternoon cup of tea.
grammar: 'Si el cuarto tuviera' – imperfect subjunctive imagines what the room lacks, with the result in 'me prepararía'.

target: Hornearía el pan y el pollo a la vez si el horno fuera un poco más grande.
english: I'd bake the bread and roast the chicken at the same time if the oven were a bit bigger.
grammar: 'Si el horno fuera' imagines an unreal oven, so the result takes the conditional – 'fuera' pairs with 'hornearía'.

target: Si me lo hubieran dicho hace diez años, no lo habría creído: yo, a caballo por las colinas de Sussex.
english: If you'd told me ten years ago I'd never have believed it: me, on horseback in the Sussex hills.
grammar: 'Si me lo hubieran dicho' sets up a past that never was, and 'habría creído' is what would have followed.

target: Si el taller tuviera agua corriente, no andaría cargando baldes desde la cocina.
english: If the workshop had running water, I wouldn't be lugging buckets from the kitchen.
grammar: 'Si el taller tuviera' – the imperfect subjunctive for a present that isn't true: there's no running water.

target: Si le preguntaras a Antoine por sus valores, citaría a un entrenador Pokémon.
english: If you asked Antoine about his values, he'd quote a Pokémon trainer.
grammar: An imagined 'si' takes 'preguntaras' – imperfect subjunctive – with the outcome in conditional 'citaría'.

target: Si hubiera sabido que cobraban por cada maleta, habría empacado más liviano.
english: If I'd known they charged for every suitcase, I'd have packed lighter.
grammar: 'Hubiera sabido' imagines a past that never was, and 'habría empacado' is what would have followed.

target: Quisiera que me devolvieran la plata, porque el aparato llegó defectuoso.
english: I'd like my money back, as the device arrived faulty.
grammar: 'Quisiera' is itself imperfect subjunctive – the polite want, and it pulls 'devolvieran' into the same mood.

target: Si el papeleo se hiciera solo, Antoine sería el hombre más eficiente de Nueva York.
english: If paperwork did itself, Antoine would be the most efficient man in New York.
grammar: 'Se hiciera solo' – the imperfect subjunctive builds the if-fantasy, and 'sería' delivers its conditional result.

target: Caliente bien el aceite antes de poner el pescado, así no se pega.
english: Get the oil properly hot before you put the fish in – that way it won't stick.
grammar: 'Caliente' is an usted command – same shape as the subjunctive, which is exactly where it comes from.

target: ¡Qué lío con las llaves! La de Bretaña es igualita a la de Sussex y siempre pruebo primero la equivocada.
english: What a muddle with the keys! The Brittany one is exactly like the Sussex one and I always try the wrong one first.
grammar: 'Qué lío' – exclamations run 'qué' + noun with no article in between, unlike English 'what a muddle'.

target: Agrega la pimienta al final, así no pierde el aroma.
english: Put the pepper in at the end – that way it keeps its aroma.
grammar: 'Agrega' only works positive – negate it and the tú command changes shape to 'no agregues'.

target: ¡Qué fila tan larga! Ve apartando lugar mientras compro algo de tomar para el viaje.
english: What a long queue! Save a place while I get us something to drink for the journey.
grammar: 'Ve apartando lugar' – 've' (go) plus the -ando form tells someone to get on with it in the meantime.

target: Que yo sepa, el museo cierra los lunes, pero mejor confirmemos antes de comprar las entradas.
english: As far as I know, the museum shuts on Mondays – but let's double-check before buying the tickets.
grammar: 'Mejor confirmemos' – the nosotros subjunctive on its own works as a command meaning let's confirm.

target: No metas los plátanos al refrigerador, déjalos madurar en la mesa.
english: Don't put the bananas in the fridge – leave them out on the table to ripen.
grammar: 'No metas' – a negative command takes the subjunctive form: 'metas', not 'metes' as in the plain present.

target: ¡Mira, una ballena! ¡Guau!
english: Oh look, a whale – wow!
grammar: 'Mira' is the tú command of 'mirar' – 'miras' minus its final -s: look.

target: Hábleme más despacio, por favor, que si no me pierdo enseguida.
english: Please speak more slowly – otherwise I get lost straight away.
grammar: 'Hábleme' – an usted command: 'hablar' swaps its -a ending for -e, then 'me' glues straight on the end.

target: Deme medio kilo de tomates y escoja los más firmes, por favor.
english: Give me half a kilo of tomatoes, and pick the firmest ones, please.
grammar: 'Deme' is 'dé' + 'me' written as one word – positive usted commands glue their pronouns on the end.

target: Por favor, mándeme a alguien que arregle la persiana. Se atascó a medio bajar.
english: Please send someone up to fix the blind – it's stuck halfway down.
grammar: 'Mándeme' – the usted command of 'mandar' swaps -a for -e and carries its pronoun on the tail.

target: ¡Talones abajo, hombros atrás y la vista al frente! Me lo voy repitiendo durante toda la clase.
english: Heels down, shoulders back, eyes up! I keep saying it to myself all through the lesson.
grammar: Riding-school commands can drop the verb: 'talones abajo' – noun plus direction does it, no verb required.

target: ¡Qué maravilla! ¡Es una absoluta maravilla!
english: How wonderful! It's an absolute marvel!
grammar: Exclaiming with 'qué' skips the article: '¡Qué maravilla!' – what a marvel, with no word for the a.

target: ¡Ponte el sombrero, que el sol de mediodía aquí quema de verdad!
english: Put your hat on – the midday sun here really does burn!
grammar: 'Ponte el sombrero, que' – after a command, 'que' slips in the reason: because the sun burns, no 'porque' needed.

target: Tapa la sartén un momento para que el vapor termine de cocinar las verduras.
english: Put the lid on the frying pan for a moment so the steam finishes cooking the vegetables.
grammar: 'Tapa la sartén' – bare commands aren't brusque in Spanish: kitchen and recipe talk runs on them.

target: ¡No limpies la pantalla con ese trapo! Busca el paño suave que venía en la caja.
english: Don't clean the screen with that rag! Find the soft cloth that came in the box.
grammar: 'No limpies' – a negative command flips to the -es form, while positive 'busca' keeps its plain shape.

target: Exprime el limón sobre la ensalada a última hora, así queda fresquita.
english: Squeeze the lemon over the salad at the last minute – that way it stays nice and fresh.
grammar: 'Exprime' is the tú command of 'exprimir' – -er and -ir verbs both close their command with -e.

target: ¡No te quedes parada en la orilla, que es peor! Eso les decimos a todas las que empiezan.
english: Don't stand about at the water's edge, it only makes it worse! That's what we tell anyone who's just starting.
grammar: 'No te quedes' – a negative command borrows the subjunctive form, and 'te' moves out in front of it.

target: Pica la cebolla bien finita y tenla lista antes de prender el fuego.
english: Chop the onion nice and fine and have it ready before you turn on the heat.
grammar: 'Tenla' – 'ten' is the irregular tú command of 'tener', with 'la' (the onion) riding on the end.

target: ¡No te olvides de apuntar los cumpleaños en el calendario nuevo, que luego pasan y ni cuenta nos damos!
english: Don't forget to put the birthdays in the new calendar – otherwise they go by and we don't even notice!
grammar: 'No te olvides' – negative commands take the subjunctive form: 'olvides', not 'olvidas'.

target: ¿No tienes frío? Ponte otra capa de ropa, por si acaso.
english: Aren't you cold? Put another layer on, just in case.
grammar: 'Ponte' – positive commands glue the pronoun onto the end; the negative splits it off: 'no te pongas'.

target: No metas el cuchillo bueno al lavaplatos, lávalo a mano y sécalo enseguida.
english: Don't put the good knife in the dishwasher – wash it by hand and dry it straight away.
grammar: 'No metas' – negative tú commands take the subjunctive form: 'metas', and plain 'no mete' won't do.

target: ¡Revisa que llevemos los pasaportes antes de salir de la casa!
english: Check we've got the passports before we leave the house!
grammar: 'Revisa que llevemos' – after a checking command, 'que' + subjunctive covers the outcome still to be confirmed.

target: ¡Tres horas dura la película que trajo Antoine! Y en ruso, claro.
english: Three hours long, the film Antoine's brought! And in Russian, of course.
grammar: 'Tres horas dura' – the startling bit jumps to the front, so the verb comes before 'la película' instead of after.

target: ¡Apúrese, que ya se puso en verde y este semáforo dura poquito!
english: Hurry up, it's just gone green and this light doesn't stay that way for long!
grammar: 'Apúrese' – the usted command of 'apurarse': pronoun glued on the end, accent keeping the stress put.

target: Mándame la foto por mensaje, que en la pantalla de la computadora la veo mucho mejor.
english: Send me the photo in a message – I can see it far better on the computer screen.
grammar: 'Mándame' – commands attach their pronoun to the end, and the extra syllable forces the written accent.

target: Pásame el destornillador, que la bisagra de la alacena está a punto de caerse.
english: Pass me the screwdriver – the cupboard hinge is about to come off.
grammar: 'Pásame' – positive commands carry their pronoun on the back: 'pasa' plus 'me' fused into one word.

target: Échale una pizca de sal a la sopa y pruébala antes de agregar más.
english: Add a pinch of salt to the soup and taste it before putting in any more.
grammar: 'Échale' and 'pruébala' – two commands in a row, each with its pronoun glued on the end, both pointing at the soup.

target: Saca la mantequilla del refri con tiempo, que si no, no se puede untar.
english: Get the butter out of the fridge in good time, otherwise it won't spread.
grammar: 'Que si no' – this 'que' is a spoken because: take it out in time, because otherwise it won't spread.

target: ¡Qué rico estuvo todo! Felicite al cocinero de nuestra parte.
english: Everything was delicious! Do give the chef our compliments.
grammar: 'Felicite' turns 'felicitar' into a polite order – the -a ending flips to -e for usted commands.

target: Tómese una tableta cada ocho horas y no la mezcle con alcohol.
english: Take one tablet every eight hours and don't mix it with alcohol.
grammar: 'Tómese' carries its pronoun on the end, but the negative sets it loose in front: 'no la mezcle'.

target: Ponga la olla a fuego medio y espere a que el agua suelte el hervor.
english: Put the saucepan on a medium heat and wait for the water to come to the boil.
grammar: 'Ponga' and 'espere' – usted commands swap vowels: -er verbs take an a, -ar verbs take an e.

target: Ese pan huele delicioso, ¡sácalo del horno antes de que se dore de más!
english: That bread smells delicious – take it out of the oven before it browns too much!
grammar: 'Sácalo' – the pronoun 'lo' glues onto a positive command, the added accent keeping the stress on 'sá'.

target: No te preocupes, que perder un bus acá no es el fin del mundo: sale otro cada hora.
english: Don't worry – missing a bus here isn't the end of the world; there's another every hour.
grammar: 'No te preocupes' – negative commands use the subjunctive form and keep the pronoun out front.

target: ¡Cómo hace llorar esta cebolla! Termina de picarla tú, por favor.
english: This onion really makes you cry! You finish chopping it, please.
grammar: 'Termina de picarla tú' – commands rarely need 'tú', so tacking it on after throws the stress onto who does it.

target: ¡No mires ahora! Los señores de la plaza nos están evaluando otra vez.
english: Don't look now! The gentlemen in the square are sizing us up again.
grammar: Negative commands change form: 'no mires' uses the subjunctive – the positive would be plain 'mira'.

target: Siéntese conmigo, por favor. Hay lugar de sobra y así conversamos un rato.
english: Do sit with me – there's plenty of room, and that way we can have a chat.
grammar: 'Siéntese' – positive commands glue the pronoun on the back: 'sentarse' gives 'siente' plus 'se', one word.

target: Guarda tu plata. Hoy invito yo y no se discute.
english: Put your money away – today it's on me and that's final.
grammar: 'Guarda tu plata' opens with a tú command – it looks exactly like the él/ella present form.

target: ¡No toques ese borde, que el óleo sigue fresco!
english: Don't touch that edge, the oil paint's still wet!
grammar: The tagged-on 'que' gives the reason: 'que el óleo sigue fresco' – a spoken because, common after commands.

target: ¡Cómo brilla el piso! ¿Con qué lo limpiaste?
english: How the floor shines! What did you clean it with?
grammar: '¡Cómo brilla el piso!' – accented 'cómo' + verb makes the exclamation: it marvels at how, no adjective needed.

target: ¡Cuidado con el escalón! Ah, no. Ya se cayó.
english: Mind the step! Ah, no. Down he goes.
grammar: '¡Cuidado con el escalón!' warns with just a noun – 'cuidado con' + the hazard, no verb required.

target: Apunte mi celular por si acaso: cero siete, ochenta y nueve, cuarenta y dos, sesenta y uno, treinta y cinco.
english: Take down my mobile number just in case: oh seven, eighty-nine, forty-two, sixty-one, thirty-five.
grammar: 'Apunte' is an usted command – the polite imperative borrows the subjunctive form, 'apunta' would be the tú one.

target: Prueba la salsa con una cuchara limpia, nunca con la que estás usando para revolver.
english: Taste the sauce with a clean spoon, never with the one you're using to stir.
grammar: 'Prueba' keeps the o→ue vowel change of 'probar' – commands inherit the present tense's stem shifts.

target: ¡Qué generoso de su parte! No tenía por qué molestarse, de verdad.
english: How generous of you! You really didn't have to go to any trouble.
grammar: '¡Qué generoso de su parte!' – 'qué' plus adjective makes a complete exclamation, no verb needed anywhere.

target: ¡Qué frío hace hoy! Llévate los guantes, que afuera está helando.
english: It's bitterly cold today – take your gloves; it's icy out there.
grammar: 'Qué frío hace hoy' – 'qué' + noun is the exclamation frame: what cold, where English says how cold.

target: Voy con veinte minutos de retraso. Empiecen sin mí, por favor.
english: I'm running twenty minutes late – please start without me.
grammar: 'Empiecen sin mí' – the ustedes command, LatAm's only plural you, with the -ar ending flipped to -en.

target: Pela los ajos debajo del chorro de agua fría, así no se te quedan pegados en los dedos.
english: Peel the garlic under cold running water – that way it doesn't stick to your fingers.
grammar: 'Pela' – affirmative tú commands borrow the él/ella present form: 'pela', not 'pelas'.

target: Discúlpeme la insistencia: revíseme la reserva otra vez, que en el correo me aparece otra fecha.
english: Forgive me for insisting – do check my booking again; the email shows a different date.
grammar: 'Revíseme' – the usted command with 'me' glued on, the written accent holding the stress in place.

target: Lava bien la lechuga hoja por hoja, que a veces trae tierra.
english: Give the lettuce a proper wash leaf by leaf – it sometimes has soil in it.
grammar: 'Lava bien' – 'bien' straight after a command is the standard way to say do it properly, give it a good wash.

target: Siga derecho tres cuadras y doble a la izquierda en el semáforo.
english: Carry straight on for three blocks and turn left at the lights.
grammar: 'Siga' and 'doble' show the polite-command swap – -ir verbs end in -a, -ar verbs in -e.

target: ¡Mira el tamaño de estas zanahorias! Arranca otras dos para la sopa.
english: Look at the size of these carrots! Pull up another two for the soup.
grammar: 'Mira el tamaño' works as an exclamation more than an order – the standard look-at-that opener.

target: ¡Mira qué azul tan profundo quedó al salir del horno!
english: Look how deep that blue has come out of the kiln!
grammar: 'Qué azul tan profundo' – exclamations run qué + noun + 'tan' + adjective, with 'tan' boosting the adjective.

target: ¡Tráigale otro flan a mi esposo, por favor! Es más fácil que discutir.
english: Bring my husband another crème caramel, please! It's easier than arguing.
grammar: 'Tráigale' – a formal usted command with 'le' glued on, and the written accent keeps the stress in place.

target: Apaga el wifi y vuelve a prenderlo. A veces con eso basta.
english: Switch the wifi off and back on – sometimes that's all it takes.
grammar: 'Apaga' and 'vuelve' are tú commands – simply the present forms 'apagas' and 'vuelves' minus the final -s.

target: ¡Esto quedó precioso! Pasen, pasen, y dejen los abrigos en el cuarto de al lado.
english: This has turned out lovely! Come in, come in – leave your coats in the room next door.
grammar: 'Pasen' and 'dejen' – commands to ustedes borrow the subjunctive form: one plural that covers every guest at once.

target: ¡Ahí va Ken otra vez con la moto! Con el casco bien puesto, eso sí.
english: There goes Ken again on the bike! Helmet firmly on, mind you.
grammar: 'Ahí va Ken' – there goes Ken: the place word leads and the verb comes before the name, much as in English.

target: Cuando empiece a subir la leche, baja el fuego para que no hierva.
english: When the milk starts to rise, turn the heat down so it doesn't boil.
grammar: 'Baja el fuego' – the tú command is simply the present 'bajas' minus its final -s.

target: Bájate conmigo en la próxima. Desde ahí queda a dos cuadras.
english: Get off with me at the next stop – it's two blocks from there.
grammar: 'Bájate' – the tú command of 'bajarse' (get off), with its 'te' glued on the end as positive commands do.

target: Por lo que cobran, esperaba que la lavandería me entregara la ropa el mismo día.
english: For what they charge, I expected the laundry to have my clothes back the same day.
grammar: 'Por lo que cobran' – 'por' marks the exchange: what you pay for what you get, classic 'por' ground.

target: En el sur de Inglaterra ya cultivan vino por el calentamiento global.
english: These days they grow wine in the south of England because of global warming.
grammar: Cause is 'por': 'por el calentamiento global' – because of the warming, where 'para' would make it a goal.

target: En la librería me cambiaron el libro por otro sin problema, para eso sirve guardar el recibo.
english: The bookshop swapped the book for another one without any bother, that's what keeping the receipt is for.
grammar: 'Por otro' – exchanges run on 'por', one book for another, while 'para eso sirve' states the receipt's use.

target: Cambié la computadora de escritorio por una portátil. Para llevarla de un cuarto a otro es una maravilla.
english: I swapped the desktop computer for a laptop. For carrying from room to room it's marvellous.
grammar: Exchanges take 'por': 'por una portátil' – while 'para llevarla' names what the new machine is for.

target: Para ser noviembre, el mar estaba de lo más amable esta mañana, ni los guantes de neopreno necesitamos.
english: For November the sea was surprisingly kind this morning, we didn't even need our neoprene gloves.
grammar: 'Para ser noviembre' – 'para' + 'ser' measures against expectations: kind, considering the month it is.

target: La sopa la hice para esta noche, pero por mí, sírvanse ya si tienen hambre.
english: I made the soup for tonight, but as far as I'm concerned you can help yourselves now if you're hungry.
grammar: 'Para esta noche' aims the soup at a time, 'por mí' means as far as I'm concerned – target versus stance.

target: Salimos con tiempo para no andar con afán, por estas calles empedradas no se puede correr.
english: We set off in good time so as not to be rushing – you can't hurry on these cobbled streets.
grammar: 'Para no andar con afán' names the aim, 'por estas calles' the ground covered – purpose against route.

target: Para ser aprendiz de carpintero, maneja las herramientas con muchísima seguridad.
english: For a carpenter's apprentice, he handles the tools with remarkable confidence.
grammar: 'Para ser aprendiz' – 'para' + ser sets the yardstick: judged against what you'd expect of an apprentice.

target: Salgo a nadar por la mañana temprano y dejo los quehaceres para la tarde.
english: I go for my swim early in the morning and leave the housework for the afternoon.
grammar: 'Por la mañana' is time you move through, 'para la tarde' a slot tasks are saved for – through versus toward.

target: Para nuestra familia, la Pascua tiene una capa extra de significado por lo de Floppy.
english: For our family, Easter carries an extra layer of meaning because of the Floppy business.
grammar: 'Para nuestra familia' marks whose view it is, 'por lo de Floppy' the cause – 'por' and 'para' split the labour.

target: Por correo normal el paquete cuesta seis libras, pero para el viernes me cobran doce.
english: By ordinary post the parcel costs six pounds, but to get it there for Friday they charge twelve.
grammar: 'Por correo' marks the means of sending – 'para el viernes' marks the deadline aimed at, route versus target.

target: Pagué una fortuna por esta camisa y a la segunda lavada perdió un botón.
english: I paid a fortune for this shirt and by the second wash it had lost a button.
grammar: 'Pagué una fortuna por esta camisa' – paying is an exchange, so the price travels with 'por', not 'para'.

target: A Angela no le convence el aire acondicionado por lo que implica para el clima.
english: Angela doesn't like the idea of air conditioning because of its climate implications.
grammar: 'Por lo que implica' gives the cause; 'para el clima' names what's affected – the classic 'por'/'para' split.

target: Pedí el presupuesto por escrito, para mi tranquilidad más que nada.
english: I asked for the quote in writing, for my own peace of mind more than anything.
grammar: 'Por escrito' is the set phrase for in writing – the medium takes 'por', the purpose 'para mi tranquilidad'.

target: Para mi gusto, a la feria hay que ir a primera hora, por la tarde ya no queda lo bueno.
english: If you ask me, you want to get to the market first thing, by the afternoon all the good stuff has gone.
grammar: 'Para mi gusto' means for my taste – opinions run on 'para', while 'por la tarde' is plain time of day.

target: ¿Andas por el centro todavía? Voy para allá en diez minutos y nos tomamos un café.
english: Are you still around the centre of town? I'm heading that way in ten minutes and we can have a coffee.
grammar: 'Por el centro' is a rough whereabouts, 'para allá' a direction headed for – area versus destination.

target: Compré un kilo de zanahorias por muy poca plata, y me alcanzan para toda la semana.
english: I got a kilo of carrots for very little money, and they'll see me through the whole week.
grammar: 'Por muy poca plata' – 'por' prices the exchange, while 'para toda la semana' marks the stretch covered.

target: El termo no es para el café, es para el agua caliente que me echo en los pies al salir.
english: The flask isn't for coffee, it's for the hot water I pour over my feet when I get out.
grammar: Intended use is 'para': 'no es para el café' – what the flask is for, where 'por' would give a cause.

target: El azulejo con la esquina rota lo uso para probar los colores antes de arriesgar una pieza buena.
english: I use the tile with the broken corner for testing colours before risking a good piece.
grammar: 'Para probar' – 'para' + infinitive expresses purpose, English's in order to in one small word.

target: Estas botas no son para la lluvia: son de gamuza y se manchan con nada.
english: These boots aren't for the rain – they're suede and they mark at the slightest thing.
grammar: 'Son de gamuza' – material takes a plain 'de': boots of suede, with no made-of verb needed in between.

target: Un abrigo liviano te sirve para casi todo el año aquí, rara vez baja de diez grados.
english: A light coat will do you for most of the year here – it rarely drops below ten degrees.
grammar: 'Para casi todo el año' – 'para' can stretch over a span of time, marking how long the coat is meant to serve.

target: ¿Puedo pagar la consulta con este seguro de viaje, o tengo que pagar por adelantado y pedir reembolso?
english: Can I pay for the appointment with this travel insurance, or do I pay upfront and claim it back?
grammar: 'Por adelantado' – 'por' covers the manner of an action: paying in advance, the same 'por' as in 'por correo'.

target: Para las cosas importantes prefiero llamar, y el chat lo dejo para mandar fotos y avisos cortos.
english: For anything important I'd rather ring – I keep the chat for photos and quick updates.
grammar: 'Para las cosas importantes' – 'para' marks purpose, what calling is for. Cause or exchange would take 'por'.

target: Los guantes finos no sirven para manejar en la madrugada, el volante amanece helado.
english: Thin gloves are no use for driving before dawn – the steering wheel is ice-cold first thing.
grammar: 'No sirven para manejar' – 'servir para' names the job something is (or isn't) up to, purpose riding on 'para'.

target: Necesito azulejos de quince por quince para el baño, y por metro cuadrado entran más de cuarenta.
english: I need fifteen-by-fifteen tiles for the bathroom, and you get more than forty to the square metre.
grammar: 'Por metro cuadrado' – rates and measures ride on 'por', the same 'por' that multiplies 'quince por quince'.

target: Para un retrato trabajo con fotos, pero para un paisaje prefiero plantarme delante con el caballete.
english: For a portrait I'll work from photographs, but for a landscape I'd rather set up in front of it with my easel.
grammar: 'Para un retrato' – 'para' names the intended end product, the purpose side of the por/para split.

target: Equivocarse de registro arruina una traducción: lo que sirve para un discurso no sirve para un folleto.
english: Getting the register wrong ruins a translation: what works for a speech doesn't work for a leaflet.
grammar: 'Sirve para un discurso' – 'servir para' states what something is fit for, with 'para' pointing at the intended use.

target: Para mí, el secreto de un buen guiso pasa por el fuego lento, no por la cantidad de condimentos.
english: For me, the secret of a good stew comes down to slow cooking, not how much seasoning goes in.
grammar: 'Pasa por el fuego lento' – 'pasar por' says what something comes down to, 'por' marking the route it runs through.

target: La traducción me ha servido para aprender vocabulario de mil temas, por eso pocas palabras me agarran por sorpresa.
english: Translation has taught me vocabulary on all sorts of subjects, that's why words hardly ever catch me out.
grammar: 'Ha servido para' – usefulness points forward at a purpose, which is exactly the job 'para' does.

target: Vine sobre todo por los paisajes, pero me quedo por la comida.
english: I came mainly for the scenery, but it's the food that's keeping me here.
grammar: 'Por los paisajes', 'por la comida' – 'por' names the motive each time: because-of, where a goal takes 'para'.

target: Siempre cruzamos con el carro lleno: herramientas para la casa, cuadros para regalar y té para los primeros días.
english: We always cross with the car full: tools for the house, paintings to give away and tea for the first few days.
grammar: 'Para la casa', 'para regalar' – each 'para' tags a destination, labelling what every item in the carload is for.

target: Por ahora me conformo con el trote, pero para el verano quiero animarme a galopar en campo abierto.
english: For now I'm happy with trotting, but by the summer I want to work up to a canter in open country.
grammar: 'Por ahora' is a loose for now, 'para el verano' a firm deadline – vague time takes 'por', a target takes 'para'.

target: Trajimos flores para la mesa principal y, por si acaso, un mantel de repuesto.
english: We brought flowers for the main table and, just in case, a spare tablecloth.
grammar: 'Para la mesa principal' points at a destination, while 'por si acaso' is a set por phrase: just in case.

target: Le dejé una copia de la llave a la vecina por si acaso, una nunca sabe cuándo hará falta.
english: I've left a spare key with the neighbour just in case, you never know when it'll be needed.
grammar: 'Por si acaso' is a fixed phrase – 'por' + 'si' literally reads for if, Spanish's standard just in case.

target: Por estas fechas del año pasado todavía andábamos de manga corta, para mí que las estaciones se están corriendo.
english: This time last year we were still in short sleeves – if you ask me, the seasons are shifting.
grammar: 'Por estas fechas' – 'por' marks a loose zone in time, around these dates, where 'para' would set a deadline.

target: Para mí el pescado del día, y de tomar, una limonada sin azúcar.
english: The fish of the day for me, and a sugar-free lemonade to drink.
grammar: 'Para mí' points the dish at its destination – 'para' marks who something is meant for.

target: Este cuadro no es para vender, lo pinté por el puro gusto de pintarlo.
english: This painting isn't for selling, I painted it for the sheer pleasure of it.
grammar: 'Para vender' is intended use, 'por el puro gusto' the motive – purpose looks forward, cause looks back.

target: Vine por especias para llevar a casa. ¿Cuáles aguantan bien el viaje?
english: I've come for spices to take home – which ones travel well?
grammar: 'Vine por especias' – 'por' marks what you came to fetch, while 'para llevar' gives the purpose.

target: Compré este adaptador para los enchufes de acá, pero por alguna razón carga solo a ratos.
english: I bought this adapter for the local sockets, but for some reason it only charges in fits and starts.
grammar: 'Para los enchufes' marks the intended use, 'por alguna razón' the cause – purpose 'para', reason 'por'.

target: Estos azulejos son para el baño de una amiga, los hice por encargo.
english: These tiles are for a friend's bathroom, I made them to order.
grammar: 'Para el baño' – 'para' points at a destination or recipient: who or what the tiles are meant for.

target: Para las videollamadas de trabajo uso audífonos: por el parlante del celular no se entiende nada.
english: For work video calls I use headphones: you can't make anything out through the phone's speaker.
grammar: Sound travels 'por': 'por el parlante' – 'por' marks the channel something comes through, not its purpose.

target: Dejé toallas limpias en el baño para ustedes, y por si refresca hay una cobija extra en el armario.
english: I've left clean towels in the bathroom for you, and in case it turns chilly there's a spare blanket in the wardrobe.
grammar: 'Para ustedes' aims the towels at a recipient – 'por si refresca' gives a possible reason, and reasons take 'por'.

target: ¿Cuánto cobran de comisión por retirar con una tarjeta extranjera?
english: How much commission do you charge for withdrawing on a foreign card?
grammar: 'Por retirar' – 'por' prices the action: the fee is what you pay in exchange for withdrawing.

target: Para estrategia, paciencia y ortografía de nombres raros, no hay escuela como Pokémon.
english: For strategy, patience and the spelling of strange names, there's no school like Pokémon.
grammar: 'Para estrategia' – 'para' here means when it comes to: it names the arena, while cause would take 'por'.

target: ¿Puedes pasar por mí a las ocho? Mi carro sigue en el taller.
english: Can you pick me up at eight? My car's still at the garage.
grammar: In Latin America 'pasar por mí' means pick me up – you come by for the person, so it takes 'por', not 'para'.

target: ¿Cuánto me cobra por llevarme al centro? Prefiero acordar el precio antes de subir.
english: How much would you charge to take me into the centre? I'd rather agree the price before getting in.
grammar: 'Antes de subir' – after a preposition Spanish uses the infinitive, never an -ing form.

target: A Ken le gusta salir en moto, pero de ahí a Hell's Angel hay un buen trecho.
english: Ken likes going out on his motorbike, but it's a fair stretch from there to Hell's Angel.
grammar: 'de ahí a' sets up a distance – paired with 'hay un buen trecho', Spanish measures how far one idea is from another.

target: El camarote lo pagamos sobre todo por descansar un rato, el cruce se hace largo.
english: We pay for the cabin mostly so we can get some rest, the crossing does drag on.
grammar: 'Por descansar' – 'por' + infinitive names the motive behind the paying, where 'para' would point at a goal.

target: Pasamos por el bosque y salimos a las colinas justo cuando se levantaba la niebla.
english: We went through the woods and came out onto the hills just as the mist was lifting.
grammar: Movement through a space takes 'por': 'pasamos por el bosque' – the woods are the route, not the destination.

target: Por culpa del Brexit, ahora necesitamos visados para las estadías largas.
english: Because of Brexit, we now need visas for longer stays.
grammar: 'Por culpa del Brexit' – 'por culpa de' is because of with blame built in.

target: Los lentes oscuros no son para manejar de noche, son para el sol fuerte del mediodía.
english: Dark glasses aren't for driving at night – they're for the strong midday sun.
grammar: 'No son para manejar' and 'para el sol' – both 'para's mark intended use: what the glasses are for, and not for.

target: Me enteré por la radio de que habrá huelga de trenes, así que mejor dejamos la salida para otra semana.
english: I heard on the radio there's going to be a train strike, so we'd better put the outing off to another week.
grammar: 'Por la radio' is the channel the news arrived through, 'para otra semana' the new target date – source versus aim.

target: Para la boda del sábado alquilé un sombrero, comprarlo para un solo día no tenía sentido.
english: For the wedding on Saturday I hired a hat – buying one for a single day made no sense.
grammar: 'Para la boda' – 'para' marks what the hat was destined for: events and purposes, not causes, take 'para'.

target: Para la audioguía de la Torre tuve que investigar muchísimo: fechas, nombres, leyendas, todo.
english: For the Tower audioguide I had to research a huge amount: dates, names, legends, all of it.
grammar: Work aimed at a goal takes 'para': 'para la audioguía' – the research had a destination.

target: Para mí, estas cosas se arreglan mejor por teléfono, los mensajes se prestan a malentendidos.
english: To my mind these things are better sorted over the phone, messages lead to misunderstandings.
grammar: 'Por teléfono' – 'por' marks the channel things travel through, while 'para mí' holds the opinion.

target: Para caminatas suaves con vistas largas, pocos lugares superan los South Downs.
english: For gentle walks with long views, few places beat the South Downs.
grammar: 'Para caminatas suaves' – 'para' marks what something is for: purpose and suitability, where 'por' would give cause.

target: En La Paz cuesta respirar al principio por la altura.
english: In La Paz it's hard to breathe at first because of the altitude.
grammar: If something's a struggle, use 'costar': 'cuesta respirar' – breathing is hard at first.

target: De vuelta pasé por la panadería y compré pan para el desayuno, todavía estaba tibio.
english: On the way back I stopped by the bakery and got bread for breakfast, it was still warm.
grammar: 'Pasé por la panadería' is a route via a place, 'para el desayuno' the bread's destination – por path, para goal.

target: Prefiero manejar por la carretera de la costa, se tarda más, pero para mí el paisaje lo vale.
english: I prefer driving along the coast road, it takes longer, but for me the views are worth it.
grammar: 'Por la carretera' – 'por' traces the route travelled along, while 'para mí' merely tags whose view it is.

target: Compré este pincel finito para los detalles del retrato: para cubrir el fondo uso uno ancho.
english: I bought this fine little brush for the detail on the portrait: for covering the background I use a wide one.
grammar: Purpose runs on 'para': 'para los detalles' and 'para cubrir' – what each brush is for, noun or infinitive.

target: Hago cursos cada tanto para mantener al día mis habilidades de traducción.
english: I go on courses every so often to keep my translation skills up to date.
grammar: Purpose takes 'para': 'para mantener al día' – in order to, the goal half of the 'por'/'para' pair.

target: Ken siempre quiere salir con dos horas de margen para el ferry, así que llegamos antes que nadie.
english: Ken always wants to leave two hours' leeway for the ferry, so we get there before anyone else.
grammar: 'Para el ferry' – 'para' points the leeway at its purpose, where 'por' would give the reason behind it.

target: Cambié el aguarrás por un disolvente sin olor, más que nada por el bien de la casa.
english: I swapped the turpentine for an odourless solvent, mostly for the sake of everyone at home.
grammar: Swaps use 'por': 'cambié el aguarrás por' – 'por' marks an exchange, one thing traded for another.

target: ¿Eso queda por el centro o para el lado del mercado? Las direcciones todavía se me complican.
english: Is that near the centre or out towards the market? Directions still trip me up.
grammar: 'Por el centro' means roughly around there, 'para el lado del mercado' points that way – area versus direction.

target: Encargué el ramo para el sábado, lo recojo el viernes a última hora.
english: I've ordered the bouquet for Saturday, I'm collecting it last thing on Friday.
grammar: 'Para el sábado' – 'para' sets the deadline the order must meet, not the day the ordering happened.

target: Gracias por traerme las manzanas, no tenías que molestarte para nada.
english: Thanks for bringing the apples over, you really needn't have gone to any trouble.
grammar: 'Gracias por traerme' – thanks name their cause with 'por', and the verb after it stays an infinitive.

target: ¿De veras salió tan barato? Por ese precio en Inglaterra no te dan ni un café.
english: Seriously, it came to that little? For that price in England you wouldn't even get a coffee.
grammar: 'Por ese precio' – 'por' handles exchange: this for that, money one way and the goods the other.

target: La casa se ve sencilla por fuera, pero por dentro es luminosa y perfecta para recibir visitas.
english: The house looks plain from the outside, but inside it's light and perfect for having people round.
grammar: 'Por fuera' and 'por dentro' mean on the outside and on the inside – rough whereabouts always ride on 'por'.

target: Compré la maleta chica para llevarla en cabina, pero igual me pasé por dos kilos.
english: I bought the small case to take in the cabin, but I still went over by two kilos.
grammar: Purpose takes 'para llevarla', but the margin takes 'por': 'me pasé por dos kilos' – over by two kilos.

target: Para ser alguien que empezó tan tarde, no voy nada mal, o al menos eso me dicen en el establo.
english: For someone who started so late I'm not doing badly at all, or at least that's what they tell me at the yard.
grammar: This 'para' means considering: 'para ser alguien que empezó tan tarde' – measured against what you'd expect.

target: Estaba por llamarte, me ganaste por un par de minutos.
english: I was just about to ring you, you beat me to it by a couple of minutes.
grammar: 'Estaba por llamarte' – in Latin America 'estar por' + a verb means to be just about to do it.

target: La verdad es que Charles de Gaulle hizo mucho por Francia.
english: The truth is, Charles de Gaulle did a lot for France.
grammar: 'Por' marks who benefits: 'hizo mucho por Francia' – doing something for France's sake is 'por', not 'para'.

target: Para monumentos y glamur, no hay como Swansea.
english: For monuments and glamour, there's nowhere like Swansea.
grammar: 'Para monumentos y glamur' – this 'para' stakes out the field being judged: as far as monuments go.

target: ¿Se le acabó la harina? Tengo de sobra, se la llevo en un momento.
english: Run out of flour? I've got plenty – I'll bring you some over in a minute.
grammar: '¿Se le acabó la harina?' – the flour ran out on you: 'le' marks the person affected, 'se' makes it nobody's fault.

target: Sobró bastante queso de la reunión, ¿te lo envuelvo para que te lo lleves?
english: There's a fair bit of cheese left over from the get-together – shall I wrap it up for you to take home?
grammar: 'Te lo envuelvo' and 'te lo lleves' – each verb gets its own pronoun pair, Spanish never leaves them out.

target: Nadie sabe cómo lo hace, pero Benoît siempre se las arregla para ganar.
english: Nobody knows how he does it, but Benoît always manages to win.
grammar: 'Se las arregla' – 'arreglárselas' means to manage, with a fixed 'las' that points at nothing at all.

target: La cuenta, por favor, ¿y nos la puede dividir en dos?
english: The bill, please – and could you split it between the two of us?
grammar: 'Nos la puede dividir' – 'nos' (for us) sits before 'la' (it, the bill), both ahead of the verb.

target: Me temo que la cuenta no está bien: nos cobraron dos veces el postre.
english: I'm afraid the bill isn't right – we've been charged for the pudding twice.
grammar: 'Nos cobraron dos veces' – 'cobrar' takes the person as 'nos': the double charge lands on us.

target: Se nos hizo tarde por el tráfico. ¿Todavía nos guardan la mesa?
english: We've been held up by the traffic – are you still holding our table?
grammar: 'Se nos hizo tarde' – the 'se' + 'nos' combo shifts the blame: lateness just happened to us, nobody's fault.

target: Nos regalaron un montón de manzanas, así que se las estoy repartiendo a medio edificio.
english: We were given a mountain of apples, so I'm handing them out to half the building.
grammar: 'Se las estoy repartiendo' – the pronouns can sit up front like this, or glue onto the end: 'estoy repartiéndoselas'.

target: Le mandé los documentos tres veces, y las tres veces 'se le traspapelaron'.
english: I sent him the documents three times, and all three times they 'got mislaid'.
grammar: 'Se le traspapelaron' – the no-fault 'se': the papers mislaid themselves, and 'le' marks who it hit.

target: La aplicación de mi hijo me ayuda a repasar todos los días.
english: My son's app helps me revise every day.
grammar: The verb 'ayudar' needs 'a' before an infinitive: 'me ayuda a repasar' = it helps me revise.

target: Si llega un paquete a mi nombre, ¿me lo pueden subir a la habitación?
english: If a parcel arrives in my name, could you bring it up to my room?
grammar: 'Me lo pueden subir' – pronoun order is fixed: 'me' (to me) always lands before 'lo' (the parcel).

target: Perdón, no le entendí el apellido. ¿Me lo deletrea?
english: Sorry, I didn't catch your surname – could you spell it for me?
grammar: '¿Me lo deletrea?' – two pronouns keep a fixed order, to-me before it: always 'me lo', never 'lo me'.

target: Pierre es consciente de los riesgos y los sopesa con cuidado.
english: Pierre is aware of the risks and weighs them carefully.
grammar: 'Los sopesa' – the 'los' picks up 'los riesgos', so the risks don't need naming twice.

target: A mi vecina le encantaron los azulejos, así que se los regalé para la entrada de su casa.
english: My neighbour loved the tiles, so I gave them to her for her hallway.
grammar: 'A mi vecina le encantaron' – Spanish names the enjoyer twice, the noun phrase plus its echo pronoun 'le'.

target: A Antoine le regalaron una de las obras de algas de Beni y le encantó.
english: Antoine was given one of Beni's seaweed pieces as a present and he loved it.
grammar: 'A Antoine le regalaron' – the receiver is named twice, pronoun and noun: Spanish doubles the indirect object.

target: Estos pinceles me los regalaron hace años, y siguen siendo los que más cuido.
english: These brushes were a gift years ago, and they're still the ones I look after best.
grammar: 'Estos pinceles me los regalaron' – putting the object first forces the echo pronoun 'los' before the verb.

target: Me gusta saber qué pasa en la vida de mis hijos, y ellos me lo cuentan casi todo.
english: I like knowing what's going on in my sons' lives – and they tell me almost everything.
grammar: 'Me lo cuentan' – with two pronouns the person comes first: 'me' (to me) before 'lo' (it), never the reverse.

target: ¿El impuesto de salida ya viene incluido en el boleto o se lo pago directamente a la aerolínea?
english: Is the departure tax already included in the ticket, or do I pay it to the airline directly?
grammar: 'Se lo pago' – 'le' (to the airline) becomes 'se' in front of 'lo': Spanish never stacks two l-pronouns.

target: Los llevaba a todas sus actividades y, de alguna manera, siempre llegábamos a tiempo.
english: I took them to all their activities, and somehow we always made it on time.
grammar: The 'los' in 'los llevaba' stands for the boys – object pronouns go in front of a conjugated verb.

target: Si me deja su número, se lo paso al resto del grupo para lo de mañana.
english: If you give me your number, I'll pass it on to the rest of the group for tomorrow.
grammar: 'Se lo paso' – 'le' becomes 'se' when 'lo' follows: Spanish never says 'le lo', the pair is always 'se lo'.

target: ¿La fecha de la reunión? No se preocupe, ahorita se la mando por mensaje, la tengo anotada en la agenda.
english: The date of the meeting? Don't worry, I'll send it over by message in a moment – I've got it noted in my diary.
grammar: 'Se la mando' – 'le' turns into 'se' before 'la': Spanish refuses 'le la', so to-you plus it comes out 'se la'.

target: El cuarto de arriba en Marescot lo tenemos para los invitados, así que avisen con tiempo.
english: The upstairs room at Marescot is kept for guests, so let us know in good time.
grammar: 'El cuarto... lo tenemos' – when the object moves to the front, Spanish repeats it as a pronoun before the verb.

target: A Swonky se le reconoce desde lejos por el cuello, ningún otro cisne del río lo tiene así.
english: You can tell Swonky from a distance by his neck, no other swan on the river has one like it.
grammar: 'Se le reconoce' – impersonal 'se' plus the pronoun 'le': people in general can tell him apart.

target: La cincha hay que revisarla dos veces: te lo enseñan el primer día y no se te olvida más.
english: You check the girth twice: they teach you that on day one and you never forget it.
grammar: Fronting the object leaves a pronoun behind: 'la cincha hay que revisarla' – 'la' picks the girth back up.

target: ¿Y tu bufanda? Te la quitaste en el restaurante y seguro quedó en el respaldo de la silla.
english: What about your scarf? You took it off in the restaurant and it's bound to still be on the back of the chair.
grammar: 'Te la quitaste' – two pronouns queue in fixed order, person before thing: 'te' (you) ahead of 'la' (the scarf).

target: En esta casa les ponemos nombres de políticos a los platos.
english: In this house we name our dishes after politicians.
grammar: The pronoun 'les' doubles 'a los platos' – Spanish names the indirect object twice, pronoun plus noun.

target: El año pasado me tocó a mí acompañarlo, y la iglesia estaba helada.
english: Last year it was my turn to go with him, and the church was freezing.
grammar: 'Me tocó a mí' – 'a mí' doubles the 'me' purely for stress: it fell to me, and no one else.

target: Cuando algo se rompe en la casa, se lo damos a Ken y en unos días está como nuevo.
english: When something breaks in the house we hand it to Ken, and within a few days it's as good as new.
grammar: 'se lo damos a Ken' – 'le' becomes 'se' in front of 'lo': Spanish never lets two l-pronouns sit side by side.

target: Ya me siento mucho mejor: el malestar de estómago se me pasó con el té que me diste.
english: I'm feeling much better now – my dodgy stomach settled down with that tea you gave me.
grammar: 'Se me pasó' – Spanish lets ailments pass by themselves, with 'me' marking whom it happened to.

target: Hay que dejar secar la arcilla antes de meterla al horno.
english: You have to let the clay dry before putting it in the kiln.
grammar: 'Meterla' – the pronoun 'la' (the clay) glues to the infinitive's end, verb and object in one word.

target: Pinté un retrato para una amiga y se lo entregué ya enmarcado.
english: I painted a portrait for a friend and handed it over already framed.
grammar: 'Le' and 'lo' can't sit together, so 'le' becomes 'se': 'se lo entregué' – handed it to her.

target: Las hembras de zorro nos dejan sus regalitos en el jardín, y el pasto quemado lo confirma.
english: The vixens leave us their little presents in the garden, and the scorched grass confirms it.
grammar: 'lo confirma' – this 'lo' points at a whole idea, not one noun: Spanish lets a pronoun stand for a clause.

target: ¿Quiere la receta? Se la mando por mensaje ahora mismo, es cortita.
english: Would you like the recipe? I'll send it to you by message right now – it's a short one.
grammar: 'Se la mando' – 'le' becomes 'se' when 'la' (the recipe) follows: two l-pronouns never sit together.

target: Ese cuchillo hay que afilarlo cada tanto, si no, termina aplastando el tomate en vez de cortarlo.
english: That knife needs sharpening every so often, otherwise it ends up squashing the tomato instead of slicing it.
grammar: 'Ese cuchillo hay que afilarlo' – the knife comes first, and 'lo' picks it back up at the end of the verb.

target: Quedaron buenísimos los frijoles, voy a congelar la mitad y me los guardo para la semana.
english: The beans turned out really good – I'm going to freeze half and keep them for the week.
grammar: 'Me los guardo' – the extra 'me' means for-myself: keeping them for my own use, with 'los' standing for the beans.

target: ¿Me pesa estas uvas? Si están dulces, me las llevo todas.
english: Would you weigh these grapes for me? If they're sweet I'll take the lot.
grammar: 'Me las llevo' lines up its pronouns – 'me' (for myself) always comes before 'las' (them).

target: Ken les hizo a los niños una preciosa arca de Noé de madera. Era amarilla y roja.
english: Ken made the kids a lovely wooden Noah's ark – it was yellow and red.
grammar: 'Una preciosa arca' – on its own it's 'un arca', but an adjective in between brings the usual 'una' back.

target: Este atajo me lo enseñó el señor de la ferretería, y ahora yo se lo enseño a todo el mundo.
english: The man at the hardware shop showed me this shortcut, and now I show it to everybody.
grammar: 'Este atajo me lo enseñó' – once the object jumps to the front, 'lo' must repeat it before the verb.

target: Mi esposo habla mucho de lo que le gustan los arenques ahumados, pero en realidad nunca los come. ¿Cómo se explica eso?
english: My husband talks a big game about liking kippers, but he never really eats them – what's that about?
grammar: The pronoun 'los' (them – the kippers) goes before the verb: 'nunca los come' = he never eats them.

target: Se me descompuso la lavadora justo cuando tenía una montaña de ropa por lavar.
english: The washing machine broke down on me just when I had a mountain of washing to do.
grammar: 'Se me descompuso' – the machine broke on its own, and 'me' pins the bad luck on its owner.

target: Son muchas naranjas para cargar, ¿me las pone en dos bolsas, por favor?
english: That's a lot of oranges to carry – could you put them in two bags for me, please?
grammar: 'Me las pone en dos bolsas' – two pronouns stack person-first: 'me' (for me) before 'las' (the oranges).

target: Déjame la toalla en la piedra plana, que yo la recojo cuando salga.
english: Leave my towel on the flat stone, I'll pick it up when I come out.
grammar: 'Déjame la toalla' – the glued-on 'me' means for me: Spanish builds leave-it-for-me into the verb.

target: Tiene sentido alquilarles un ala de la casa de Josselin a los huéspedes.
english: Renting out a wing of the house at Josselin to guests makes sense.
grammar: Even with 'a los huéspedes' spelled out, the 'les' stays glued to 'alquilarles' – Spanish likes the double mention.

target: Me sobraron dos metros de tela y se los llevé a la costurera, me va a hacer dos cojines para el sofá.
english: I had two metres of fabric left over and took it to the seamstress, she's making me two cushions for the sofa.
grammar: 'Se los llevé' – pronoun order is fixed, person before thing: 'se' the seamstress, then 'los' the fabric.

target: Al plomero ya le pagamos la mitad: el resto se lo damos cuando termine el trabajo.
english: We've already paid the plumber half – we'll give him the rest when he finishes the job.
grammar: 'Se lo damos' – 'le' would collide with 'lo', and Spanish never stacks two l-pronouns, so 'le' becomes 'se'.

target: Las fotos del paseo me las mandó mi hijo anoche, y esta mañana se las reenvié al resto de la familia.
english: My son sent me the photos from the walk last night, and this morning I forwarded them on to the rest of the family.
grammar: 'Se las reenvié' – 'les' changes to 'se' before 'las', two pronouns starting with l- can't sit side by side.

target: Antoine le llenó la espalda de ganchos de ropa a Pierre para convertirlo en erizo.
english: Antoine covered Pierre's back in clothes pegs to turn him into a hedgehog.
grammar: Body parts skip 'su': 'le llenó la espalda' – the 'le' already says whose back it was.

target: ¿Me pasas el tenedor grande? Lo necesito para darle vuelta a la carne.
english: Can you pass me the big fork? I need it to turn the meat over.
grammar: 'Lo necesito' but 'darle vuelta' – pronouns sit before a conjugated verb and hang after an infinitive.

target: El vestido rosado me lo probé ayer y hoy vengo decidida a llevármelo.
english: I tried the pink dress on yesterday, and today I've come back determined to take it.
grammar: 'El vestido rosado me lo probé' – when the object opens the sentence, Spanish repeats it as 'lo' before the verb.

target: El archivo se lo adjunté al correo esta mañana. Si no le aparece, con gusto se lo reenvío.
english: I attached the file to the email this morning. If it hasn't come through, I'll gladly send it again.
grammar: 'Se lo adjunté' – Spanish never says le lo: in front of 'lo', the 'le' changes to 'se'.

target: ¿El comprobante me lo pueden mandar por correo electrónico? Así no lo pierdo.
english: Could you send me the receipt by email? That way I won't lose it.
grammar: 'El comprobante me lo pueden mandar' – front the noun and 'lo' echoes it: Spanish says the object twice.

target: Nada de tirar el aceite usado por el desagüe: déjalo enfriar y bótalo a la basura.
english: None of this pouring used oil down the drain – let it cool and put it in the bin.
grammar: 'Déjalo enfriar' – the pronoun hangs off the command 'deja', not off the infinitive that follows.

target: Todo lo que Antoine sabe de la vida se lo enseñó Pokémon.
english: Everything Antoine knows about life, Pokémon taught him.
grammar: 'Se lo enseñó' – 'le' becomes 'se' whenever it lands next to 'lo': two l-pronouns never sit side by side.

target: Se me acabaron las pastillas para la presión y necesito comprar más antes del fin de semana.
english: I've run out of my blood pressure tablets and need to buy more before the weekend.
grammar: 'Se me acabaron' – the no-fault 'se': the tablets ran out by themselves, and 'me' marks who it happened to.

target: Pierre ayuda a conseguirles vivienda a las personas sin hogar.
english: Pierre helps house homeless people.
grammar: 'Conseguirles' already means get-for-them – the 'les' stays even with 'a las personas' spelled out.

target: Los huevos ya están batidos, mézclalos con la harina poco a poco.
english: The eggs are already beaten – mix them into the flour little by little.
grammar: 'Mézclalos' – 'los' is the eggs from the sentence before: object pronouns pick up what was just named.

target: Las llaves de la casa de Bretaña se las dejamos a una vecina que nos avisa si algo pasa.
english: We leave the keys to the Brittany house with a neighbour, who lets us know if anything happens.
grammar: 'Se las dejamos' – 'le' (to the neighbour) becomes 'se' in front of 'las': Spanish never allows 'le las'.

target: ¿Tiene cambio de un billete de cien? Nadie me lo quiere recibir.
english: Do you have change for a hundred? Nobody will take it off me.
grammar: 'Me lo quiere recibir' – the pronoun pair climbs ahead of 'quiere' instead of hanging off 'recibir'.

target: Estar en Bretaña nos facilita mucho ver a la familia.
english: Being in Brittany makes it much easier to see family.
grammar: Spanish slips an 'a' in before people: 'ver a la familia' – the 'a' adds no meaning, but it's required.

target: Cuando hay una exposición buena, se lo comento a mis amigas y armamos grupo.
english: When there's a good exhibition on, I mention it to my friends and we make a group of it.
grammar: Before 'lo', the pronoun 'les' turns into 'se': 'se lo comento a mis amigas' – never 'les lo'.

target: A los dueños de casa les trajimos un detalle, ¿se lo damos ahora o al final?
english: We've brought the hosts a little something – shall we give it to them now or at the end?
grammar: 'Se lo damos' – 'les' can't stand before 'lo', so it turns into 'se': se lo, never 'les lo'.

target: A Lassie la saca a pasear Dave todas las mañanas, sin falta.
english: Dave takes Lassie out for her walk every morning, without fail.
grammar: 'A Lassie la saca' – when the object opens the sentence, a pronoun must echo it: 'la' doubles Lassie.

target: Pierre les ponía nombres rarísimos a sus peluches: Alavanille, Courtpartout, Sautepartout.
english: Pierre used to give his soft toys the strangest names: Alavanille, Courtpartout, Sautepartout.
grammar: The 'les' points ahead to 'a sus peluches' – Spanish doubles an indirect object as pronoun and full noun.

target: La dirección me la apuntó el recepcionista en un papel, por si el celular se quedaba sin batería.
english: The receptionist jotted the address down for me on paper, in case my phone died.
grammar: Starting with 'la dirección' forces an echo: 'me la apuntó' – 'la' repeats the fronted address before the verb.

target: Pierre cuenta chistes buenísimos y nos hace reír muchísimo.
english: Pierre tells excellent jokes and makes us all laugh a lot.
grammar: 'Nos hace reír' – 'hacer' + infinitive builds make-someone-do-it: he makes us laugh, no linking word needed.

target: El glosario del proyecto se lo mandé al revisor apenas quedó listo, para que usáramos los mismos términos.
english: I sent the project glossary over to the reviser as soon as it was ready, so we'd be using the same terms.
grammar: 'Se lo mandé' – 'le' changes to 'se' in front of 'lo': Spanish never says le lo.

target: El corte de pelo de Pierre le recuerda a su hermano a Margaret Thatcher.
english: Pierre's haircut reminds his brother of Margaret Thatcher.
grammar: The 'le' in 'le recuerda' points at who gets reminded – 'a su hermano' just spells the same person out.

target: De nuestros años en Lyon me quedó el gusto por el buen pan y las caminatas junto al río.
english: From our Lyon years I kept a taste for good bread and walks along the river.
grammar: 'Me quedó el gusto' – the taste is the subject and 'me' the keeper: what remains stays to you in Spanish.

target: El técnico dijo que la computadora todavía servía y que el problema era el cable de la impresora.
english: The technician said the computer was still perfectly good – the problem was the printer cable.
grammar: After 'dijo que' the tense steps back: 'todavía servía' – imperfect for what held true as he spoke.

target: El plomero dijo que había que cambiar el calentador entero, que ya no valía la pena repararlo.
english: The plumber said the whole water heater needed replacing – it wasn't worth repairing any more.
grammar: 'Dijo que había que cambiar' – reported speech backshifts 'hay que' (you have to) into 'había que'.

target: Henri dice que las abejas reconocen su voz. Nadie se atreve a contradecirlo.
english: Henri says the bees recognise his voice. Nobody dares contradict him.
grammar: 'Dice que' hands the claim on in the indicative – 'reconocen' stays plain even when nobody believes it.

target: ¿Me repite lo que dijo del horario? No entendí la última parte.
english: Could you repeat what you said about the timetable? I didn't catch the last part.
grammar: 'Lo que dijo' – what you said needs 'lo que' (the thing that): 'que' on its own can't stand in for a missing noun.

target: La señora del puesto me dijo que mañana estarían listos los aguacates.
english: The lady on the stall told me the avocados would be ready tomorrow.
grammar: After 'dijo', the future steps back – 'estarían listos' is would be ready, the future seen from the past.

target: Nos advirtió el abogado que guardáramos copia de todo lo que firmáramos.
english: The lawyer warned us to keep a copy of everything we signed.
grammar: 'Que guardáramos' – this passes on an order (keep copies!), not a fact, so the verb takes a special form.

target: Me llamó una amiga para contarme que se había ganado una canasta en la rifa del pueblo.
english: A friend rang to tell me she'd won a hamper in the village raffle.
grammar: 'Que se había ganado' – after 'contarme', her own words 'me gané' step one tense back into the pluperfect.

target: En la aduana nos preguntaron cuánto tiempo pensábamos quedarnos en Francia.
english: At customs they asked us how long we were planning to stay in France.
grammar: 'Preguntaron cuánto' – a reported question needs no 'que': the question word itself does the joining.

target: Antoine sostiene que Pokémon le enseñó más que la escuela, y cuesta llevarle la contraria.
english: Antoine maintains Pokémon taught him more than school, and it's hard to argue with him.
grammar: 'Sostiene que' reports a claim held as fact, so the indicative stays – 'enseñó', with no subjunctive doubt.

target: El chico del soporte técnico me preguntó si la pantalla parpadeaba o se ponía negra de repente.
english: The lad from technical support asked whether the screen was flickering or suddenly going black.
grammar: 'Me preguntó si la pantalla parpadeaba' – 'si' is whether, turning the question into reported speech.

target: La enfermera me preguntó si era alérgica a algún medicamento antes de ponerme la inyección.
english: The nurse asked whether I was allergic to any medication before giving me the injection.
grammar: 'Preguntó si era alérgica' – 'si' means whether, and 'are you allergic' shifts into the past: 'era'.

target: Me preguntaron si podía adelantar la reunión, pero ya tenía el día completo.
english: They asked me if I could bring the meeting forward, but my day was already full.
grammar: 'Me preguntaron si podía' – reporting a past question backshifts the verb: their '¿puedes?' becomes 'podía'.

target: Llamé a la clínica para confirmar la hora y me dijeron que la doctora ya no atendía los viernes.
english: I rang the clinic to confirm the time and they told me the doctor no longer does Fridays.
grammar: 'Ya no atendía' – reporting steps the tense back: the clinic's live 'ya no atiende' turns imperfect after 'dijeron'.

target: Todos juran que leyeron el libro, pero las miradas al piso dicen otra cosa.
english: Everyone swears they read the book, but the eyes on the floor say otherwise.
grammar: 'Juran que' takes the indicative 'leyeron' – verbs of swearing report claims as flat statements of fact.

target: ¿Le preguntaste al carpintero cuánto cobraría por hacer una repisa para ese rincón?
english: Did you ask the carpenter how much he'd charge to make a shelf for that corner?
grammar: 'Cuánto cobraría' – a reported question shifts future to conditional: how much will he charge becomes would-charge.

target: El electricista dijo que vendría el martes, pero todavía no aparece.
english: The electrician said he'd come on Tuesday, but he still hasn't turned up.
grammar: Reported promises turn conditional: 'dijo que vendría' – his I'll come on Tuesday becomes he would come.

target: Scout resolvió la crisis de los misiles con una sola mirada, según cuenta la familia.
english: Scout resolved the missile crisis with a single look, or so the family says.
grammar: 'Según cuenta la familia' credits the tale to its tellers – attribution with no promise that it is true.

target: Me agradecieron mil veces por acompañarlos a la estación, y les dije que no hay de qué, que me quedaba de camino.
english: They thanked me over and over for seeing them to the station, and I told them not to mention it, it was on my way.
grammar: 'Que no hay de qué, que me quedaba' – spoken Spanish restarts each reported remark with its own fresh 'que'.

target: Le pregunté al carnicero cómo se asaba ese corte y me lo anotó en un papelito.
english: I asked the butcher how to roast that cut and he jotted it down on a slip of paper for me.
grammar: 'Cómo se asaba' – after past 'pregunté', the reported question shifts back a tense: 'se asa' becomes 'se asaba'.

target: El de la tienda me preguntó qué modelo de computadora tenía y no supe qué contestar.
english: The man at the shop asked me what model of computer I had, and I hadn't a clue what to say.
grammar: 'No supe qué contestar' – a question word straight onto an infinitive: what to answer, no extra verb needed.

target: Me dijeron en la tienda que este esmalte aguanta bien la segunda cocción.
english: They told me at the shop that this glaze stands up well to a second firing.
grammar: After 'me dijeron' the reported verb stays present – 'aguanta' still holds true, so no shift to the past is needed.

target: Me han dicho que a esta hora el bus tarda el doble, así que más vale irnos caminando.
english: I've been told the bus takes twice as long at this time of day, so we're better off walking.
grammar: 'Me han dicho que' reports hearsay – an unnamed they have told me, the source left vague.

target: Ken pregunta si hay postre antes de mirar el resto del menú.
english: Ken asks whether there's pudding before looking at the rest of the menu.
grammar: A reported yes/no question hangs on 'si': 'pregunta si hay postre' – asks whether, and this 'si' has no accent.

target: ¿Sabe si el caldo se prepara con carne o solamente con verduras?
english: Do you know whether the broth is made with meat or just with vegetables?
grammar: 'Sabe si' folds one question inside another – this 'si' means whether, not the if of conditions.

target: Ken jura que este año los topos no le van a ganar la batalla del jardín.
english: Ken swears the moles are not winning the battle for the garden this year.
grammar: 'jura que' – verbs of asserting keep the indicative after 'que': the claim is served up as fact, mood unchanged.

target: Dicen que los bolivianos son sumamente amables.
english: I've heard Bolivians are extremely friendly.
grammar: 'Dicen que' means they say, no one in particular – Spanish passes on hearsay with an unnamed they.

target: Mi profesor de pintura decía que primero se mira y después se pinta.
english: My painting teacher used to say you look first and paint second.
grammar: 'Decía que' – the imperfect suits sayings repeated over the years, not one single remark.

target: Cuando algo sale mal, mi esposo solo dice 'not to worry'.
english: Whenever something goes wrong, my husband just says 'not to worry'.
grammar: 'Cuando' + present states a habit – 'algo sale mal' really happens; a future event would need 'salga'.

target: Una pregunta: ¿sabe si por aquí se llega a la catedral, o me devuelvo?
english: Quick question – do you know if this is the way to the cathedral, or should I turn back?
grammar: A question folded inside a question uses 'si' (whether): 'sabe si por aquí se llega' – plain indicative throughout.

target: Los chicos me dijeron que acercara el celular, que casi no me veían.
