english: The boys told me to hold the phone closer – they could hardly see me.
grammar: 'Dijeron que acercara' – where English says 'told me to hold', Spanish reports a request with the past subjunctive.

target: Pregunté en el mostrador si podíamos adelantar el vuelo, pero me dijeron que la tarifa no lo permite.
english: I asked at the desk if we could bring the flight forward, but they told me the fare doesn't allow it.
grammar: Reported questions step back a tense: 'si podíamos adelantar' – asked in the past, so can becomes could.

target: El guía nos aseguró que valía la pena, pero a mí me pareció una trampa para turistas.
english: The guide swore it was worth it, but it struck me as a tourist trap.
grammar: Reported speech steps back a tense: 'aseguró que valía la pena' – the guide's it's worth it became it was.

target: En la reunión de vecinos alguien preguntó por las obras, y el administrador respondió que empezarían el lunes siguiente.
english: At the residents' meeting someone asked about the building work, and the manager replied that it would start the following Monday.
grammar: 'Empezarían' – a reported future turns conditional: the manager's live 'empezarán' steps back after 'respondió'.

target: A PapyLou le encantó el globo: dice que desde arriba se veía todo el valle.
english: PapyLou loved the balloon: he says you could see the whole valley from up there.
grammar: Reported speech keeps its link word: 'dice que desde arriba se veía' – Spanish never drops the 'que'.

target: Antoine insiste en que esta vez la película japonesa sí nos va a gustar. Ya veremos.
english: Antoine insists that this time we really will like the Japanese film. We'll see.
grammar: 'insiste en que' – 'insistir' hangs on to its 'en' even before 'que', and the assertion stays indicative.

target: El recepcionista me preguntó de dónde era y cuánto tiempo pensaba quedarme.
english: The receptionist asked me where I was from and how long I was planning to stay.
grammar: 'Me preguntó de dónde era' – reporting a question backshifts it: the original are-you-from becomes past 'era'.

target: El guía dijo que el retablo era de mil seiscientos cuarenta, pero el letrero marca otra fecha.
english: The guide said the altarpiece was from sixteen forty, but the sign gives a different date.
grammar: 'Dijo que el retablo era' – inside reported speech the tense steps back to imperfect: the guide himself said 'es'.

target: Dicen que el agua fría es buena para la circulación.
english: They say cold water is good for your circulation.
grammar: 'Dicen' – they say, without saying who: the unnamed they is how Spanish passes on general wisdom.

target: El chofer nos avisó que la ruta de siempre estaba cerrada y que iba a tomar un desvío.
english: The driver let us know the usual route was closed and that he was going to take a detour.
grammar: 'Y que iba a tomar' – each reported remark restarts with its own 'que': Spanish repeats it where English drops it.

target: Cada Navidad, Pierre y Antoine insisten en que el pastel lo decoran ellos.
english: Every Christmas, Pierre and Antoine insist that they're the ones who decorate the cake.
grammar: 'insisten en que' – 'insistir' hangs on to its 'en' even before 'que', and the claim stays matter-of-fact.

target: ¿Me da la clave del wifi? Nunca sé si va con mayúsculas o todo junto.
english: Could I have the wifi password? I never know whether it's got capitals or is all one word.
grammar: 'Si va con mayúsculas' – this 'si' is whether, not if: it folds a yes-no question inside the sentence.

target: Dicen que a uno de nuestros antepasados se lo comieron los caníbales.
english: One of our ancestors was supposedly eaten by cannibals.
grammar: 'Se lo comieron' – 'a uno de nuestros antepasados' comes first, so 'lo' has to repeat him on the verb.

target: Mi esposo me asegura que no hay nada de qué preocuparse.
english: My husband assures me there is nothing to be concerned about.
grammar: 'Nada de qué preocuparse' – the 'de' of 'preocuparse de' moves up in front of 'qué', never to the end.

target: Según mi esposo, todo está absolutamente bajo control.
english: According to my husband, everything is absolutely under control.
grammar: 'Según mi esposo' hands the claim to its source – the word means 'according to' and never changes form.

target: Mi esposo insiste en que no hay ningún problema.
english: My husband insists there is no problem whatsoever.
grammar: 'Insiste en que' – 'insistir' keeps its 'en' even when a whole statement follows. Dropping the 'en' is the classic slip.

target: Si de verdad no hubiera nada de qué preocuparse, mi esposo no lo repetiría tanto.
english: If there really were nothing to worry about, my husband wouldn't repeat it so often.
grammar: 'Hubiera' pairs with 'repetiría' – 'si' + imperfect subjunctive sets the unreal condition, conditional the result.

target: 'Not to worry', dice mi esposo, por enésima vez.
english: 'Not to worry', says my husband, for the umpteenth time.
grammar: 'Dice mi esposo' – after a quotation the verb jumps ahead of the speaker; says-my-husband is the standard order.

target: El cajero no me devolvió la tarjeta. ¿Sabe usted a quién puedo acudir?
english: The cash machine didn't give my card back – do you know who I can turn to?
grammar: 'A quién puedo acudir' is a question tucked inside another – 'quién' keeps its accent all the same.

target: La dueña del establo me contó que con el barro del invierno casi nadie había salido a pasear en semanas.
english: The owner of the yard told me that with the winter mud hardly anyone had been out hacking for weeks.
grammar: After past 'me contó que', the report steps back a tense too: 'había salido' – had been out, not has.

target: El veterinario dice que el caballo necesita herraduras nuevas.
english: The vet says the horse needs new shoes.
grammar: 'Dice que' + indicative – reporting a plain statement keeps 'necesita' in the ordinary present.

target: Pregúntale al vendedor si este cargador le sirve también a la cámara, así no andamos con dos.
english: Ask the assistant whether this charger works for the camera too – that way we're not carrying two around.
grammar: 'Si este cargador le sirve' stays present – the asking happens now, so nothing pushes the tense back.

target: En la farmacia me dijeron que este jarabe ya no se vende sin receta.
english: At the chemist's they told me this syrup isn't sold without a prescription any more.
grammar: The report stays present tense when the fact still holds: 'ya no se vende' – true then, and still true now.

target: Cuando reservé, me aseguraron que el desayuno estaba incluido, y ahora me dicen otra cosa.
english: When I booked, they assured me breakfast was included, and now they're telling me otherwise.
grammar: 'Me aseguraron que' pushes their words into the past – the original 'está' backshifts to 'estaba incluido'.

target: Pregunté si el museo abría los lunes y me dijeron que dependía de la temporada.
english: I asked whether the museum opened on Mondays, and they told me it depended on the season.
grammar: 'Me dijeron que dependía' – reporting a past answer knocks the verb back one step: 'depende' becomes 'dependía'.

target: Esta mañana el panadero me contó que el pan integral se acaba antes de las diez.
english: This morning the baker told me the wholemeal bread runs out before ten.
grammar: 'Se acaba' stays present inside 'me contó que' – a fact still true today keeps its tense when reported.

target: Pregúntele al electricista si también puede revisar el timbre, que lleva meses sin sonar.
english: Ask the electrician if he can check the doorbell too – it hasn't rung for months.
grammar: 'Si también puede revisar' – a reported yes-no question hangs on 'si' (whether), no question mark needed inside.

target: El mate de coca ayuda con el soroche, o eso dicen.
english: Coca tea helps with altitude sickness, or so they say.
grammar: 'O eso dicen' – or so they say: the subjectless 'dicen' tags the whole claim as hearsay.

target: Nuestros amigos nos dijeron que lleváramos solo el traje de baño, que ellos ponían todo lo demás.
english: Our friends told us just to bring our swimming things – they'd sort out everything else.
grammar: 'Que lleváramos' – reporting an instruction, Spanish uses 'que' + past subjunctive where English uses 'to bring'.

target: Pierre sabe exactamente cuánto gastó en octubre de hace cuatro años. Le pregunté para comprobarlo.
english: Pierre knows exactly what he spent in October four years ago. I asked, to check.
grammar: Indirect questions keep the accent: 'cuánto gastó' – the mark stays even with no question marks around.

target: El pronóstico decía que iba a despejar, pero amaneció nublado otra vez.
english: The forecast said it was going to clear up, but it dawned cloudy yet again.
grammar: 'Decía que iba a despejar' – reporting shifts 'va a' back to 'iba a': it will clear became it would.

target: Dicen que el pueblo de al lado es más auténtico, pero eso mismo decían del anterior.
english: They say the next village along is more authentic – but that's exactly what they said about the last one.
grammar: 'Dicen' gives today's hearsay and 'decían' yesterday's – the unnamed they just changes tense.

target: Cada vez que se van, les pregunto si llevan comida para el camino.
english: Every time they leave, I ask if they're taking food for the journey.
grammar: 'Les pregunto si llevan' – asking whether uses plain 'si', and 'llevan' stays in its ordinary everyday form.

target: Dicen que París le copió el estilo a Swansea, y yo me lo creo.
english: They say Paris copied its style from Swansea, and I believe it.
grammar: 'Dicen que' – rumour needs no named source: an unnamed they does the reporting all by itself.

target: Mi vecina me contó que había visto un zorro en su jardín dos noches seguidas.
english: My neighbour told me she'd seen a fox in her garden two nights running.
grammar: 'Había visto' – 'me contó' pushes her original 'vi' one step back: a reported past turns into the pluperfect.

target: Un policía nos indicó que no se podía estacionar ahí y que mejor moviéramos el carro a la otra cuadra.
english: A police officer told us we couldn't park there and that we'd best move the car to the next block.
grammar: 'No se podía' reports a fact, 'moviéramos' an instruction – only the order gets pushed into the subjunctive.

target: Quedé de preguntar si el festejo era en la casa o en un salón de eventos, nadie estaba seguro.
english: I said I'd ask whether the do was at home or in a function room – nobody was sure.
grammar: Reporting a question needs 'si' – 'preguntar si el festejo era', with the verb shifted back into the past.

target: No sé cómo se cambia la contraseña del correo. Me lo explicaron una vez por teléfono y no me quedó nada.
english: I don't know how you change the email password. They explained it to me once over the phone and none of it stuck.
grammar: Question words keep their accent when reported: 'cómo se cambia' – a real asking, no question marks in sight.

target: Llamé para preguntar a qué hora cierran la puerta principal y me explicaron que hay portero toda la noche.
english: I rang to ask what time they lock the front door, and they explained there's a porter all night.
grammar: The accent survives reporting: 'preguntar a qué hora cierran' – 'qué' keeps its mark in the indirect question.

target: Yo sé dónde se puede encontrar una gran reserva de revistas en Angers.
english: I know where a large store of magazines can be found in Angers.
grammar: 'Dónde' keeps its accent in a reported question – knowing where still counts as asking, so the mark stays.

target: Las leyendas aztecas hablan de una yegua sagrada. Los expertos coinciden: se referían a Brannagh.
english: Aztec legends speak of a sacred mare. Experts agree: they meant Brannagh.
grammar: After a colon the report drops straight in, no 'que': 'los expertos coinciden: se referían a Brannagh'.

target: El coordinador me explicó que el documento saldría publicado en seis idiomas a la vez.
english: The coordinator explained that the document would be published in six languages at once.
grammar: 'Saldría' – in reported speech the original future shifts to the conditional, the future seen from the past.

target: Un señor que paseaba a su perro nos preguntó si no teníamos frío, y le dijimos que sí, pero que una se acostumbra.
english: A man walking his dog asked whether we weren't cold, and we said yes, but you get used to it.
grammar: 'Preguntó si' – reported yes/no questions hang on 'si', which works as whether rather than a condition.

target: En el curso me explicaron que el barniz se aplica meses después, cuando el óleo ya secó por dentro.
english: On the course they explained that the varnish goes on months later, once the oil paint has dried right through.
grammar: 'Me explicaron que' reports a general truth – timeless facts keep their present tense, so 'se aplica' stays as it is.

target: Ken dice que encontró otro carro antiguo en perfecto estado. Yo tengo mis dudas.
english: Ken says he's found another vintage car in perfect condition. I have my doubts.
grammar: 'dice que encontró' – after 'decir que' the report keeps its indicative, even when the listener has her doubts.

target: Le pregunté al policía de la esquina y me explicó que la calle estaba cerrada por una carrera.
english: I asked the policeman on the corner and he explained the street was closed for a race.
grammar: Reporting goes beyond 'dijo': 'me explicó que' works the same, with 'estaba' shifted back into the past.

target: Vengo diciendo desde enero que voy a ordenar los papeles, y ya estamos en abril.
english: I've been saying since January that I'm going to sort out the paperwork, and it's already April.
grammar: 'Vengo diciendo' – 'venir' + gerund tracks something you've kept doing right up to now, since January and counting.

target: ¿Hace cuánto que no revisa la fecha de vencimiento de su pasaporte? A mucha gente se le pasa.
english: How long has it been since you checked the expiry date on your passport? It slips a lot of people's minds.
grammar: 'Hace cuánto que no revisa' asks how long since the last check – the verb stays present right across the gap.

target: Aprender español lleva su tiempo.
english: Learning Spanish takes time.
grammar: Duration runs on 'llevar': 'lleva su tiempo' – tasks 'llevan' time, while people 'se toman' their time.

target: Dejé la traducción a tiempo completo hace años, y todavía extraño el ambiente de las conferencias.
english: I gave up full-time translating years ago, and I still miss the buzz of the conferences.
grammar: 'Hace años' after a past tense means 'years ago' – 'hace' plus a span of time counts back from today.

target: Desde el Brexit, hay más papeleo en la aduana.
english: Since Brexit, there's more paperwork at customs.
grammar: 'Desde el Brexit' – 'desde' + an event means since it happened; durations use 'desde hace'.

target: Llevamos años quedándonos en la misma casa de huéspedes cuando cruzamos en ferry, y ya nos tratan como de la familia.
english: We've been staying at the same guesthouse for years when we cross on the ferry, and by now they treat us like family.
grammar: 'Llevamos años quedándonos' – 'llevar' + time + gerund packs 'we have been staying for years' into the present.

target: Llevo un mes con el mismo retrato y el parecido por fin empieza a aparecer.
english: I've been on the same portrait for a month, and the likeness is finally starting to come through.
grammar: 'Llevo un mes con' – 'llevar' + a length of time says how long something has been going on, no perfect tense needed.

target: Lleva semanas de mal genio: desde que le cambiaron el turno no es la misma persona.
english: He's been in a foul temper for weeks – ever since they changed his shift he hasn't been the same person.
grammar: 'Lleva semanas de mal genio' – 'llevar' carries duration: literally he carries weeks of bad temper.

target: Si sigue lloviendo así, tendremos que cambiar los planes del fin de semana.
english: If it keeps raining like this, we'll have to change our weekend plans.
grammar: 'Sigue lloviendo' – 'seguir' + gerund means to keep on doing: rain carrying on, not starting up.

target: Hace media hora que estoy esperando el código de verificación y no llega nada.
english: I've been waiting half an hour for the verification code and nothing's come through.
grammar: 'Hace media hora que estoy esperando' – 'hace' + time + 'que' stays in the present: the wait still counts as now.

target: Ese foco del pasillo lleva semanas parpadeando. Hoy sí lo cambio.
english: That hall bulb has been flickering for weeks – today I'm changing it, no excuses.
grammar: 'Lleva semanas parpadeando' – 'llevar' + a time + gerund measures how long something has been going on.

target: En el súper están vendiendo adornos navideños desde noviembre, cada año empiezan más temprano.
english: The supermarket has been selling Christmas decorations since November – every year they start earlier.
grammar: 'Desde noviembre' pins the start date, and the present 'están vendiendo' shows it still going – no 'has been' needed.

target: Ken y yo llevamos años arreglando estas casas, y la lista de pendientes no se acaba nunca.
english: Ken and I have been doing up these houses for years, and the list of jobs never ends.
grammar: 'Llevar' + time + gerund measures how long so far: 'llevamos años arreglando' – present tense, years deep.

target: ¡Dios santo, acabo de ver una ballena! ¡Fue absolutamente increíble!
english: Good lord, I just saw a whale – it was absolutely incredible!
grammar: 'Acabo de ver' – I have just seen: 'acabar de' plus a verb is how Spanish says it happened a moment ago.

target: Llevo más de veinte años traduciendo y todavía aprendo palabras nuevas casi todas las semanas.
english: I've been translating for over twenty years and I still learn new words almost every week.
grammar: 'Veinte años traduciendo' – 'llevar' + a gerund measures time spent on an activity that's still going.

target: Lleva quince años trabajando de policía en este barrio, por eso saluda a todo el mundo por su nombre.
english: He's been working as a police officer in this neighbourhood for fifteen years – that's why he greets everyone by name.
grammar: 'Lleva quince años trabajando' – present tense in form, but it means he has been working for fifteen years.

target: Uso la misma sartén desde hace años y me funciona mejor que las nuevas, ya está curada.
english: I've used the same frying pan for years now and it does a better job than new ones – it's well seasoned by now.
grammar: 'Uso la misma sartén desde hace años' – still going on, so Spanish stays present where English says I have used.

target: Hace mucho que dejamos Lyon, pero cada vez que vuelvo reconozco las calles como si nunca nos hubiéramos ido.
english: It has been a long time since we left Lyon, but whenever I go back I know the streets as if we had never left.
grammar: 'Hace mucho que dejamos Lyon' – with a past tense after 'que', 'hace' counts the time since it happened.

target: Llevo años haciendo azulejos y todavía guardo el primero que pinté, con todo y sus defectos.
english: I've been making tiles for years and I still keep the first one I ever painted, flaws and all.
grammar: 'Llevo años haciendo' – 'llevar' plus a stretch of time and a gerund: still at it, so no past tense is needed.

target: El puesto de jugos de la esquina lleva cerrado desde febrero y nadie sabe si va a volver a abrir.
english: The juice stall on the corner has been shut since February, and nobody knows whether it'll open again.
grammar: 'Lleva cerrado' – 'llevar' + an adjective stretches a state over time, with 'desde febrero' dating its start.

target: Llevo tres inviernos nadando en el mar casi todas las mañanas, hasta el día que amaneció nevando.
english: I have been swimming in the sea almost every morning for three winters, even the day we woke up to snow.
grammar: 'Llevo' is simple present, yet it covers three winters – 'llevar' + gerund replaces English 'I have been swimming'.

target: Ese letrero lleva meses apagado, ya nadie lo prende de noche.
english: That sign's been off for months – nobody turns it on at night any more.
grammar: 'Lleva meses apagado' – 'llevar' + time works with an adjective too: it has been off for months now.

target: Hace años que no toco un cheque de viajero. Ahora todo se paga con el celular.
english: I haven't touched a traveller's cheque in years – these days you pay for everything with your phone.
grammar: 'Hace años que no toco' – 'hace' + a span + 'que' counts time since, with the verb kept present.

target: Hace años que nadamos todo el año, y aun así hay mañanas de febrero en que dudo hasta el último segundo.
english: We've been swimming all year round for years now, and even so there are February mornings when I hesitate right up to the last second.
grammar: 'Hace años que' + present covers a stretch still running: 'nadamos' does the work of we've-been-swimming.

target: Llevo dos días con dolor de cabeza y no se me quita con nada.
english: I've had a headache for two days and nothing will shift it.
grammar: 'Llevo dos días con dolor' – 'llevar' + a time + 'con' carries a state you've had, and still have, ever since.

target: ¿Cuánto hace que no revisan el ascensor? Hace un ruido rarísimo.
english: How long has it been since the lift was looked at? It makes the strangest noise.
grammar: 'Cuánto hace que no' + present asks how long since something last happened: 'revisan', not a past tense.

target: Aquí llevamos años celebrando los cumpleaños con un almuerzo largo en vez de fiesta, y funciona de maravilla.
english: Here we've been celebrating birthdays with a long lunch instead of a party for years now, and it works a treat.
grammar: 'Llevamos años celebrando' – three words that pack 'we have been celebrating for years' into the present.

target: La llave del baño gotea desde hace días. Voy a intentar arreglarla yo misma antes de llamar al plomero.
english: The bathroom tap has been dripping for days – I'm going to have a go at fixing it myself before calling the plumber.
grammar: 'Desde hace' + a duration keeps the verb present: 'gotea desde hace días' – started days ago, still dripping.

target: Llevo casi una hora en la sala de espera y todavía no me llaman.
english: I've been in the waiting room for nearly an hour and they still haven't called me in.
grammar: 'Llevo casi una hora' – 'llevar' + a stretch of time counts an ongoing wait, no have-been needed.

target: Llevamos semanas planeando esta reunión y por fin llegó el día.
english: We've been planning this get-together for weeks, and the day has finally arrived.
grammar: 'Llevamos semanas planeando' – 'llevar' + time + the '-ndo' verb is how Spanish says we have been planning for weeks.

target: Entiendo que estén ocupados, pero llevamos cuarenta minutos sin que nadie nos atienda.
english: I understand you're busy, but we've been here forty minutes without anyone serving us.
grammar: 'Llevamos cuarenta minutos' – 'llevar' + a time span measures the wait, with 'sin que' naming what hasn't happened.

target: Llevamos media hora dando vueltas y todavía no encontramos la entrada del mercado.
english: We've been going round in circles for half an hour and we still can't find the way into the market.
grammar: 'Llevamos media hora dando vueltas' – present tense in Spanish for we have been going round for half an hour.

target: Los frijoles los compro secos desde hace años, rinden mucho más que los enlatados.
english: I've been buying my beans dried for years – they go much further than tinned.
grammar: 'Los compro' stays present even with 'desde hace años' – Spanish keeps a still-live habit in the present.

target: Hacía años que no veía una tormenta tan fuerte como la de anoche.
english: I hadn't seen a storm as fierce as last night's in years.
grammar: 'Hacía años que no veía' – both verbs sit in the imperfect: it had been years since I'd seen one.

target: ¿Hace cuánto vives por acá? Se nota que conoces la zona como la palma de tu mano.
english: How long have you lived round here? You clearly know the area like the back of your hand.
grammar: '¿Hace cuánto vives por acá?' – the question sits in the present tense because the living carries on now.

target: Ken lleva semanas restaurando la cómoda del pasillo, y le está quedando preciosa.
english: Ken has been restoring the hallway chest of drawers for weeks, and it's coming up beautifully.
grammar: 'lleva semanas restaurando' – 'llevar' + time + gerund says has-been-doing, all in the present tense, no 'ha' needed.

target: La computadora lleva veinte minutos actualizándose y la barrita no avanza nada.
english: The computer's been updating for twenty minutes and the little bar hasn't moved at all.
grammar: 'Lleva veinte minutos actualizándose' – 'llevar' + time + gerund: been at it twenty minutes and counting.

target: Hace seis meses que el sobre del banco espera a Antoine en la mesa de entrada.
english: The envelope from the bank has been waiting for Antoine on the hall table for six months.
grammar: 'Hace seis meses que' + the plain present 'espera' – Spanish uses the present where English says has been waiting.

target: Soy del sur de Inglaterra, pero desde hace años pasamos temporadas largas en Bretaña.
english: I'm from the south of England, but for years now we've been spending long spells in Brittany.
grammar: 'Desde hace años' – a length of time needs 'desde hace'. Plain 'desde' alone marks a start point, like 'desde 2019'.

target: Llevamos un buen rato esperando el postre. ¿Habrá pasado algo en la cocina?
english: We've been waiting a good while for the pudding – has something happened in the kitchen, I wonder?
grammar: 'Llevamos un buen rato esperando' – 'llevar' + a stretch of time + gerund says how long you've been at it.

target: Hace veinte años que vamos a Latour de France y todavía somos 'los nuevos'.
english: We've been going to Latour de France for twenty years and we're still 'the new people'.
grammar: 'Hace veinte años que vamos' – present 'vamos', because the visits still run: hace + que counts up to now.

target: Hace mucho que no oigo hablar del bidé de Antoine.
english: It's been a long time since I heard anything about Antoine's bidet.
grammar: 'Hace mucho que no oigo' – present tense in Spanish, but it means it's been ages since I heard.

target: En Sussex ya no nieva tanto como antes.
english: It doesn't snow in Sussex as much as it used to back in the day.
grammar: 'Ya no nieva tanto como antes' – 'ya no' + 'como antes' does the work of used-to, no past tense needed.

target: Hace más de un mes que no hacemos una videollamada todos juntos, ya toca organizar otra.
english: It's been over a month since we last had a video call all together – time we organised another.
grammar: 'Hace más de un mes que no hacemos' – the present tense stays, because the not-calling still holds right now.

target: Llevamos tres horas en la terminal de buses y nada que sale nuestro bus.
english: We've been at the bus terminal for three hours and there's still no sign of our bus leaving.
grammar: 'Llevamos tres horas en la terminal' – 'llevar' plus a stretch of time means have been there, all in one verb.

target: Llevan veinte años 'a punto de apagar la consola'.
english: They've spent twenty years 'just about to turn off the console'.
grammar: 'Llevan veinte años' – 'llevar' + a stretch of time says how long it has been going on, no 'they have been' needed.

target: Estamos en plena estación de lluvias y aun así hace dos meses que no llueve de verdad.
english: We're right in the middle of the rainy season, and even so it's been two months since we had any proper rain.
grammar: 'Hace dos meses que no llueve' – 'hace... que' plus a present verb measures how long the not-happening has run.

target: Le sigo diciendo a Antoine que tiene que dibujar más, pero créanme: Antoine lo intenta.
english: I keep telling Antoine he has to draw more – but believe me, Antoine is trying.
grammar: 'Sigo diciendo' – 'seguir' + gerund means to keep on doing: the telling just keeps rolling.

target: Este viaje me está encantando. Hacía años que no me sentía tan libre.
english: I'm absolutely loving this trip – I hadn't felt this free in years.
grammar: 'Hacía años que no me sentía' – the past-tense twin of 'hace... que': it had been years since.

target: Llevaba años queriendo aprender español.
english: I'd been wanting to learn Spanish for years.
grammar: 'Llevaba años queriendo' – 'llevar' + time + gerund: I'd been wanting to for years.

target: ¿Lleva mucho tiempo vendiendo aquí? Todo se ve buenísimo.
english: Have you been selling here long? Everything looks wonderful.
grammar: 'Lleva mucho tiempo vendiendo' – 'llevar' + gerund asks how long something has been going on.

target: ¿Qué quiere decir 'ahorita'? Llevo semanas escuchándola y todavía no sé si es ahora o dentro de un rato.
english: What does 'ahorita' actually mean? I've been hearing it for weeks and I still don't know if it's now or in a while.
grammar: 'Llevo semanas escuchándola' – 'llevar' + time + gerund does the work of English have-been-doing, in the present.

target: Llevo toda la mañana dándole vueltas a una sola frase del informe.
english: I've spent the whole morning going back and forth over a single sentence in the report.
grammar: 'Llevo toda la mañana' – with 'llevar' the time comes first and the activity follows as a gerund: 'dándole vueltas'.

target: Llevan meses arreglando el puente peatonal, mientras tanto toca pasar por abajo entre los carros.
english: They've been repairing the footbridge for months – meanwhile you have to go under it, in among the cars.
grammar: 'Llevan meses arreglando' – 'llevan' is plural because the fixers are 'they', even though nobody says who.

target: Hace siglos que los rebaños pastan en estas colinas, y se nota en el paisaje.
english: Flocks have grazed these hills for centuries, and you can see it in the landscape.
grammar: 'Hace siglos que' + present 'pastan' could equally be 'pastan desde hace siglos' – same open span, two shapes.

target: Hace años que repartimos la vida entre los dos países y ya tenemos el sistema bien afinado.
english: We've been splitting our life between the two countries for years, and we've got the system down to a fine art.
grammar: 'Hace años que' + present 'repartimos' – time still running takes today's tense, where English reaches for have-been.

target: Páseme el hilo morado, el que está junto a las tijeras.
english: Pass me the purple thread – the one next to the scissors.
grammar: 'El que está junto a las tijeras' – 'el que' means the one that: article + 'que', with no noun repeated.

target: Nuestra familia venera a nuestro gran antepasado Louis Vagneur, que cayó en batalla.
english: Our family worships our great ancestor Louis Vagneur, who fell in battle.
grammar: 'Que cayó en batalla' – 'que' reaches people too: where English shifts to who, Spanish keeps 'que'.

target: El sendero que sube detrás de la caballeriza tiene la mejor vista de todo el valle.
english: The path that climbs up behind the stables has the best view in the whole valley.
grammar: In 'el sendero que sube', 'que' is the subject of its own clause – the path that climbs, nothing added.

target: Brannagh es la yegua de la que hablarán las generaciones futuras.
english: Brannagh is the mare future generations will speak of.
grammar: After a preposition, 'que' needs its article: 'de la que hablarán' – the mare of whom they'll speak.

target: Este verde no era el que quería, así que voy a mezclar otro.
english: This green wasn't the one I wanted – I'm going to mix another.
grammar: 'El que quería' – 'el que' means the one that: no need to repeat 'verde', the little 'el' stands in for it.

target: PapyLou canta desafinado, pero con un entusiasmo que contagia a toda la iglesia.
english: PapyLou sings out of tune, but with an enthusiasm that spreads through the whole church.
grammar: 'Que' hangs a whole clause off a noun: 'un entusiasmo que contagia' – enthusiasm that spreads.

target: HowTheLightGetsIn es un gran festival de ideas que se celebra en Londres.
english: HowTheLightGetsIn is a great festival of ideas held in London.
grammar: 'Que se celebra en Londres' – one little 'que' does the job of both 'which' and 'that', no second word needed.

target: Al llegar a Inglaterra, lo primero que buscamos fue un club de judo en Storrington.
english: When we got to England, the first thing we looked for was a judo club in Storrington.
grammar: 'Lo' + adjective + 'que' names a thing by its quality: 'lo primero que buscamos' – the first thing we sought.

target: De todas las cortinas, me quedo con las que vienen en rosado claro, esas alegran más el cuarto.
english: Out of all the curtains I'd go for the ones that come in pale pink – they brighten the room up more.
grammar: 'Las que vienen en rosado claro' – 'las que' means the ones that, feminine plural to match 'cortinas'.

target: PapyLou recoge toda la basura que encuentra en el suelo.
english: PapyLou picks up every bit of rubbish he finds on the floor.
grammar: Unlike English, 'que' can't be dropped: 'la basura que encuentra' – the rubbish (that) he finds.

target: ¿Hay alguna casa de cambio por aquí que abra los domingos?
english: Is there a bureau de change round here that opens on Sundays?
grammar: 'Que abra los domingos' describes a bureau you hope exists – unconfirmed, so 'abra', not 'abre'.

target: Magali vive en Lyon, que queda bastante lejos.
english: Magali lives in Lyon, which is quite far away.
grammar: For where a place sits, Spanish likes 'quedar': 'que queda bastante lejos' = which is quite far away.

target: Los mundos que inventaban en el trampolín tenían reglas que solo ellos dos entendían.
english: The worlds they made up on the trampoline had rules only the two of them understood.
grammar: 'Que inventaban' points at the worlds and 'que solo ellos dos entendían' at the rules – two 'que' links, one sentence.

target: El Brexit tuvo más consecuencias de las que la gente esperaba.
english: Brexit had more consequences than people expected.
grammar: 'Más consecuencias de las que' – 'las' is feminine plural because it points back at 'consecuencias'.

target: El Jaguar que compramos era precioso, pero desde el primer día me dio un poco de vergüenza.
english: The Jaguar we bought was beautiful, but from day one it embarrassed me a little.
grammar: 'que compramos' – that we bought: the relative needs no extra pronoun, the buyer lives in the verb ending.

target: Nos cruzamos con Dave y Lassie casi siempre en el mismo tramo del camino, la ruta que hacen todos los días.
english: We nearly always cross paths with Dave and Lassie on the same stretch of the path, the route they do every day.
grammar: 'la ruta que hacen' – English can skip that (the route they do), Spanish can't: 'que' always stays in place.

target: Un buen diccionario es como un colega que nunca se cansa.
english: A good dictionary is like a colleague who never gets tired.
grammar: 'Nunca se cansa' – 'nunca' before the verb needs no 'no': one negative word does the whole job.

target: ¿Cuál prefieres, el bolso marrón o el que trae la correa negra?
english: Which do you prefer – the brown bag or the one with the black strap?
grammar: 'El que trae la correa negra' – the one that has the black strap: 'traer' covers what an item comes fitted with.

target: El cargador que compré en el puesto de la esquina duró tres días. Lo barato sale caro.
english: The charger I bought from the corner stall lasted three days. Cheap ends up costing you dear.
grammar: 'El cargador que compré' – English may drop that (the charger I bought), the Spanish 'que' never goes.

target: Las palabras que más trabajo dan son las que todo el mundo cree entender.
english: The words that cause the most trouble are the ones everyone thinks they understand.
grammar: 'Las que' stands alone as the ones that – the article does the noun's work and 'que' does the linking.

target: El manzano de Marescot, que ya está en las últimas, todavía da unas cuantas manzanas cada otoño.
english: The apple tree at Marescot, which is on its last legs, still gives us a few apples every autumn.
grammar: Commas turn the clause into an aside: 'que ya está en las últimas' adds a detail without defining the tree.

target: Justo cuando nos estamos sentando a cenar, aparecen peregrinos jóvenes que nadie invitó.
english: Just as we're sitting down to dinner, young pilgrims nobody invited turn up.
grammar: 'Que nadie invitó' – English can say 'pilgrims nobody invited' and drop the link, Spanish always keeps 'que'.

target: El vuelo que sale al mediodía cuesta el doble. Tomemos el de la mañana aunque toque madrugar.
english: The midday flight costs twice as much – let's take the morning one even if it means getting up early.
grammar: 'El vuelo que sale al mediodía' – the 'que' clause pins down which flight, so no commas fence it off.

target: Los historiadores no mencionan a Scout, lo cual dice mucho sobre los historiadores.
english: Historians don't mention Scout – which says a lot about historians.
grammar: 'Lo cual' points back at the whole previous clause – the not-mentioning itself, not any one noun.

target: El pasaje de los murales es el que sale al río, no tiene pierde.
english: The alleyway with the murals is the one that comes out at the river – you can't miss it.
grammar: 'El que sale al río' – 'el que' is the one that: the article stands in for the alleyway itself.

target: Me encanta regalar los retratos y paisajes que pinto.
english: I love giving away the portraits and landscapes I paint.
grammar: 'Que pinto' – no yo needed inside the clause: the '-o' ending alone says who does the painting.

target: ¿Y qué es lo que más te ha gustado del viaje hasta ahora?
english: So what have you enjoyed most about the trip so far?
grammar: 'Lo que más te ha gustado' – 'lo que' means the thing that: 'lo' is the catch-all for ideas with no noun to lean on.

target: Cada vez que visitamos la Torre de Londres, pienso en las horas que pasé con esa audioguía.
english: Every time we visit the Tower of London, I think of the hours I spent on that audioguide.
grammar: Time nouns still take plain 'que': 'las horas que pasé' – the hours I spent, with no 'cuando' in sight.

target: En Newbury hay un cisne que se llama Swonky: lo atropelló un carro y le quedó el cuello torcido.
english: In Newbury there's a swan called Swonky: he was hit by a car and his neck ended up with a bend in it.
grammar: 'Que' covers who and which alike: 'un cisne que se llama Swonky' – one word does both jobs.

target: Ken es de esas personas que arreglan cualquier cosa: una gotera, un enchufe, una silla coja.
english: Ken is one of those people who can fix anything: a leak, a socket, a wobbly chair.
grammar: 'esas personas que arreglan' – the relative agrees with 'personas', so plural 'arreglan' even though it's about Ken.

target: Hay una peluquería en el centro donde te atienden sin cita, por eso siempre está llena.
english: There's a hair salon in the centre where they see you without an appointment – that's why it's always packed.
grammar: 'Donde te atienden' – for places 'donde' means where, tying the salon to what happens there: no 'que' needed.

target: Ese plato que le acaban de servir a la mesa de al lado, ¿qué es?
english: That dish they've just served to the next table – what is it?
grammar: 'Ese plato que le acaban de servir' – the 'que' clause singles out exactly which dish you mean.

target: A Béa el techno le da la energía que el café no le alcanza a dar.
english: Techno gives Béa the energy that coffee can't quite manage.
grammar: 'La energía que' – the relative 'que' is compulsory: English drops that, Spanish never does.
ttsText: A Bea el techno le da la energía que el café no le alcanza a dar.

target: Tengo todo tipo de temas de los que puedo conversar con mis hijos y mi esposo.
english: I have all kinds of topics I can chat about with my sons and my husband.
grammar: 'Temas de los que puedo conversar' – the 'de' goes up front, Spanish can't leave 'about' dangling at the end.

target: Siempre contesto los mensajes que llegan al grupo de la familia, aunque sea con un par de palabras.
english: I always answer the messages that come through on the family group chat, even if it's only a couple of words.
grammar: 'Que llegan' is plural – inside a relative clause the verb agrees with 'los mensajes', the noun it points back to.

target: El señor que arregla zapatos en la esquina también hace copias de llaves.
english: The man who mends shoes on the corner also cuts spare keys.
grammar: 'El señor que arregla zapatos' – a 'que' clause can work as a job title: Spanish often names people by what they do.

target: Las que venimos a nadar no siempre somos las mismas, pero hay un grupito fijo que nunca falla.
english: Those of us who come to swim aren't always the same ones, but there's a solid little core who never miss.
grammar: 'Las que venimos' keeps first-person agreement – those of us who come, so 'venimos', never 'vienen'.

target: Mis hijos parecen bastante contentos con la mamá que les tocó.
english: My sons seem pretty happy with the mum they ended up with.
grammar: 'La mamá que les tocó' – 'tocar' is the verb for what life deals you: the one they happened to get.

target: Quisiera algo para la tos que no dé sueño, porque mañana tengo que manejar temprano.
english: I'd like something for a cough that won't make me drowsy – I have to drive early tomorrow.
grammar: 'Que no dé sueño' – the remedy hasn't been found yet, so its relative clause takes subjunctive 'dé', not 'da'.

target: De todos los nombres que inventó Pierre, mi favorito siempre fue Sautepartout.
english: Of all the names Pierre invented, my favourite was always Sautepartout.
grammar: Inside a relative clause the subject may follow its verb: 'que inventó Pierre' – that Pierre invented.

target: La señora que atiende de noche en la recepción me consiguió otra cobija. Las noches acá son heladas.
english: The lady who works reception at night found me an extra blanket – the nights here are freezing.
grammar: People take plain 'que' too: 'la señora que atiende' – the same 'que' covers people and things alike.

target: ¿Este es el bus que va hacia la terminal o tengo que cruzar al otro lado?
english: Is this the bus that goes to the terminal, or do I need to cross to the other side?
grammar: 'El bus que va' – a relative clause about a real, specific bus keeps the indicative 'va', not 'vaya'.

target: Gilles Darmont tiene opiniones firmes sobre absolutamente todo, incluidos los temas que desconoce.
english: Gilles Darmont has firm opinions on absolutely everything, including subjects he knows nothing about.
grammar: 'Que desconoce' needs no he – inside a relative clause the verb ending alone names the subject.

target: Nos quedamos en un ryokan en las montañas de Nagano, donde todo era silencio y madera clara.
english: We stayed in a ryokan in the mountains of Nagano, where everything was silence and pale wood.
grammar: 'donde todo era silencio' – after a place, 'donde' does the relative work: no 'en el que' machinery needed.

target: El único horario que me queda libre es el viernes después de las cuatro.
english: The only slot I've got free is Friday after four.
grammar: 'Que me queda libre' – the relative 'que' is compulsory where English can drop that: the slot I've got free.

target: Quien trabaja con público tiene una paciencia que yo no tengo.
english: Anyone who works with the public has a patience I simply don't have.
grammar: 'Quien trabaja con público' – 'quien' by itself means anyone who, no noun needed in front of it.

target: La arcilla que compro ahora viene ya preparada, así que me ahorro todo un paso.
english: The clay I buy now comes ready to use, which saves me a whole stage of the job.
grammar: 'La arcilla que compro' – English can drop that (the clay I buy) but Spanish never skips the 'que'.

target: Los bomberos que llegaron primero evacuaron el edificio sin que nadie se lastimara.
english: The firefighters who arrived first evacuated the building without anyone getting hurt.
grammar: 'Los bomberos que llegaron primero' – the relative clause sits straight after its noun to say which firefighters.

target: Antoine vive en Park Slope, que la verdad es una zona encantadora.
english: Antoine lives in Park Slope, which really is a charming area.
grammar: 'La verdad' dropped into a sentence means honestly – a free-floating truth-be-told, no verb attached.

target: Si algo bueno tuvo la pandemia, fue todo el tiempo que pasamos en familia.
english: If the pandemic had one upside, it was all the time we spent as a family.
grammar: 'El tiempo que pasamos' – Spanish never drops the relative 'que', unlike English 'the time (that) we spent'.

target: Los amigos que nos hospedaron el fin de semana pasado nos despidieron con un desayuno enorme y fruta para el camino.
english: The friends who put us up last weekend saw us off with an enormous breakfast and fruit for the journey.
grammar: 'Los amigos que nos hospedaron' – plain 'que' covers 'who' for people too, no need to reach for 'quien'.

target: ¿No habría un cuarto que no dé a la avenida? Anoche no pegué el ojo.
english: Might there be a room that doesn't look onto the main road? I didn't sleep a wink last night.
grammar: 'Un cuarto que no dé' – the room is only wished for, so its relative clause goes subjunctive, not 'da'.

target: La caja donde guardamos los papeles del viaje va siempre en el asiento de adelante.
english: The box where we keep the travel papers always goes on the front seat.
grammar: 'La caja donde guardamos' – for places 'donde' means where, sparing you the heavier 'en la que'.

target: Tanta gente me agota. Busquemos un parque donde una pueda sentarse tranquila.
english: Crowds this size wear me out – let's find a park where you can sit in peace for a bit.
grammar: 'Un parque donde una pueda sentarse' – the park is still hypothetical, so its verb goes subjunctive.

target: Prefiero la camisa que tiene rayas grises, la de flores es muy llamativa para mí.
english: I prefer the shirt with the grey stripes – the flowery one's a bit loud for me.
grammar: 'La de flores' – the article plus 'de' stands in for the noun: the flowery one, with 'camisa' left unsaid.

target: La casa que buscamos es la que tiene el portón naranja, no tiene número.
english: The house we're looking for is the one with the orange gate – there's no number on it.
grammar: 'La que tiene el portón naranja' – where English says the one with, Spanish prefers a clause: the one that has.

target: En eso coincido contigo. Con lo que no estoy de acuerdo es con cambiar el plan a última hora.
english: There I agree with you – what I can't get behind is changing the plan at the last minute.
grammar: 'Con lo que no estoy de acuerdo' – 'lo que' points at a whole idea (changing the plan), not a named thing.

target: Otra vez se trabó el cajón donde guardo las cucharas y los tenedores.
english: The drawer where I keep the spoons and forks has stuck again.
grammar: 'El cajón donde guardo' – 'donde' does the job of where, much lighter than saying 'en el que'.

target: El día que Antoine recibió su Game Boy Advance fue, según él, el mejor de su vida.
english: The day Antoine got his Game Boy Advance was, according to him, the best of his life.
grammar: 'El día que' – for days and dates, plain 'que' does the work of 'when': no 'cuando' needed.

target: Es una región donde los pueblos todavía se organizan alrededor de la iglesia y el pub.
english: It's a region where villages are still organised around the church and the pub.
grammar: 'Una región donde' – 'donde' works just like English 'where', and saves you the clunkier 'en la que'.

target: Hay dos versiones de Antoine: la que conocemos y la que habría existido con GTA VI. Mejor no pensarlo.
english: There are two versions of Antoine: the one we know and the one that would have existed with GTA VI. Best not to think about it.
grammar: 'La que conocemos' – the article alone recalls 'versiones', so 'la que' means the one that we know.

target: ¿Dónde encuentro ese pan de maíz que me recomendó usted ayer?
english: Where can I find that corn bread you recommended to me yesterday?
grammar: 'Que me recomendó usted' – 'que' ties the bread to the recommending, and Spanish never drops it.

target: El ingeniero que revisó la obra terminó pidiendo que reforzaran las columnas.
english: The engineer who inspected the building work ended up asking for the columns to be reinforced.
grammar: 'El ingeniero que revisó la obra' – the 'que' clause singles him out, so it takes no commas around it.

target: La enfermera que me atendió en urgencias tuvo una paciencia infinita conmigo.
english: The nurse who looked after me in A&E had endless patience with me.
grammar: 'La enfermera que me atendió' – plain 'que' does the whole job of 'who', nothing extra is needed for people.

target: Las algas que Beni recoge en la playa terminan convertidas en cuadros que da gusto mirar.
english: The seaweed Beni gathers on the beach ends up as pictures that are a joy to look at.
grammar: 'que Beni recoge' – a relative clause can carry its own subject: 'Beni' slots in between 'que' and the verb.

target: Estoy muy orgullosa de la aplicación que creó Antoine.
english: I'm very proud of the app Antoine built.
grammar: 'Que creó Antoine' – Spanish happily puts the doer after the verb: it means that Antoine created, not the reverse.

target: ¿Conoces alguna aplicación que sirva para traducir menús? La que tengo confunde todo.
english: Do you know an app that's any good for translating menus? The one I've got muddles everything up.
grammar: 'Que sirva' is subjunctive – that app is only hoped-for. The one in hand, 'la que tengo', stays indicative.

target: La playa donde nos juntamos tiene una rampa que baja suave, ideal para entrar sin resbalarse.
english: The beach where we meet has a ramp with a gentle slope, ideal for getting in without slipping.
grammar: 'La playa donde nos juntamos' – for places 'donde' does the relative work that 'que' + preposition would need.

target: Según mi instructora, voy avanzando bien. Sin embargo, el trote levantado todavía me cuesta.
english: According to my instructor I'm coming along nicely. Rising trot still gives me trouble, though.
grammar: 'Sin embargo' means however – it accepts the first sentence, then weighs in against it.

target: Igual el internet aquí va y viene, así que no te preocupes si no contesto de inmediato.
english: The internet here comes and goes anyway, so don't worry if I don't reply straight away.
grammar: 'Igual' up front means anyway, not equal – Latin American speech uses it for either-way, come what may.

target: O sea, ¿la tarifa era por persona y no por habitación? Con razón no me cuadraban las cuentas.
english: Hang on – so the rate was per person, not per room? No wonder my sums weren't adding up.
grammar: 'O sea' is the everyday in-other-words – it opens the rephrase while the penny drops.

target: Los caracoles de la cargolade de Papy Bey no eran precisamente una maravilla, la verdad.
english: The snails at Papy Bey's cargolade weren't exactly wonderful, truth be told.
grammar: Tacked on at the end, 'la verdad' means truth be told – a spoken-Spanish softener for a verdict.

target: Montar a caballo fortalece la espalda, aunque a veces también la castiga.
english: Riding strengthens your back, though sometimes it punishes it too.
grammar: 'Aunque a veces también la castiga' – it really does happen, so after 'aunque' the verb keeps its ordinary form.

target: Nos encanta recibir visitas. Ahora bien, a veces los invitados se quedan más de la cuenta.
english: We love having people to stay. That said, sometimes guests stay a bit too long.
grammar: 'Ahora bien' is a pivot connector – it accepts the first statement, then introduces the catch, like 'that said'.

target: Mire, no quiero exagerar, pero la comida llegó fría otra vez y así no se puede.
english: Look, I don't want to make a fuss, but the food arrived cold again and that's just not on.
grammar: 'Mire' softens the complaint before it lands – a command in form, a discourse opener in function.

target: Si el trámite demora más de una hora, lo dejamos para mañana y ya.
english: If the paperwork takes more than an hour, we'll just leave it for tomorrow and that's that.
grammar: 'Y ya' closes the matter – a tiny discourse tag meaning that's that, end of discussion.

target: En realidad, la receta original lleva más pimienta, pero yo le bajo un poco porque queda muy fuerte.
english: Actually the original recipe calls for more pepper, but I ease off a little because it comes out too strong.
grammar: 'En realidad' fronts a correction – it flags that the truth is otherwise, the Spanish counterpart of actually.

target: Al agua entramos todas juntas. A la salida, en cambio, cada una tiene su ritmo.
english: We all go into the water together. Coming out, though, everyone has her own pace.
grammar: 'En cambio' pivots between the two halves – on the other hand, a contrast marker gentler than 'pero'.

target: Total, si perdemos la conexión, la aerolínea tiene que reubicarnos. Al menos eso dice el reglamento.
english: Anyway, if we miss the connection the airline has to put us on another flight – at least that's what the rules say.
grammar: Opening with 'total' is spoken Spanish for anyway, at the end of the day – it waves the whole worry off.

target: Las opiniones de Scout sobre el Brexit no eran precisamente matizadas.
english: Scout's views on Brexit were not exactly nuanced.
grammar: Understatement runs on 'precisamente': 'no eran precisamente matizadas' = not exactly nuanced.

target: En teoría el viaje toma un día entero, pero en la práctica nunca sale exactamente como lo planeamos.
english: In theory the journey takes a whole day, but in practice it never goes quite the way we plan it.
grammar: 'En teoría' sets up the claim and 'en la práctica' undercuts it – a paired frame for expectation versus reality.

target: Antipático no es, al contrario: lo que pasa es que es de pocas palabras.
english: He's not unfriendly, quite the opposite – it's just that he's a man of few words.
grammar: 'Lo que pasa es que' – the stock cushion before an explanation: literally what-happens-is-that, it's just that.

target: El taxista no estuvo muy amable que digamos, pero tampoco era para amargarse el día.
english: The taxi driver wasn't what you'd call friendly, but it was hardly worth letting it spoil the day.
grammar: 'Que digamos' tacks onto a negative to understate it – 'no estuvo muy amable que digamos' is not exactly friendly.

target: Por cierto, allá las estaciones van al revés: cuando aquí es invierno, ellos están en pleno verano.
english: By the way, the seasons are the other way round there – when it's winter here, they're in high summer.
grammar: 'Por cierto' is a topic-changer meaning by the way – nothing to do with certainty, despite its look.

target: Entiendo su punto, pero siento que estamos generalizando demasiado.
english: I see your point, but I feel we're generalising rather a lot.
grammar: Concede first, then push back: 'entiendo su punto, pero' – the polite Spanish frame for disagreeing.

target: Perdimos el tren de las nueve y el siguiente venía lleno, total que llegamos al almuerzo con una hora de retraso.
english: We missed the nine o'clock train and the next one was packed, so the upshot was we arrived at lunch an hour late.
grammar: 'Total que' is a spoken wrap-up connector – it closes a chain of mishaps and delivers the end result in one go.

target: Por lo visto, el nuevo maestro es exigente, pero los alumnos lo respetan un montón.
english: Apparently the new teacher is strict, but the pupils really respect him.
grammar: 'Por lo visto' hedges the whole claim – you're passing on what's said about the teacher, not vouching for it.

target: Al final, la vuelta larga valió la pena: pasamos por unas callecitas de casas pintadas que no conocíamos.
english: In the end the long way round was worth it – we went along some little streets of painted houses we didn't know.
grammar: 'Al final' delivers the verdict – in the end, how it turned out – rather than the end of any street.

target: Tenemos muchos amigos tanto en Pulborough como en Josselin.
english: We have lots of friends in both Pulborough and Josselin.
grammar: The pair 'tanto' … 'como' means both … and: 'tanto en Pulborough como en Josselin'.

target: O sea, ¿el trámite se hace en línea y no aquí en la oficina? Quiero estar segura de haber entendido.
english: So the paperwork gets done online, not here at the office? I want to be sure I've understood.
grammar: 'O sea' opens a double-check – you say back what you think you heard: so, in other words.

target: Mira que cuesta convencerla, ¿eh? Pero al final siempre termina cediendo.
english: She really takes some persuading, doesn't she? But she always comes round in the end.
grammar: 'Mira que cuesta convencerla' – 'mira que' opens spoken emphasis (it really does), no actual looking involved.

target: Mis sobrinos tienen los trabajos más variados, la verdad es que es impresionante.
english: My nieces and nephews do a huge variety of jobs – it really is quite something.
grammar: 'Sobrinos' covers nieces and nephews in one word – a masculine plural sweeps in both genders by default.

target: Según mis hijos, los videojuegos 'desarrollan la coordinación'. Ajá.
english: According to my sons, video games 'develop coordination'. Right.
grammar: 'Según mis hijos' hands the claim to them – you report their view without signing up to it yourself.

target: Según Gilles Darmont, los satélites controlan el clima. Según nosotros, Gilles necesita pasatiempos.
english: According to Gilles Darmont, satellites control the weather. According to us, Gilles needs a hobby.
grammar: 'Según' takes subject pronouns – 'según nosotros', and it would be 'según tú', never 'según ti'.

target: Está bien tener un hijo bautizado católico y el otro anglicano: así cubrimos todas las posibilidades.
english: It's good to have one child baptised Catholic and the other Anglican – that way we cover our bases.
grammar: 'Así cubrimos' – 'así' means that way, one small word wrapping up the plan just described.

target: No cabe duda de que Twig tiene muchísima energía.
english: There's no doubt Twig has masses of energy.
grammar: 'No cabe duda de que' – literally doubt doesn't fit – is the set way to say there's no doubt that.

target: Al final no era para tanto: la comida alcanzó y nadie se quiso ir temprano.
english: In the end there was nothing to worry about: the food went round and nobody wanted to leave early.
grammar: 'No era para tanto' is the fixed way to say something wasn't worth the worry – 'tanto' stands alone, no noun.

target: Las bodas chilenas son impresionantes, aunque no siempre las mejor organizadas.
english: Chilean weddings are impressive, but not always the best-run affairs.
grammar: 'Las mejor organizadas' drops 'bodas' – in a superlative, the article alone can stand in for the noun.

target: Manejar por las montañas de Georgia no es precisamente relajante: el motor casi explota en una subida.
english: Driving through the mountains in Georgia is not exactly relaxing: the engine nearly blew on one climb.
grammar: 'no es precisamente relajante' – understatement by 'precisamente': deny the mild word instead of stating the harsh one.

target: No termino de entender la Francia de Macron.
english: I can't quite make sense of Macron's France.
grammar: 'No termino de entender' – negative 'terminar de' means can't-quite: the understanding never fully arrives.

target: De todos modos me llevo la papaya. Ya veré qué hago con tanta fruta.
english: I'll take the papaya anyway – I'll work out what to do with all that fruit later.
grammar: 'De todos modos' is the anyway connector – it concedes the point, then carries on regardless.

target: Lo difícil no es el frío, sino decidirse a entrar.
english: The hard part isn't the cold – it's making yourself get in.
grammar: 'Sino' – after the negative 'no es el frío', but-rather must be 'sino': plain 'pero' can't correct like that.

target: El dibujo lo tengo decidido desde el principio. Los colores, en cambio, los voy eligiendo sobre la marcha.
english: The design is settled before I start. The colours, on the other hand, I choose as I go.
grammar: 'En cambio' draws the contrast between the two halves – on the other hand, tucked in after 'los colores'.

target: Estaba riquísimo, de verdad. Lo que pasa es que ya no puedo más.
english: It was absolutely delicious, honestly – it's just that I can't manage another bite.
grammar: 'Lo que pasa es que' cushions the excuse – the set thing-is opener before the real reason.

target: En resumen: el hotel bien, la comida regular y los paisajes, de otro mundo.
english: In short: the hotel was fine, the food nothing special, and the scenery out of this world.
grammar: 'Regular' as a verdict means so-so or nothing special – the polite middle notch, not English regular.

target: Según ellos no hacía falta llevar nada, sin embargo llegamos con vino y flores, como debe ser.
english: According to them we didn't need to bring anything, but we turned up with wine and flowers all the same, as you should.
grammar: 'Según ellos' pins a claim to its source, their view only – which lets 'sin embargo' overturn it straight after.

target: Para serte sincera, el cambio de planes me cayó fatal, pero ya se me pasó.
english: To be honest with you, the change of plan didn't sit well with me at all – but I'm over it now.
grammar: 'Para serte sincera' – a set opener: 'para' plus infinitive states purpose, with 'te' glued straight onto 'ser'.

target: Explicar el trabajo de Antoine: del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho.
english: Explaining Antoine's job is easier said than done.
grammar: 'Del dicho al hecho hay mucho trecho' – the proverb: from the saying to the deed there's a long stretch.

target: Según el encargo, era un texto sencillo. Sin embargo, la terminología me tomó tres días completos.
english: According to the brief it was a simple text. Even so, the terminology took me three full days.
grammar: 'Sin embargo' pivots to a contrast – a neutral however that opens its sentence and takes a comma after it.

target: Incluso desde Francia, llegar a Reunión lleva casi un día entero, y eso que es Francia.
english: Even from France, getting to Réunion takes nearly a full day – and that's despite it being France.
grammar: 'Y eso que' tacks a spoken concession onto the end – and that's despite, strengthening the point just made.

target: Queremos mucho a los animales del jardín. Sin embargo, con las hembras de zorro y sus regalitos cuesta un poco.
english: We love the garden's animals dearly. With the vixens and their little presents, though, it takes some effort.
grammar: 'Sin embargo' – the formal however: it sets the whole sentence against the previous one, heavier than 'pero'.

target: La verdad, no es nada grave. Es más que nada para quedarme tranquila.
english: Honestly, it's nothing serious – it's mainly just to put my mind at rest.
grammar: 'Más que nada' – literally more than anything – is the spoken way to say mainly or above all.

target: Bueno, visto así, reconozco que mi plan tiene sus fallas.
english: Well, put like that, I'll admit my plan has its flaws.
grammar: 'Visto así' – literally seen that way – is the two-word version of if you put it like that.

target: Yo no digo que no al carro antiguo, pero convencida, lo que se dice convencida, no estoy.
english: I am not saying no to the vintage car, but convinced – really convinced – I am not.
grammar: 'lo que se dice convencida' – the set phrase 'lo que se dice' weighs the word it repeats: convinced in the full sense.

target: La habitación es sencilla, eso sí, pero la cama es comodísima y el agua sale bien caliente.
english: The room is simple, mind you, but the bed is wonderfully comfortable and the water runs properly hot.
grammar: 'Eso sí' is the mind-you tag – it grants the downside before 'pero' swings back to the room's strong points.

target: ¿Exageramos con Brannagh? Según los aztecas, los chinos y los saudíes, no.
english: Are we overdoing it with Brannagh? According to the Aztecs, the Chinese and the Saudis: no.
grammar: 'Según' hands the verdict to its source: 'según los aztecas' – according to, with no verb needed after it.
